overview: Physics Sim is a browser-based MuJoCo rigid-body physics simulator. Scenes are defined as a tree of SceneNode bodies, each with primitive geoms and joints. The simulator compiles scenes to MJCF XML and runs MuJoCo WASM in the browser. Coordinate system: X=right, Y=forward/depth, Z=up. Ground plane at Z=0.
workflow: 1. Call physics_get_schema to understand available geom/joint types and fields.
2. Use physics_build_scene (easy, auto-fills defaults) or physics_update_scene (full control).
3. For an organic or particular shape (a face, an animal, a worn tool) use physics_create_sculpt and physics_sculpt rather than primitives or OpenSCAD. See schema.sculpting.
4. For a crisp dimensioned part (a bracket, a housing, a mount) use physics_create_lattice and physics_lattice_extrude: exact coordinates on a grid. See schema.lattice.

5. Use physics_run_headless to simulate N ticks and verify behaviour programmatically: check final positions, velocities, or trajectory shape against expected values. Do this before relying on visual inspection.
6. Call physics_play to show the simulation to the user once you have confirmed it behaves correctly via headless run.

7. Call physics_set_note_cards to put a card on the scene describing what was built: its title, its dimensions, and the physics it demonstrates. A scene without one is not finished; see that tool's description for the shape of a good card.
8. Use physics_set_environment to adjust gravity, wind, floor friction, and fluid density.
9. When the user wants to print what was built, physics_export_print with out_dir writes an STL or 3MF and returns its path: give them the path (see gotchas, HANDING OVER A PRINTABLE FILE).

core: DO NOT add a body with a plane geom as a floor. MuJoCo provides a built-in ground plane at Z=0 automatically. Adding a plane body causes a silent compile error: the scene loads but physics_play returns ok:true while isPlaying stays false. Omit the floor body entirely.

After calling physics_play, immediately call physics_get_state and check that isPlaying is true. If it is still false, the scene failed to compile (likely a bad geom, duplicate name, or plane body conflict). Fix the scene and try again.

Ensure geom size arrays match the required element count for each primitive: 'capsule' requires 2 elements [radius, half_length] (or use fromto), 'cylinder' requires 2 elements [radius, half_height], 'box' requires 3 elements [hx, hy, hz], and 'sphere' requires 1 element [radius]. A 1-element capsule with no fromto does NOT error and does NOT disappear: the MJCF writer falls back to half_length = radius, so the intended rod/spoke/arm silently becomes a tiny stub pill at the geom's pos. Since such geoms usually also default to pos:[0,0,0], several of them (e.g. the five arms of a star) stack into ONE small blob at the body origin. A single unexplained capsule at the centre of a body is almost always this, not a renderer or simulator fault. Inspect the geoms with physics_get_object and look for 1-element capsule sizes.
When constructing or updating hinge joints, always explicitly specify the rotation axis (e.g. axis:[0,1,0]). Omitting axis causes MuJoCo to default to [0,0,1], breaking planar hinge motion.

When mutating or generating scene nodes, preserve existing capsule span attributes (fromto or 2-element size), collision flags (contype:0/conaffinity:0), and joint axes so rods and pivots do not disappear or jam after scene updates.

Do not use rgba alpha to hide a helper/bounds geom. Alpha below 1 draws a geom translucent, and 0 makes it invisible, but either way it still collides and still has mass: an invisible bounds box is a wall nothing can pass through. If a geom should not be there, delete it. Collision geometry you should not see (a proxy) takes `role: 'collision'`: it collides and has mass but is never drawn. A geom you should see but nothing should hit takes `role: 'visual'` (contype 0/conaffinity 0 does the same, and also leaves its mass in).

THE VIEWPORT IS NOT A VALIDATOR. A scene that looks right can still be unusable: open edges, inverted winding, zero-area triangles and shells that merely touch instead of overlapping are all invisible on screen and all break an export. physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt report `watertight` on every reply for exactly this reason — read it. A raw mesh geom you built yourself has no such guard, so check it before you rely on it, and prefer physics_create_lattice or physics_create_sculpt when the thing is going to be made rather than only looked at.

A screenshot is evidence about APPEARANCE and nothing else. It cannot show you that a mesh is closed, that a wall is the thickness you asked for, that two parts are joined rather than overlapping, or that a dimension is what you intended. Use physics_measure for distances, the `watertight` flag for solidity, and the export tools' own warnings for whether a part can actually be made.

A COMMAND THAT TIMED OUT MAY STILL HAVE RUN. The app is handed the command before the MCP server starts waiting, and it keeps working on it when the wait gives up: a slow physics_build_scene, physics_update_object or physics_add_object can land seconds after the 'Timeout waiting for ...' error. So a timeout does not mean nothing happened, and retrying blindly builds the scene twice (or adds the body twice). Before retrying, check the state: physics_get_scene_summary (or physics_get_objects) shows whether the bodies are there and whether the model built; retry only what did not land.
collision: HOLLOW SHAPES NOW COLLIDE AS HOLLOW SHAPES, so do not build proxy walls. MuJoCo itself collides a mesh as its CONVEX HULL, which fills in any cavity — a cup, bowl, open-top box, funnel or housing would be solid and a ball dropped in would rest on an invisible lid at the rim. The app now measures each body's SOLIDITY (true volume over hull volume) and breaks anything below ~0.92 into convex pieces automatically, for every kind of mesh body: imported STL, sculpt, lattice, relief, SCAD, boolean. Model the container as a container. physics_get_scene_summary reports `collidesAs` and `solidity` per body, and `cavityFilled` when a hollow body is still colliding as its hull. Override with `collision`: 'hull' forces the old filled-in behaviour, 'decompose' forces the split. A NARROW SLOT CAN STILL BE BRIDGED by one piece while the body looks healthy ("9 convex pieces"): the app cuts each mesh into chunks before decomposing it — again and again while a chunk is long and thin for its wall or its pieces still fill a cavity — so a coiled chute, a gutter or a track gets pieces along its whole length, and a SEALED hollow (a closed drum, a rattle, a ball in a cage) is opened by the cut and stays hollow, so bodies started inside it stay inside. Every piece is then pulled in to the real surface, so floors are smooth enough to roll on and walls are flat. Any filled cavity left is reported as `cavitiesFilled` (centre, extent and volume in mm, and the collider covering it) in physics_get_scene_summary. THIN WALLS LANDING ON THIN WALLS (nesting bowls, cups dropped into cups, shells stacked): the default contact (solref [0.02, 1]) is soft enough that a part landing at ~1 m/s sinks ~20 mm into what it hits and passes through a 4 mm wall; set `solref: [0.005, 1]` on those mesh geoms (their convex pieces inherit it). Free-jointed bodies are capped at 64 pieces by default for speed, so their pieces can stand 1-2 mm proud on a large curved part; raising `collisionHulls` costs simulation speed roughly in proportion. TIGHT FITS: a concavity with flat walls (a square pocket, a slot, an open-top box) is cut exactly along its inside corners and is not narrowed at all; pieces still stand a little proud on curved bores and in curved inside corners; the summary reports `openingsNarrowedMm` (and `openingsNarrowed`, a sentence saying where) — a peg, ball or slider fitted with less clearance than that will jam. `surfaceUncoveredMm` (and `surfaceUncovered`) is the opposite fault: surface no piece covers, which contact sinks into by that much (a part sinking into the floor, a ball dropping into a solid); a millimetre or two on a curved wall is V-HACD's voxels, more is worth reporting. Each mesh geom of a body is decomposed on its own, at its own pos and euler, and a mesh with contype 0 and conaffinity 0 is left as it is. If a filled cavity remains or a fit jams, raise `collisionResolution` (V-HACD voxels per chunk, default up to 25000; Fine is 50000, Finest 100000) on the body rather than adding hidden proxy boxes; `collisionHulls` caps the total piece count (default up to 512) and setting it low makes things worse. Decomposing takes a few seconds per body, up to ~20 s for a long coiled part: physics_get_scene_summary reports `collisionPending` until it lands, and physics_run_headless waits for it. (Proxy collision geometry is for the few cases this cannot handle — a rounded mesh resting flat, or a SCAD part's own `$physbox_collision` proxies — and is a geom with `role: 'collision'`, never one hidden with alpha.) ONE CONSEQUENCE: a decomposed hollow body is weighed by its true volume rather than its hull's — often a third as much — so set `mass` or `collisionMass` if you wanted the heavier figure.

Bodies that should NOT collide with each other (e.g. windmill blades, rotor hub, nacelle) MUST have contype:0 AND conaffinity:0 on ALL their geoms. Without this, sibling bodies that overlap near a shared parent origin generate huge contact-constraint forces that oscillate and prevent scripted torques from accumulating. Even a few millimetres of geom overlap near the hub causes ±1 rad/s oscillation that prevents spin-up.

Visual geoms and bodies (such as capsule rods, hub rings, bearings, and axle pins) mounted near shared joint pivot origins MUST have contype:0 AND conaffinity:0 set on their geoms. Without contype:0/conaffinity:0, overlapping geoms near the pivot origin generate strong contact interpenetration forces that lock the joint and cause high-frequency wobbling in place instead of smooth swinging. This includes geoms on a STATIC parent, not only sibling bodies: MuJoCo skips contacts between a body and its parent only when the parent itself moves. A parent welded to the world (no joint on it or above it) gets no such filtering, so a shaft or bracket on a fixed frame collides with the hinged child it passes through.

Lowering friction on one geom does nothing if the other is at the default. MuJoCo takes the LARGER of the two geoms' friction, not the average (geom priority is not supported here), so make BOTH sides slippery, including the floor via physics_set_environment floorFriction. See schema.contactPhysicsTips.howFrictionIsCombined.

A CURVED OR ROUNDED MESH RESTING FLAT ON A BOX OR ANOTHER MESH CAN START MOVING BY ITSELF. MuJoCo 3.8's convex collision gives a mesh-on-box or mesh-on-mesh pair ONE contact point, so a flat-bottomed rounded part (a phone, a tile, a puck) is balanced on a point: measured on a 75 x 150 x 8.5 mm rounded slab lying on a box, it sat still for 2.5 s and then slid and spun at about 6 mm/s and 7 deg/s. The same slab on the floor plane stays put, and as a box primitive on the box it gets four contacts and stays put. A leaning mesh also creeps (0.17 mm/s down a wall). The fix is a box collision proxy on the resting body — a box geom sized to the flat face with `role: 'collision'` (collides, never drawn; give it the part's mass or density, since the visual mesh then weighs nothing), and `role: 'visual'` on the mesh so only the box collides — not solver settings: an elliptic cone stops the leaning creep but makes the flat case worse, and disabling native CCD fixes the flat case but quadruples the creep. physics_run_headless's `final` (settled/rocking) tells you whether a resting pose really is at rest.
scripting: Script functions require the 'api.' prefix. Writing getTime() instead of api.getTime() throws ReferenceError and silently breaks the script. All api calls must be api.functionName(...).

To give a body an initial velocity, use a script with a first-tick guard: if (api.getTime() === 0) { api.setVelocity([...], 'bodyName'); }. Using === 0 fires exactly on the first tick. Or give the joint an initialVelocity (schema.jointFields.initialVelocity). To start a hinge or slide away from 0: if (api.getTime() === 0) api.setPosition([theta], 'bodyName').

A SCRIPT THAT FAILS DOES NOT STOP THE SIMULATION, so look for it: physics_update_object / add_object / build_scene replies carry scriptWarnings for a script that does not compile; physics_get_state.worker.scriptProblems lists runtime errors and unknown body, joint and actuator names live, with the sim time each started and how many steps it failed on; physics_run_headless returns them as warnings. api.log output is in physics_run_headless `logs` and physics_get_telemetry `scriptLogs`; api.state is in telemetry `scriptState`. If live play is slow, physics_get_state.worker.realtimeFactor and scriptMsPerStep say whether the scripts are why.

The script field on a SceneNode is a single string: 'script': '...'. It is NOT an array. Passing scripts:[{code:'...'}] or scripts:['...'] will silently be ignored and the script will never run. Always use the singular 'script' key with a flat string value.

api.getOrientation() returns the 9-element row-major rotation matrix of the body the script is attached to (xmat). Column 0 = [R[0], R[3], R[6]] is the body's local X-axis in world space. For a rotor with hinge axis=[1,0,0], project wind onto this axis to get the effective wind speed: Vw = windX*R[0] + windY*R[3].
joints_and_gears: A TORQUE-LIMITED VELOCITY ACTUATOR IS A SLIP CLUTCH. Give a velocity actuator a forceLimit and the app drives its joint from a hidden driver through dry friction equal to the limit: below the limit the joint holds its set speed (drooping by load/kv, as before); above it the clutch slips at exactly the limit torque, which is a stalled motor. It is stable at any inertia, so NO armature is added any more (it used to be 1.5*kv*0.001, which on a NEMA17 was 240 times its rotor and capped its acceleration at a few hundred rad/s^2): a joint accelerates at forceLimit / its real inertia. A coupled chain stopped by an end stop stalls the motor at its limit rather than slipping the coupling. A velocity actuator's ctrlValue is the target speed (rad/s hinge, m/s slide), and a script drives it with api.setActuatorControl('<jointName>_actuator', value). See schema.jointFields.actuator.

GEARS ARE COUPLED BY PROXIMITY, not by their teeth touching. Any body whose id contains 'gear' and has a hinge is coupled to another such body when (1) their hinge axes are parallel, (2) a wheel of each overlaps the other's along the axis, i.e. they lie in the same plane, and (3) the axes are between 0.5 and 1.2 times the sum of those two wheels' radii apart; the ratio is -r_other/r_this. A WHEEL is, in this order: each cylinder or capsule geom (its radius; geoms with role 'visual' or csg 'difference' do not count); else a cut gear's pitch circle (physics_build_mechanism); else each mesh geom, which includes an 'extrude' polygon, a lathe or an OpenSCAD part: its widest radius from the hinge, or, when its outline has teeth (counted around the axis, at a gear's depth for that count), its pitch radius tip*N/(N+2), and two toothed wheels couple at the exact ratio of their teeth. A body with only boxes has no wheel and is never coupled. An arbor with a wheel and a pinion at different heights offers each separately. A RACK is a slide body marked isRack: true (a rack cut by physics_build_mechanism is one already); its name does not matter. It couples to any hinged wheel (a round geom, or a cut gear's pitch circle) whose hinge axis is square to the slide, that lies in the rack's plane over its length, with the rack's face toward it within 30% of the wheel's radius from the axis (a cut rack's origin is its pitch line); the ratio is theta = x/r, signed by the side the rack is on, so a rack above a pinion and one below it run opposite ways. A marked rack that nothing meshes with is named in couplingWarnings. Bodies already tied together by coupleTargetId, directly or along a chain, are left to those couplings, so an explicitly chained train is never coupled again across a fold. Set allowCoupling: false on a body to keep it out of all of this.
scad_and_patterns: OpenSCAD designs in this simulator must be scaled to meters (scale([0.001, 0.001, 0.001]) { ... }) at the top-level. Leaving them in default millimeters causes meshes to render 1000x too large, breaking camera zoom bounding boxes and physics stability.

FOR LETTERING ON A PART, USE physics_apply_pattern WITH pattern: 'text', NOT OpenSCAD text() AND NOT HAND-BUILT LETTERS. It engraves or embosses real lettering in any Google font (fontFamily, fontWeight, heightMm), straight, round an arc, along a wave or any SVG path, on any face of any body — flat, curved or a cylinder's side — and it exports to STL, 3MF, relief carving and machining like the part. Or pass it at build time as `patterns: [{ at, normal, pattern: 'text', options: { text, fontFamily, heightMm }, depthMm }]` on the body. OpenSCAD's text() is unreliable in the browser compiler (it can compile silently to empty geometry), and stroke-built letters are a workaround from before the text pattern existed.

When performing CSG difference operations in OpenSCAD (such as cutting slots, grooves, or recesses), ensure the subtracted geometries extend slightly past the outer boundaries of the main body. Perfectly coplanar faces at the cutting limits can cause degenerate triangles or rendering artifacts (like flickering or jagged ridges) in the WebGL renderer.

When generating parametric OpenSCAD scripts (such as sine waves, splines, or ribbons), ALWAYS declare design parameters (e.g. wave_length = 50; // [10:5:200], thickness = 2.0; // [0.5:0.5:10]) on separate lines at the VERY TOP of the SCAD code, outside any scale(), module, or function blocks. Include Customizer range annotations // [min:step:max] so the app can automatically parse them into interactive UI sliders.

A body with a 'scad' script compiles to exactly ONE mesh geom that IS the entire part. The SCAD source is the single source of truth for that body's shape. When converting a primitive-built body to SCAD, or rewriting its SCAD, you MUST also replace its geoms array with just that one mesh geom. Leftover primitives from the previous version are not ignored: they still render and still collide on top of the mesh, and because they are typically unpositioned (pos:[0,0,0], no fromto) they pile up at the body's centre as stray blobs and discs that look like simulator artefacts. Note that physics_update_object with a 'scad' payload only refills the existing mesh geom; it does NOT prune sibling primitives, so send an explicit geoms array to remove them. A dynamic mesh already collides via its convex hull, so do not keep primitives around 'for collision' unless you want a proxy. In that case position it explicitly and mark it role: 'collision' (never drawn), or better, draw it in the SCAD with $physbox_collision (openScadNotes.collisionProxies).
scene_and_export: A body that looks TRANSPARENT or see-through is rarely a transparency setting. Check its rgba alpha (below 1 draws translucent); if that is 1, the usual cause is inside-out face winding, because mesh geoms are drawn single-sided: the near surface is culled and you are looking at the inside of the far wall through the gap where it should be. Call physics_get_scene_summary and read `windingInverted` on the geom before you touch colours or materials.

physics_update_scene's sceneGraph parameter is a bare array of SceneNode objects (matching physics_build_scene's bodies convention) for new bodies, or the whole object physics_get_scene returned for a round trip. Only the object form brings back the environment and the note cards.

physics_build_scene and physics_update_scene wait for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for a final MJCF recompile before responding, and report the real result as { ok, error?, nodeCount }. There is no need to poll physics_get_state afterward. The call can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies (each compiles sequentially).

physics_get_state.lastCompileError holds the most recent MJCF/MuJoCo compile error message (or null on success). Check this after loading a scene to see the real underlying failure reason instead of just a generic ok:false.

To visually verify layout, spacing, or alignment of a scene, use the physics_get_screenshot tool directly rather than launching a Puppeteer or browser instance. Spawning browser instances is slow, resource-heavy, and redundant when the direct viewport screenshot tool is available. The one exception is testing alongside a person or another agent: then open a tab of your own (it registers as a session; see list_sessions) and pass its id as `session` on every command, so nothing lands in theirs.
To load a user preset, use the 'user:presetName' format (e.g. 'user:mukada') in the physics_load_preset parameter. The bridge handles this automatically by pulling from localStorage.

If a dynamic mesh's visual representation is misaligned or hovering compared to its collision behavior, verify the renderVertices: they should be a direct swap: (x, -z, y) of the Y-up collision vertices without subtracting the centroid (since MuJoCo handles centroid offset internally).

Never bypass the MCP API surface by creating raw browser agents or Puppeteer connections to query state or localStorage, and do not modify source code files simply to add telemetry/debug commands. Use the existing MCP endpoints to query state (e.g. physics_get_state) and apply updates (e.g. physics_update_scene).
Copilot response parsing rule: diagnostic 'questions' arrays (containing question/options keys) must NEVER be treated as scene 'nodes'. Scene nodes require valid body/geom/scad structure.

MOLDS INVERT. A casting copies the master, but the mold is turned over to pour into: whatever the master stands on in a pour box becomes the casting's pour face, and the master's top ends up at the bottom of the mold. For anything with a right way up (text, a logo, a face, relief art), settle which end of the finished casting is its top before building the master, and when checking a simulated cast, turn it the way it will stand first. Neither physics_make_pour_box nor physics_add_simulation knows which way up the piece is meant to be used.

HANDING OVER A PRINTABLE FILE: physics_export_print (STL or 3MF) with out_dir writes the file to disk and replies with its path; give the user that path. Pick a directory they will find (their project folder or Downloads, not a temp directory), say what is in the file (which bodies, size in mm, which way up), and note anything left out (bought-in hardware is never printed). Check physics_get_scene_summary `watertight` on every mesh first. Without out_dir nothing is written: you only learn names and sizes. A cast pattern (physics_export_cast) and a pour box (physics_make_pour_box) are handed over the same way, with out_dir. The person can also press Export STL / Export 3MF in the app's toolbar themselves.

coordinateSystem.mujocoWorldSpace: X=right (+X right, -X left), Y=forward into screen (+Y away, -Y toward viewer), Z=up (+Z height). Ground plane at Z=0. Gravity default: Z=-9.81.
coordinateSystem.geomPos: pos field on geoms is a local offset from the body origin in MuJoCo Z-up space.
coordinateSystem.bodyPos: pos field on bodies is relative to parent body (or world origin for root bodies).
coordinateSystem.meshVertices: EXCEPTION: mesh geom vertices are in Three.js Y-up world space (X=right, Y=up, Z=toward camera). See mesh section.
coordinateSystem.cameraOrientation: CAMERA Y-AXIS RULE: In MuJoCo world space, -Y is in front of the object toward the viewer, and +Y is behind the object. To frame a front-on view of an object at target [0, 0, z], set position to a NEGATIVE Y coordinate (e.g. position: [0, -2.5, z], target: [0, 0, z]). Passing a positive Y coordinate (e.g. [0, 2.5, z]) places the camera behind the object looking into empty space.
coordinateSystem.defaultCamera: physics_get_screenshot always renders whatever the viewport camera currently shows. Use physics_set_camera(position, target), both MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z], to point the camera at a specific body/face before screenshotting. To frame a front-on view of an object at [x,y,z], place position at a negative Y offset relative to target (e.g. position:[0, y-2.5, z], target:[x, y, z]). For a square-on view of the whole scene, preset 'front', 'side' or 'topDown' gives an orthographic drawing view, and dims:true marks it in mm. The default 'perspective' preset is a diagonal 3/4 pose. physics_get_camera returns the camera's live pose.

tools.list_sessions:
List the browser tabs connected to each app, and say which one commands are going to.

Several tabs of the same app can be open at once. Without this the hub could only shout at all of them and keep whichever answered first, which makes the app look haunted: a body created by one call is missing from the next, a preset saved over a good one comes back empty, a screenshot shows a scene from twenty minutes ago. Each tab now has an id and a label, and every command goes to exactly one of them.

The most recently connected tab is selected by default, so with one tab open there is nothing to do. With several, call this and then either use_session to pin one, or pass its id as `session` on each command. `session` is the one to use when more than one agent works in the same app: a pin is shared by everyone talking to the hub, so two agents pinning their own tabs take the pin from each other between calls, while `session` is per command. A tab keeps its id across a reload.

physics_add_object.summary:
Add ONE body to the scene, leaving everything already in it alone. `body` is a single body descriptor, exactly the shape of one element of physics_build_scene's `bodies` array, and the same defaults are filled in.

Pass `parent` (existing body id/name) to attach inside that body (rigidly fixed if `joints` is omitted; `free` joint only allowed at top level). Duplicate ids get a numeric suffix. Returns compile status and any `scriptWarnings` and `referenceWarnings`.

details.parenting_and_compilation:
Use this instead of reading the scene back and posting it again through physics_update_scene. On a scene holding a sculpt or a boolean that round trip is megabytes each way, and it overwrites anything another client changed in between. physics_delete_object is the other half of the pair.

parent (an existing body's id or name) puts the new body inside that one instead of at the top level. Its pos is then relative to the parent, and with no joints given it is fixed rigidly to the parent and moves with it. Give it a hinge or slide joint to let it turn or slide; a free joint is refused, because MuJoCo allows one only at the top level. The same rule holds for nested children in physics_build_scene: a child with no joints is fixed to its parent.

An id that is already taken is given a numeric suffix rather than refused, and the reply says what the body was actually called. The reply also carries the real MJCF compile result, so a body that failed to build says so rather than reporting ok and leaving you to find out. A script that does not compile is still saved, and the reply carries scriptWarnings: ["Script on '<body>' does not compile: <error>. ..."]; runtime errors surface in physics_get_state.worker.scriptProblems and in physics_run_headless warnings.

physics_build_scene.summary: Build and load a scene from simplified `bodies` descriptors with auto-filled defaults (`bodies: []` clears the scene). Waits for OpenSCAD bodies and MJCF compilation and returns `{ ok, error?, scriptWarnings?, referenceWarnings?, collisionPending?, nodeCount, topLevelCount }`. Frames the camera on the scene and starts at t = 0. Follow with `physics_set_note_cards` to describe the scene.

details.compilation_and_notes: Returns once the scene is built, without waiting for hollow bodies' convex pieces: when some are still being worked out (a few seconds a body, up to ~20 s for a long coiled part, one body at a time) the reply lists them as `collisionPending` with a note. That is not an error and the scene is built; do not build it again. physics_run_headless waits for them. Build and load a scene from simplified body descriptors. Auto-fills safe defaults. `bodies: []` clears the scene: every body goes, and the reply is { ok: true, nodeCount: 0, topLevelCount: 0 }. Easier than physics_update_scene. Waits for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for MJCF to settle before responding. The response is { ok, error?, scriptWarnings?, referenceWarnings?, nodeCount, topLevelCount } (referenceWarnings: one per target id - coupleTargetId, weldTargetId, connectTargetId, leftTargetId, rightTargetId, pulleyWheelId, weldLastToId - that names no body, names a body where its id is needed, or couples to a body with no joint; such a reference does nothing. nodeCount is every body, nested children included; topLevelCount only the top level), so check `ok`/`error` directly rather than polling physics_get_state. Can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies. The camera is then framed on the whole scene, every nested body included, as it is when a preset loads; physics_set_camera afterwards to look somewhere else. After the scene lands, write its note card with physics_set_note_cards; nothing else does. The default card says "Interactive 3D rigid-body physics scene". Replace it as part of building the scene. A script that does not compile is still saved, and the reply carries scriptWarnings: ["Script on '<body>' does not compile: <error>. ..."]; runtime errors surface in physics_get_state.worker.scriptProblems and in physics_run_headless warnings. A new scene starts from t = 0 with an empty telemetry history. A reply of 'Timeout waiting for ...' does not mean the command failed: it may still have run, or still be running. Check physics_get_scene_summary before retrying.

physics_carve_scene.summary:
Machine the scene that is loaded. Needs the machine armed. This is the one that cuts.

Runs ONE `side` at a time (operator must flip, re-fixture, and re-zero Z between sides). Shaped by `toolDiaMm` (default 3), `sides`, `stockThicknessMm`, and `material`. Refuses if >5% of the part is unreachable unless `acceptUnreachable: true`. Poll `physics_machine_status` for time-based progress.

details.sides_reachability_and_streaming:
A solid is machined from more than one SIDE, and the sides are separate programs with the part re-fixtured in between — so this runs ONE side and says which. `side` picks it; the default is the first. Do not treat a carve as a single button press: tell the user the part has to be turned over and the next side run separately, and that Z must be re-zeroed after it is.

`toolDiaMm` (default 3), `sides`, `stockThicknessMm` and `material` shape the program. It refuses if more than 5% of the part cannot be reached by the chosen tool — that comes out as an unmachined lump and the operator finds out three hours in; use a smaller tool, cut from more sides, or pass `acceptUnreachable: true` if that is understood and wanted.

Over a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself and the carve survives the laptop being shut. Over USB this browser is the streamer and the job lives as long as the tab. Poll physics_machine_status for progress — and note that progress is reported as an elapsed clock against an estimate, not as a line count, because a rapid across the stock and a raster pass are both one line and take wildly different times. Without stockThicknessMm it carves in the bench stock (physics_set_environment) when the part fits in it, and says so; a part taller than the bench stock gets stock sized from the part. A framing lap frames the same job the last carve asked for.

tools.physics_check_collisions:
Check which bodies start inside one another (or inside the floor) at t=0, before running the simulation. It asks MuJoCo itself: the scene is compiled on a model of its own and stepped once, and the contacts the solver generates are read back, so the answer is exactly what the simulation will see, and the live view is left alone (`method: 'contacts'`). If the worker cannot run the scene it falls back to world-space boxes round each colliding geom, built from its real shape and pose (`method: 'bounds'`; conservative, since a box round a diagonal strut is bigger than the strut).

Either way, pairs the solver never collides are left out: a body and the body it hangs off by a joint (and anything fixed to either), two bodies fixed into one rigid piece (two bodies both fixed to the world, say), geoms with contype and conaffinity 0 or role 'visual', and pairs whose contact bits do not meet. Penetration under 0.1 mm counts as resting contact.

Returns { hasInterpenetrations, bodyCount (every body, nested ones included), method, toleranceMm, overlappingPairs: [{ bodyA, bodyB, geomA, geomB, depthMm }] }, one entry per pair of bodies at its deepest; bodyB 'floor' is a body sunk into the ground. `filledCavities` lists hollow bodies still colliding as their convex hull.
tools.physics_clear_paint: Remove brushed paint. With no id, strips every stroke in the scene; with an id, that body; with an id and a geomName, that geom. Base colours set by physics_set_color are left alone.
tools.physics_combine:
Merge other bodies into this one and apply a boolean between them. This is how two things you have already built and positioned become one part.

A boolean is a program over ONE body's shapes, so two bodies can never cut each other however they overlap. This brings them together: each merged body's shapes are rewritten into the target's frame — keeping their exact place in the world — marked with the operation, and the bodies they came from are removed, along with anything parented to them.

op 'union' leaves them as ordinary added shapes, which is a compound body needing no boolean at all. 'difference' cuts them out of the target; 'intersection' keeps only the overlap. Both of those turn the boolean on and the result is compiled like any other, so physics_get_object will report csgVolume and the generated source once it has.

Anything can be merged in: a primitive, a lattice part, a sculpt, an imported STL. Build the shape you want to remove, put it where you want it, and subtract it. The target keeps its own id, joints and name.

physics_create_lattice.summary:
Add a lattice body (a shape built by connecting points on a grid) and return its id. This is the only way to make one: a primitive, an imported STL, an OpenSCAD body and a sculpt cannot be converted into one.

Use this rather than sculpting for anything CRISP and DIMENSIONED: a bracket, a housing, a mount, a part that has to be 40 mm across and meet another part squarely.

Starts as a closed box `sizeMm` across (default 40 mm, or `empty: true` for no faces) with the cage origin at `pos` (default [0, 0, 0.2], or relative to `parent`). Build an entire part in one call by passing `ops: [{op, ...}]`, `subdiv` (0|1|2 Catmull-Clark passes, default 0), and `thicknessMm` (wall thickness for open shells). All lattice tools use millimetres in the cage frame on a 0.1 mm grid.

details.placement_and_frames:
It starts as a closed box `sizeMm` across (default 40 mm), centred on the cage origin. pos is where the CAGE ORIGIN goes in world space (default [0, 0, 0.2]), so with ops a face drawn at x = 150 mm ends up 150 mm from pos; it is dropped in with a free joint, so it falls when the simulation runs. parent (an existing body's id or name) puts it inside that body instead: pos is then relative to the parent, and it is fixed rigidly to the parent. edit:true also opens the lattice tools in the viewport. Only do that when a person is about to carry on by hand: it takes over the viewport and pauses the simulation.

Returns the id and the cage's counts, bounds and size in millimetres. It replies as soon as the body is built: a concave shape's convex pieces are worked out in the background, and until they land the reply (and physics_get_scene_summary) says collisionPending and the body collides as its hull. physics_run_headless waits for them. Do not retry a create that timed out without first checking physics_get_objects for the body. All lattice tools take and return millimetres in the cage's frame, on a 0.1 mm grid. The cage frame stays fixed to the shape through every edit. The body's own origin is the shape's centre of mass, which moves as the shape is edited (the body's `pos` moves with it, so the shape stays where it was drawn). Joint anchors and child bodies are positioned in that body frame. The reply's `cageOriginMm` (also in physics_get_lattice and the scene summary) is where the cage origin sits in the body frame, so a hinge at cage point c goes at c + cageOriginMm (as millimetres, then metres). Edits keep existing joint anchors and child bodies where they were on the shape.

It weighs its own volume at 1000 kg/m³ (water), not a fixed kilogram, and the figure follows the shape as it is edited; a lattice in physics_build_scene honours the body's `density` or `mass`. A shape that is not closed is weighed by its convex hull, so wall or cap it before trusting the mass. physics_get_scene_summary's `inertial.massKg` is the figure the solver uses.
details.one_call_ops:
BUILDING IT IN ONE CALL. These optional fields make the whole part in the create, with no round trip per edit:
- `empty: true` starts with no faces at all instead of the box (so does sizeMm 0). A create whose first op is a revolve and that passes no sizeMm starts empty too.
- `ops` is a list applied in order to the starting cage, each `{op: <name>, ...fields}`, with the same fields and in millimetres as the tool named in brackets: `extrude` (physics_lattice_extrude: face, distanceMm, axis, mirror), `inset` (physics_lattice_inset: face, amountMm, mirror), `bevel` (physics_lattice_bevel: face, amountMm, mirror), `bevel_edges` (physics_lattice_bevel_edges: edges, radiusMm, mode 'chamfer' or 'fillet', loop, mirror), `faces` (physics_lattice_faces: faces, mirror), `delete_faces` (physics_lattice_delete_faces: faces, mirror), `sharpen` (physics_lattice_sharpen: edges, sharp, loop, mirror), `circle` (physics_lattice_circle: centre, diameterMm, axis, sides, mirror), `revolve` (physics_lattice_revolve: profile, axis, degrees, closed, throughMm, segments), `bridge` (physics_lattice_bridge: faceA, faceB), `dimension` (physics_lattice_dimension: corners, axis, mode 'size' or 'position', valueMm), `orient` (physics_lattice_orient, no fields), `smooth` (level, as subdiv below) and `wall` (thicknessMm, as below). An unknown op name fails the whole call and nothing is created. The reply's `opsApplied` counts them; read the shape back with physics_get_lattice.
- `subdiv` is the SMOOTHING level, Catmull-Clark passes over the mesh built from the cage (physics_lattice_smooth): 0 the cage itself with flat faces and hard edges (the default), 1 or 2 rounder. It is NOT a grid subdivision, and anything above 2 is taken as 2. A box smoothed twice is a rounded blob, so leave it at 0 for a crisp part.
- `thicknessMm` is a wall thickness for an OPEN surface (physics_lattice_wall): the offset runs inwards and closes it into a shell. A closed shape ignores it.

physics_create_sculpt.summary:
Add a free-form sculptable body, started from clay, and return its id. To brush a shape that already exists - an imported STL, a mesh loaded from a scene file, a compiled OpenSCAD part - pass its id straight to physics_sculpt instead: any mesh body can be brushed. A primitive (box, sphere, cylinder...) and a boolean body cannot; neither has a mesh a stroke would last on.

`base` picks the starting shape (default 'sphere'; 'head', 'humanoid' facing +X, 'quadruped', 'bird', 'fish', 'hand', 'cube', 'cylinder'). `pos` is world position (default [0,0,0.3], or relative to `parent`); `sizeMm` is the longest side in mm (default 100).

details.bases_sizing_and_mass:
base picks the starting shape (default 'sphere'); see schema.sculpting.bases for the nine and what each is for. Start from the closest base: 'head' is a bust on its shoulders, 'humanoid' a standing mannequin facing +X. pos is the body's position in world space (default [0, 0, 0.3]); the body is dropped in with a free joint, so it falls when the simulation runs. parent (an existing body's id or name) puts it inside that body instead: pos is then relative to the parent, and it is fixed rigidly to the parent.

Returns the id, the base, and the mesh's vertex/face counts, bounds and size in metres. sizeMm is the clay's longest side in millimetres (default 100). Make it the size of the thing being made - a 70 mm pumpkin is sizeMm 70 - rather than sculpting big and scaling later. physics_resize_sculpt changes it afterwards. physics_sculpt's default radius is a sixth of the body's longest side; go smaller for detail.

It weighs its own volume at 1000 kg/m³ (water), not a fixed kilogram, and the figure follows the clay through every stroke and resize; a sculpt in physics_build_scene honours the body's `density` or `mass`. physics_get_scene_summary's `inertial.massKg` is the figure the solver uses.

physics_cut.summary:
Cut a shape out of a body: a round hole, a rectangular slot, or a spherical dish. Works on ANY body — a primitive, a lattice part, a sculpt, an imported STL — because a cut is an ordinary negative shape added to that body's boolean program.

ON A SCULPT BODY, USE physics_sculpt_cut INSTEAD: a cut made here turns the sculpt into a boolean, and it can no longer be brushed.

`at` is a point in the body's own frame in mm and `normal` is the outward surface normal there (default [0,0,1]). `depthMm` is measured from where the ray meets material (0 or omitted = right through). Basic shapes: 'hole' (`diameterMm`, optional `threadPitchMm`), 'slot' (`widthMm`, `lengthMm` in the cut's local frame), 'dish' (`diameterMm`, blind). Also supports 'pocket', ISO hardware pockets ('nut_trap', 'nut_slot', 'counterbore', 'insert', 'insert_boss', 'bearing'), O-ring glands ('oring', 'seal_cord'), and linear-motion seats ('rail_seat', 'rod_clamp', 'lm_housing'). Two meeting cuts should overlap by ~0.1 mm.

details.coordinates_and_booleans:
THIS IS THE ONLY WAY TO PUT A SHAPE ON A BODY THAT ALREADY EXISTS. A body's geoms are its boolean program, so two separate bodies can never cut each other; physics_combine merges them first if that is what you want.

You say WHERE the cut goes and HOW DEEP, not where the cutter's middle is and how long it is. `at` is a point in the body's own frame in millimetres and `normal` is the outward direction of the surface there (default [0,0,1], straight down onto the top). A line is cast along that normal through `at` to find the material, and `depthMm` is measured from wherever it meets — so 10 mm means 10 mm into the low arm of a bracket as much as into the top of a block. depthMm 0, or omitted, goes right through. The cutter itself is made a little longer than the hole, because a cut ending flush with a surface leaves coincident faces and a boolean of those is not reliably a solid.

`diameterMm` sizes a hole or a dish; `widthMm` and `lengthMm` size a slot, across the surface it enters. A dish is always blind — a ball has no length to run.

The reply gives the point the cut actually landed on, which is not always the point asked for: the line was cast through it to find the surface. NOTE for a lattice body: `at` is the BODY's frame, while physics_get_lattice reports the cage's; the two differ by however far the mesh was recentred on its centre of mass, which physics_get_object reports as latticeOrigin.

WIDTH AND LENGTH ARE IN THE CUT'S OWN FRAME, not the world's. The cutter is made by turning its +Z onto `normal`, so widthMm runs along the surface's local X and lengthMm along its local Y. Cutting straight down (normal [0,0,1]) that is world X and world Y; cutting into a wall facing +Y it is world X and world Z.

TWO CUTS THAT MEET SHOULD OVERLAP, not touch. Negatives that share an exact face leave coincident surfaces in the boolean, and a boolean of those is not reliably a solid. Give neighbouring slots a tenth of a millimetre of overlap and the union comes out clean.

A body that ends up thin and full of through-cuts — a stencil, a fretted plate — may be worth setting to `collision: 'hull'`, which collides it as one filled hull instead of many thin pieces; see the gotcha about hollow shapes.

The cut solid stays exactly where its shapes are: a point measured with physics_measure is cut at by subtracting the body's `pos` (and, for a lattice body, adding its `latticeOrigin`).
details.threads: A TAPPED HOLE: give a hole `threadPitchMm` and it is cut with an ISO 60° thread of that pitch, right-handed unless `threadLeft` is true. `diameterMm` is then the thread's MAJOR diameter — the bolt's name — so an M6 is diameterMm 6, threadPitchMm 1; M3 is 3 × 0.5, M4 is 4 × 0.7, M5 is 5 × 0.8, M8 is 8 × 1.25, M10 is 10 × 1.5. The hole is cut at nominal size: a printed part that must take a real bolt may want a tenth or two of a millimetre on the diameter. Ignored for a slot or a dish. Compiles in well under a second, like any other cut.
details.hardware: HARDWARE: `shape` can also be 'nut_trap', 'nut_slot', 'counterbore', 'insert', 'insert_boss' or 'bearing', each cut into the part at `at`/`normal` as one feature, sized from ISO tables by `size`: a bolt size 'M2' to 'M24' ('insert' and 'insert_boss' run M2 to M8), or for 'bearing' one of 623, 624, 625, 626, 688, 608, 6000, 6001. nut_trap: a hex pocket the nut drops into (across flats + fitMm, nut height + fitMm deep, default fitMm 0.2) over an ISO 273 clearance hole right through. nut_slot: the nut slides in from the side instead: a clearance hole right through, and a slot as wide as the nut across its flats and as tall as the nut, buried 2 mm under the face on the bolt's line and running out to the nearest side wall (the reply's `pieces` are shank and slot). Refused when the part is too thin to bury the nut (2 mm cover + nut + 1 mm floor). Turn it to another side in the Cut panel. counterbore: a socket-head recess (DIN 974-1) over a shank hole; `bore` 'clearance' (default) or 'tapped'. insert: a blind hole for a heat-set insert. insert_boss: a round post stood on the face, bored for an insert; `bore` 'insert' (default), 'tapped' or 'clearance'. bearing: a blind pocket at the outer diameter, as deep as the bearing is wide, over a through hole that leaves a ledge under the outer race. `fitMm` is a diametral clearance on what fits in it. The reply gives `group` and the `pieces` it is made of; physics_get_object lists them with a `hardware` tag. Moving or deleting any piece moves or deletes the whole feature. Bolt sizes are not threads: for a plain tapped hole use shape 'hole' with threadPitchMm. `threadFitMm` adds a diametral clearance to a tapped hole.
details.orings: O-RING GROOVES: shape 'oring' cuts a groove for a stocked O-ring, size 'ID×cord' in mm (e.g. '20×2'; cords 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 5). Where it seals is read off where it is put, or forced with `seal`: on the side of a cylinder it is a 'piston' seal round that boss (sealing inside the bore it goes into); on the wall of a hole a 'bore' seal (sealing on a shaft through it); anywhere else a 'face' seal under a lid, centred on a round face and in the middle of the wall of a round cavity open into it. shape 'seal_cord' cuts a groove that follows the rim of a rectangular face, for O-ring cord cut to length (size = cord diameter, '1.5' to '5'), in the middle of the wall when a box cavity is open into the face. Leave `size` out and it picks the ring or cord that fits. Depth and width are the cord's static gland. A size that cannot fit, or a spot with no room, is refused with the reason. physics_add_hardware kind 'oring' then lays the ring in the groove, and `sealCheck` (in physics_cut's reply and physics_add_hardware's for the ring, and per groove as `sealChecks` in physics_get_object, which is where to look once the lid or bore is in place) says whether it seals against whatever is placed over or round it, with what to change if not: squeeze 15-30%, groove under 85% full, under 5% stretch, and the mating part covering the whole ring.
details.linear_motion: LINEAR MOTION SEATS: shape 'rail_seat' (size MGN9/MGN12/MGN15, `lengthMm` the rail's, `turned` true to run across the face; `bore` 'insert' (default), 'tapped' or 'clearance' for the bolt holes) cuts a 1.5 mm channel that locates the rail straight with a hole at every bolt. 'rod_clamp' (size the rod's diameter) is a blind socket two diameters deep. 'lm_housing' (size the rod's diameter) is a pocket for its LM-UU bushing with the rod's way right through.
details.pocket: A SMOOTH POCKET OR DISH: shape 'pocket' cuts a recess from its outline, depth and floor, as a dense mesh, so a shallow 112 mm dish comes out smooth instead of stepped like a scaled sphere. outline 'rect' (a rounded rectangle: widthMm, lengthMm, cornerRadiusMm) or 'ellipse' (widthMm, lengthMm; or diameterMm for a round one); depthMm; floor 'flat' (a flat floor meeting the wall in a fillet of floorRadiusMm, default a quarter of the depth) or 'bowl' (a smooth dish). Placed like any cut, by at/normal; widthMm runs along the surface's local X. The reply's `pocket` echoes what was built. In SCAD, `use <physbox/pocket.scad>` gives the same cutter as a module: pocket(width, length, depth, corner_r=0, floor=\"flat\", floor_r=-1, outline=\"rect\"), rim at z=0 going down, millimetres — subtract it with difference().

physics_add_hardware.summary:
Put a piece of BOUGHT hardware in the scene: a ball bearing, a socket head cap screw, a hex nut or a ground shaft. Bought parts are drawn and simulated but left out of every print, mold and machining export and of the DFM check: they are what goes into the part, not the part.

`kind`: 'bearing' (623, 624, 625, 626, 688, 608, 6000, 6001) | 'screw' (M2 to M24, `lengthMm` under the head from the ISO 4762 lengths, `washer` true for an ISO 7089 washer under the head) | 'nut' (M2 to M24) | 'shaft' (diameter '3' to '12' mm, `lengthMm`) | 'oring' (only seated, `into` a body and `group` an O-ring or rim-seal groove: sized and shaped by the groove; cord is cut to the groove's length).

Usually seated in a cut from physics_cut via `into` (body id) and `group` (cut group, e.g. 'bearing1'), or placed at `at` (world mm). Also supports linear motion ('mgn_rail', 'linear_rod', 'drawer_runner' with `fixTo`), aluminium extrusion ('extrusion', 'tnut', 'corner_bracket', 'joint_plate', 'end_tap', 'vslot_carriage' with `between`), and 'spring' / 'stepper'.

details.seating_and_mounting:
SEATED IN A HARDWARE CUT is the usual way: give `into` (the body) and `group` (the cut's group from physics_cut's reply, e.g. 'bearing1'). The part becomes a child of that body, sized by the cut, placed in it (a bearing flush in its pocket, a nut on the floor of its trap, a screw bearing on its counterbore's floor), rigid to it, and taken out of the contact solver, because the cut holds it, not contacts. It follows the cut when the cut is moved or resized. A bearing's inner race is a body of its own on a hinge along the bore (reply: `innerRaceId`), so whatever is fixed to it turns. A screw in a counterbore is sized to reach into the next hole along its line in another body, and WELDS that body to the one it sits in (reply: `fastens`); with nothing below it reaches 1.5 diameters past the part. Deleting the screw removes the weld it made. `into` without `group` takes the body's first empty cut that fits. `into` a bearing with kind 'shaft' puts a shaft of its bore through the inner race.

Otherwise the part stands on its own at `at` (world, mm, exactly: a part put on top of something is not lifted) with a free joint and normal contacts. `into` a body that has no cut this part fits MOUNTS it there instead: it stays at `at` and is welded rigidly to that body (reply: `weldedTo`), as a motor is bolted to its frame or a spring stands on its plate.

Changing a seated part's size changes its cut's size too.

WHAT TO BUY: physics_get_scene_summary's `hardwareList` counts every bought part (`rows`) and packs bar stock onto the bar lengths it is sold in (`bars`).
details.linear_motion: LINEAR MOTION. kind 'mgn_rail' (MGN9, MGN12, MGN15; `lengthMm`), 'linear_rod' (rod Ø6-20 with its LM-UU bushing; `lengthMm`), 'drawer_runner' (full-extension, 250-600 mm; size is the length). Each has a moving piece — the rail's carriage, the rod's bushing, the runner's drawer member — that is a body of its own (`<id>_carriage`) on a limited slide, so it stops at the ends. Seat a rail `into` a body's 'rail_seat' cut `group`, a rod into a 'rod_clamp'. Put a body on the moving piece with `fixTo` (its id): it is welded to the piece and slides with it; for a part already in the scene pass `id` (the part) and `fixTo` and nothing else. A body with an 'lm_housing' cut rides the rod on that housing's line: `into` the body, `group` the housing, any kind; the rod's bushing is moved to the housing and the body welded to it, or the reply says why not (no rod on that line, past its travel). DRAWERS: kind 'drawer_runner' `into` a drawer body that stands in its cabinet puts a pair on the drawer's sides, sized to its depth, out of the side it is flush with, the runners fixed in the smallest body round the drawer (as children of it) and the drawer welded to one runner's slide, the other runner following it. The DFM check measures each runner's side space against 12.7 mm.
details.extrusion: ALUMINIUM EXTRUSION: kind 'extrusion' (size '2020', '2040', '3030', '4040', or '2020V' for V-slot; `lengthMm` any length, cut to suit) is a T-slot profile along its own +Z, the real section drawn and its envelope colliding, weighing the maker's kg/m. 'tnut' (size 'M4/6', 'M5/6', 'M5/8', 'M6/8': thread/slot) stands on its own. 'corner_bracket', 'joint_plate' and 'end_tap' JOIN two profiles: give `between: [aId, bId]` (either order). The end of one must stand square on a side face of the other; the piece is fixed to the profile whose side is met and carries a weld to the other (reply: `weldedTo`), so a frame holds together, and deleting the piece removes its weld. A bracket goes in the inside corner (toward the middle of the met profile), a plate across the outside face the two share (`size` 'L20'/'T20'/... to choose; left out, an L near an end and a T across a middle), an end-tap screw through the met profile into the other's tapped end. Sizes follow the profiles. Two profiles that do not meet are refused with the reason. 'vslot_carriage' with `into` a '2020V' profile puts a three-wheel plate on it on a slide joint along the profile, limited to stop clear of both ends. Slots are mate features, so a T-nut or screw dragged to a profile snaps onto a slot's line.
details.springs_and_motors: SPRINGS AND MOTORS: kind 'spring' (Ø6×20 to Ø20×60, at its real rate) — its top is a moving piece (`<id>_carriage`, reply: `carriageId`) on a slide with that stiffness, resting at its free length and stopping at solid height; `fixTo` a body and it is sprung. A given `size` is applied before `fixTo`, so the body rides the right top. Its seat and top weigh at least a few grams more than bare wire (8*rate*1e-6 kg and 4*rate*1e-6 kg, rate in N/m), so a stiff spring under a heavy part does not ring faster than the 1 ms step and punch through what it stands on. kind 'stepper' (NEMA17 40, NEMA17 48, NEMA23 56) — face at its origin, shaft up +Z, the shaft (`<id>_shaft`, reply: `shaftId`) on a hinge driven by a velocity actuator (`<id>_spin_actuator`) limited to the motor's holding torque, so it stalls under a load past it; its rotor is the maker's inertia, with nothing added. Give `into` the body it is bolted to (and `at`) to mount it; otherwise it arrives free. Set its speed as you would any actuator's ctrl.

physics_build_mechanism.summary: Build a standard transmission or linkage into the scene with joints, couplings, and drive: `family` is 'gear', 'gear_pair', 'rack_pinion', 'gt2_belt', 'leadscrew', 'cam_follower', or 'four_bar'. Common args: `origin` [x,y,z] in metres, `idPrefix`, `actuate` (default true, creates `<jointName>_actuator`), `speed` (rad/s or m/s), `torqueLimitNm`, `arborId` + `axialOffsetMm` (for compound gears), and family-specific fields in `spec`.

details.families_and_common_options:
Build a transmission or linkage into the scene from real standards, with its joints, couplings and drive set up: family 'gear' (one involute spur gear on a hinge), 'gear_pair' (two in mesh, the driven one coupled to the driver at -z1/z2), 'rack_pinion', 'gt2_belt' (two GT2 pulleys and the belt), 'leadscrew' (a T8 screw on a hinge and its brass nut on a slide, side by side in a fixed mount; the nut travels lead/2pi per radian and does not turn, so a carriage fixed to it slides; ends of travel are hard stops), 'cam_follower' (a profiled cam on a hinge and a roller follower on a slide, held to the cam by a spring; the cam pushes it through contact, so it rises and falls with the profile; metrics.followerPreloadN is the spring's push at the bottom and top of the stroke), 'four_bar' (Grashof-classified, the loop closed by a pin). ADDS TO THE SCENE AS IT IS: nothing already there is removed, except a body with the same id as one being built (so building again with the same idPrefix rebuilds it in place). 

COMMON OPTIONS, every family: `origin` [x,y,z] METRES (the driver's hinge, the screw's middle, the four-bar's ground pivot; left out, a default spot above the floor, so give it when building more than one); `idPrefix` (ids made from it instead of random ones: gear_pair with idPrefix 's1' makes 'gear_s1' and 'gear_s1_2', joints '<id>_hinge', so later calls can name them); `actuate` (default true: the driver carries a velocity motor, actuator '<jointName>_actuator'; false leaves it undriven); `speed` (its target, rad/s, or m/s on a slide); `torqueLimitNm` (the most the motor puts out, N*m or N: it stalls past it).
details.compound_gears: COMPOUND GEARS: `arborId` (an existing hinged body) with `axialOffsetMm` (along that body's own +Z) puts family 'gear', or gear_pair's DRIVER, onto that body, which then carries both gears on its one hinge; a pair's driven gear is placed beside it in the arbor's frame (`meshAngleDeg` says which way) and coupled to the arbor. A multi-stage train is a gear_pair, then a gear_pair onto the first pair's driven gear, and so on; each stage is coupled explicitly, so no stage is ever proximity-coupled to another across a fold. The reply's `arborId` names it.
details.family_specs_and_reply:
FAMILY FIELDS go in `spec` (sent at the top level): gear: moduleMm, teeth, pressureAngleDeg, thicknessMm, backlashMm, profileShift, boreKind ('none'|'round'|'d_shaft'|'hex'|'bearing_608'), boreDiameterMm. gear_pair: driver and driven (each a gear's fields), or moduleMm, driverTeeth, drivenTeeth; meshAngleDeg. rack_pinion: pinion (gear fields) and rack ({moduleMm, teeth, thicknessMm, baseHeightMm}), or moduleMm, pinionTeeth, rackTeeth. gt2_belt: driverTeeth, drivenTeeth, centerDistanceMm, beltWidthMm, boreDiameterMm. leadscrew: lengthMm (at least 40), leadMm (any value from 1 mm per turn up; 2, 4 and 8 are the stock T8 leads), pitchMm (at least 1), diameterMm (at least 4). cam_follower: kind ('eccentric'|'snail'|'heart'|'harmonic'), baseRadiusMm, liftMm, thicknessMm. four_bar: groundMm, crankMm, couplerMm, rockerMm, crankAngleDeg, linkWidthMm, thicknessMm, pinDiameterMm. 

The parts COLLIDE with the floor and other bodies (a four-bar's foot can touch the ground), but not with what they are coupled or pinned to. Reply: family, addedIds (every body added, children included), arborId when one was built onto, and metrics (centre distance, ratio, belt length, travel, Grashof class, as the family has them). A figure the builder could not make as asked (a lead under 1 mm, a gear under 6 teeth) is changed to the nearest it makes, and listed in adjusted: [{ field, requested, used }] with a warning each: work the mechanism out from `used`. ok is false, with error, when the scene then fails to compile.

tools.physics_get_edges:
List the edges of a body that can be rounded or bevelled, with an id for each. Call this before physics_round_edges when you want particular edges rather than a group.

Edges are found on the body AS MODELLED — holes cut, booleans done, but before any rounding — so ids stay the same while its roundings change. Each is a straight `line` (fromMm/toMm) or a round `circle` rim (centreMm, diameterMm, axis): the edge of a box, the rim of a hole or a boss. Everything is in the body's own frame in millimetres. `groups` says which of top / bottom / vertical it belongs to (by the world's up, whatever way the body is turned), or 'inside' for an inside corner, where rounding ADDS material (`convex` false). `maxRoundMm` / `maxBevelMm` is the largest size that fits that edge on its own: half the narrower face beside it, or half the gap to the next edge on that face. `roundedBy` is the index of the rounding that already has it.

`unroundable` counts edges that are neither straight nor a full circle (a sculpted crease, a helix) — they are left alone. Sculpt bodies are refused with the reason. OpenSCAD and imported parts work; if an OpenSCAD part's source is edited so that a rounded edge is no longer there, that edge's rounding is dropped (physics_get_object shows edgeRoundsLost) rather than cut where the edge used to be.

physics_round_edges.summary:
Round (fillet) or bevel (chamfer) edges of any part except a sculpt — a primitive, a boolean with holes cut in it, a lattice part, an OpenSCAD or imported part. The finishing step that makes a block look made rather than modelled.

`edges` is 'all' (default: every OUTSIDE edge), 'top', 'bottom', 'vertical' (outside edges too), 'inside' (the inside corners, where rounding adds material — a fillet at the foot of a rib makes it stronger), or a list of ids from physics_get_edges. `sizeMm` is the fillet's radius, or for a bevel how far back along each face the cut starts. `mode` 'round' (default) or 'bevel'. A size bigger than fits is refused, with the largest that does. `remove: true` takes the rounding off those edges instead (no size needed).

FOR PRINTING, BEVEL THE BOTTOM EDGES rather than rounding them: edges 'bottom', mode 'bevel', 0.5 mm — a rounded bottom edge is an overhang.

details.boolean_and_corner_behavior:
Each call adds one rounding to the body (listed in the reply's `roundings`); an edge belongs to one rounding at a time, so rounding an edge again at a new size moves it to the new one. The rounding is part of the body's boolean program, so the drawn mesh, the colliders, the mass and every export (STL, CNC, casting) get the rounded shape. A rounded part with no hole collides as its own hull, so a filleted block really does roll off its corners. Where three rounded edges of the same size meet square (a box corner) the corner comes out as a ball's eighth. Where an outside edge runs into an inside corner that is also rounded (the top of a gusset meeting the fillet at its foot) the outside rounding stops at the top of that fillet, leaving its last few millimetres sharp: separate roundings cannot blend into each other there.

Resizing a box through its size moves its roundings with it. The reply includes the new volumeMm3.

physics_repair_mesh.summary:
Repair non-manifold, open, degenerate, or inconsistently wound triangle meshes in the scene.

Welds vertices within weld_tolerance_mm (default 0.01 mm), removes zero-area degenerate triangles and duplicate/opposite-wound triangle pairs, resolves non-manifold edges (3+ incident triangles), fills open boundary edge loops, and fixes inverted shell winding so meshes are watertight and ready for 3D CSG booleans, slicing, or simulation.

id is the body id or name to repair; omit to repair all mesh bodies in the scene. geom_name targets a specific mesh geom on the body. weld_tolerance_mm sets the vertex welding distance threshold in mm (default 0.01). fill_holes (default true) caps open boundary loops with triangulated patches. fix_winding (default true) orients connected shells consistently with positive enclosed volume. remove_duplicates (default true) strips duplicate and zero-volume folded face pairs. remove_degenerates (default true) strips zero-area and collinear sliver triangles.

A weld that would destroy the part (a tolerance near its own edge length) is refused and NO mesh is changed.

details.weld_safety: A WELD THAT WOULD DESTROY THE PART IS REFUSED. Welding merges every pair of vertices closer than the tolerance, so a tolerance near the part's own edge length merges its corners (a 20 mm cube welded at 20 mm became a tetrahedron, at 25 mm nothing). A weld_tolerance_mm above the default may be at most half the part's shortest edge and 1% of its size; a larger one is refused with the most that part takes. Every result is also checked before it replaces the part: no triangles left, more than 5% of the surface squashed by the weld, the bounding box moving by more than 10% of the part's size, or the volume of an already closed part changing by more than 10%. Any of those returns ok: false, with `error` and `failures` naming each mesh and why, and NO mesh is changed: a call over several meshes is all or nothing.

tools.physics_delete_object: Remove a body from the scene by id, along with everything parented to it. Returns what was deleted and how many children went with it. The person can undo it in the app (Ctrl+Z), but there is no undo over MCP, so confirm with the user first unless they asked for it.
tools.physics_set_constraint:
Weld one body to another, attach it with a pin, or say what it takes to break the weld off.

`weldTo`/`connectTo` take a body id, null to clear. A weld holds two bodies rigidly wherever they happen to be; a connect pins one point and lets the body swivel about it.

`breakForceN` and `breakTorqueNm` are what the weld survives, in newtons and newton-metres. MuJoCo reports the force it spends holding every weld, so these are real units rather than a made-up scale: a 1 kg body hanging off a weld pulls about 10 N, a few hundred is a sturdy joint, a few tens is decorative. Either limit alone is enough; a weld given only a force limit ignores torque. Pass null to make the weld unbreakable again.

`breakHoldSteps` (default 3) is how many steps in a row the overload must last. A hard contact makes the solver spike for a single step, and without the hold that spike snaps welds that were never really loaded.

BREAKING IS TRANSIENT. It is a simulation event, not an edit: the scene graph still says the part is welded on, so physics_get_scene, exports and share links are unchanged, and physics_reset puts the object back together. Use physics_get_breaks to see what has come apart.

physics_set_impact.summary:
What a body does when it is hit hard: come apart, take a dent, or neither.

Thresholds are in newton-seconds — IMPULSE, i.e. momentum — not force. Contact force in a hard solver is a spike whose height depends on the timestep as much as on the collision, so a force threshold changes meaning when the timestep does. Momentum does not: 0.2 kg arriving at 5 m/s and stopping dead is 1 N*s whatever the solver was doing.

Set `shatterImpulseNs` (Voronoi fracture into `shatterPieces` 2..24, `shatterPattern`, `shatterSpread`, `shatterSeed`, `shatterDepth` 0..2) and/or `dentYieldNs` (`dentDepthPerNs`, `dentRadius`, `dentMaxDepth`, `pierceImpulseNs`, `deformCollision`, `geomName`). Damage is transient (reset restores the body; inspect with physics_get_breaks).

details.shattering: SHATTERING. `shatterImpulseNs` is the blow that breaks the body up; null clears it. The pieces are Voronoi cells of the body itself, cut out of its real shape (not its convex hull), so a chair breaks into pieces of seat, leg and back with nothing in the air between the legs. Together they weigh what it weighed and start where it was, each carrying the velocity of the part of the body it used to be. A piece of a concave body collides as its own convex hull. physics_run_headless shatters and dents too, at the same blow and into the same pieces as the live run; its reply lists them in `shattered` and `dented`. `shatterPieces` is 2..24 (default 8), `shatterPattern` is 'radial' (small pieces crowded around the impact, the default) or 'uniform', `shatterSpread` adds outward speed in m/s, and `shatterSeed` fixes which pieces so a scene breaks the same way twice. `shatterDepth` (0 by default, 2 at most) lets the PIECES break again when they land: each shard inherits a threshold scaled to its own share of the body, because a chip held to the whole body's threshold can hardly ever be hit hard enough and reads as armour plating. Pieces of pieces come apart into at most four, and those chips do not collide with EACH OTHER (they still land on and hit everything else), which is what keeps a cascade running in real time. The world holds at most 60 shards at once: a break that would go over cuts fewer pieces, or does not happen. The body must be able to move: something bolted to the scenery cannot be hit hard enough to matter.
details.denting_and_piercing:
DENTING. `dentYieldNs` is the blow that leaves a permanent crater; null clears it. `dentDepthPerNs` is metres of depth per newton-second over the yield, `dentRadius` the crater's radius in metres, `dentMaxDepth` a hard cap. A dent is a displacement of vertices, so a PRIMITIVE has nothing to push in — a box is six numbers the solver evaluates, not eight corners. Setting a yield on one CONVERTS it to the mesh it already looked like, and the reply says so with `convertedToMesh`. Name the surface with `geomName` if the body has several. A plane cannot be dented at all; it is infinite in the solver. A plate given a yield is unmarked by anything under it and cratered by anything over, which is the point: the same plate, two blows, two outcomes.

`pierceImpulseNs` is a second, higher limit past which the surface is HOLED rather than dented — the material under the striker is removed. Keep it well clear of the yield, or there is no range in which the thing behaves like a sheet. The crater's width and shape come from the STRIKER (a flat-ended slug leaves a flat-bottomed pit its own width, a ball a spherical cap) and grow wider as well as deeper with the blow, so the depth rate should be set so that typical impulses land well under dentMaxDepth — a rate that reaches the cap just past the yield makes every blow leave an identical mark and mass stop mattering.
details.deform_collision_and_transience:
`deformCollision` makes the damage REAL to the solver instead of only visible: things fall through the holes, and an edge worn away stops holding what it used to. It is off by default because it is genuinely expensive — damage reaches MuJoCo by rebuilding the model, and the surface must also be broken into convex pieces each time, since MuJoCo collides a mesh as its convex hull and a hull fills every crater and every hole straight back in. Expect a hitch per blow. Without it:

DENTS AND HOLES ARE COSMETIC. The contact solver keeps using the undented shape, because feeding a deformed mesh back to it means rebuilding the model and that cannot happen at the rate blows arrive.

All of it is TRANSIENT, like a broken weld: the scene graph still holds the whole body, so physics_get_scene, exports and share links are unchanged, and physics_reset makes it whole and unmarked again. physics_get_breaks reports what has actually come apart or been dented.

tools.physics_set_crumple:
A crumple zone: a joint that is rigid until it is overloaded, and then folds and STAYS folded.

Set on a JOINT, because that is what folds — name it with `jointName`, or the body's first hinge or slider is used. A free or ball joint has no single axis to fold about and is refused.

`crumpleTorqueNm` is the torque past which it gives, in newton-metres; null clears it. `crumpleRangeDeg` is how far it may fold afterwards, in degrees, as [min, max]. `crumpleDampingAfter` is the damping written into the joint at the moment it gives — high, normally, so it settles into its new shape rather than swinging into it; without it a released joint reads as a hinge coming undone rather than as metal taking a set.

It costs almost nothing because it is not a new mechanism: the joint is held still by an ordinary weld equality, and giving way is the same release that shears a handle off a mug.

ONE THING TO WATCH: a joint only folds if something is still loading it after it gives. A post standing straight up gives gravity no lever, so once its base yields it simply goes on standing there. A cantilever — an arm held out sideways, already carrying its own weight — folds the moment its root lets go.

TRANSIENT, like every other kind of damage here: the scene graph is untouched and physics_reset straightens it. physics_get_breaks reports it as a key of the form 'crumple:<jointName>'.
tools.physics_get_breaks:
What has sheared off during this run. Returns `broken` (stable keys: 'weld:<nodeId>-><targetId>' for a weld, 'crumple:<joint>' for a crumple zone, 'member:<nodeId>' for a body with loadStrength that snapped or bent under load, 'join:<blobId>><nodeId>' / 'pin:<blobId>><nodeId>' for a part that came out of a join blob) and `last`, the most recent break with the time and the load it was carrying when it went, plus `cause` for loads: 'pulled', 'sheared', 'bent' or 'buckled'. Nothing breaks in the first 0.25 s while a scene settles; `shattered`, the bodies currently in pieces and how many pieces each is in, with `lastShatter`; and `dented`, each marked surface with how many blows it has taken and the deepest in millimetres.

Breakage never reaches the scene graph, so this is the only way to observe it. An empty list means nothing has broken, not that nothing can.
tools.physics_restore_break: Put a broken weld back. With `key`, restores that one joint where the body is now, without disturbing the rest of the run. With no key, resets the whole simulation, which restores everything.
tools.physics_delete_preset: Delete a custom user physics preset by name.

physics_export_cast.summary: Produce a metal casting pattern (`method`: 'sand' or 'lost-pla'; `metal`: 'aluminium'|'brass'|'bronze'|'silver') for `master_id` and report part volume, cast weight, shrink-scaled pattern, parting height, gating sizes, and undercut share. Pass `out_dir` to write the pattern STL.

details.draft_shrink_and_parting:
Produce a metal casting pattern, as the Mold dialog's Sand and Lost PLA tabs do, and report what the pour needs: part volume, cast weight in the chosen metal, the pattern grown by that metal's shrink, the parting height, the gating sizes, and the share of the part that will not draw from the sand.

What is cast is master_id (a body, or several comma-separated, children included, where they stand), else every body that is not a simulation; unlike the dialog it never follows the UI selection. The reply's molded names what was used (label, ids).

method is 'sand' (default) or 'lost-pla'. metal is one of aluminium, brass, bronze, silver; anything else is refused. draft_deg tapers the printed pattern from the parting plane and leaves the model as it is: 2 by default for sand, so the pattern draws, and 0 for lost PLA, which burns out. If physics_set_cast_prep has put draft in the model already, none is added and summary.draftDeg reports the model's, and the pattern parts where that draft was tapered from whatever partingFromBaseMm says (a warning names both). shrink_percent replaces the metal's own shrink allowance. partingFromBaseMm is a height in millimetres from the base of the part, or 'auto' to let it choose. On a part that is symmetric about its own mid-height, parting at the base makes the entire lower half re-entrant, so 'auto' is worth taking.

Pass out_dir to have the pattern STL written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file sizes only: the mesh itself is never returned into the conversation.

physics_make_pour_box.summary: Make a printed pour box (mother mold: base plate with groove, sleeve, and optional hole pin) for casting a silicone mold of `body_id`. NOTE: a pour-box mold is inverted when used (the face the master stands on becomes the open pour face, unless `hole='pour'`). Key args: `body_id`, `shape` ('fit'|'round'|'box'), `hole` ('none'|'wick'|'pour'|'fixing'), `silicone` ('platinum'|'tin'), `apply` (true adds static bodies + fill line to scene), `out_dir`.

details.orientation_and_inversion: Make a printed pour box (mother mold) for casting a silicone mold of a master, the same as the Mold dialog's Silicone tab: a base plate the master stands on with a groove round it, a sleeve that drops into the groove and holds the silicone, and optionally a printed pin that leaves a hole through the silicone, from a point on the master's top to 1 mm above the fill line. The master is taken as it stands (poured from above, standing on its lowest point). A pour-box mold is used the other way up from how it was made: the face the master stands on becomes the silicone's open pour face, and the master's top (where a wick or fixing hole is) is at the bottom of the mold while the casting is poured. Only a pour hole changes that: the mold is then poured through the hole the way it was made, standing on the base. So for a part with a right way up (text, a logo, a face, relief art), settle which end of the finished casting is its top before building the master, and ask the user if it isn't clear. Art meant to read upright with the pour face as the casting's top goes on the master upside down.
details.parameters: body_id is the master (comma-separated for several bodies; defaults to every body that is not a simulation or a pour box, never the UI selection). cover_mm (8) is the silicone round the sides and over the top; wall_mm (2.4) the sleeve wall; clearance_mm (0.2) the gap each side of the sleeve in its groove; base_mm (6) and groove_mm (3) the plate and the groove's depth; freeboard_mm (2) the sleeve above the fill line. shape is 'fit' (default: the master's outline grown by the cover, least silicone), 'round' or 'box'. hole is 'wick', 'pour' or 'fixing' (or 'none', the default): a wick or fixing hole is plugged during the pour, a pour hole is poured through. hole_dia_mm defaults by purpose (wick 2.5, pour 8, fixing 3; a pour hole under 6 mm is refused when simulated); hole_at_mm is a point [x, y] in plan, world mm, on the master's top (default its highest point), refused when nothing of the master is under it. The older pin=true and pin_dia_mm still make a wick hole. silicone is 'platinum' (1.08 g/cm3, 1:1) or 'tin' (1.15 g/cm3, 10:1).
details.reply_and_simulation: Returns fillHeightMm (above the base, where the master stands), fillZMm, pourDepthMm (the fill as physics_add_simulation kind mold_cast measures it, from the groove floor; a pour into the box uses it by default), sleeveHeightMm, grooveMm (as built: no deeper than the base less 1 mm, with a warning when that is shallower than asked), the sleeve and base footprints, siliconeMm3, siliconeG and partAG/partBG to weigh out, and with a hole its purpose and diaMm and holeTopMm, where it comes out. apply=true adds the base and sleeve to the scene as static bodies and a hole's pin as a rigid child of the master (added.holePinId) (one undo step, a note card section), and leaves master, base and sleeve selected (the reply's selected), as the Mold dialog does.
