The base and sleeve carry the fill line, so physics_add_simulation kind mold_cast with body_id '<master>,<base>,<sleeve>' casts the silicone from the top to that line with no fill_mm needed (the reply's fillFrom says so); a later mold or pour box leaves them out. If the master is moved within its box, or the box is turned, pass fill_mm. Pass out_dir to have pour-base.stl and pour-sleeve.stl written there, and pour-<purpose>-pin.stl for a hole's pin. A pour hole under 6 mm, or a wick or fixing hole too big to plug, comes back as a warning.

physics_set_cast_prep.summary: Prepare every part in the scene for casting in-model: chamfers outside edges, fillets inside corners, and for `method='sand'` bakes `draft_deg` (default 2°, `draft_mode` 'add'|'remove') away from `parting_from_base_mm`. Pass `off=true` to restore originals or `bake=true` to keep prepared shapes permanently.

details.draft_edges_and_options:
Prepare every part in the scene for casting, in the model itself, the same as the Prepare for Casting switch under Mold > Sand or Lost PLA > Advanced. For draft on the printed pattern alone, leaving the model as it is, use physics_export_cast's draft_deg instead. Outside edges are chamfered and inside corners filleted (fillet 1.5x the chamfer); for method 'sand' every wall is also given draft away from the parting plane, and the parting face's edges stay sharp. Draft is baked into the parts as meshes, with the originals kept so that off=true restores them; while draft is on, edits to any body are refused with an error naming this tool. Edges go on as ordinary roundings, which physics_get_edges and physics_round_edges see.

method is 'sand' (default) or 'lost-pla' (edges only: a burnt-out pattern needs no draft). draft_deg defaults to 2, draft_mode is 'add' (walls grow toward the parting line, nothing undersize; default) or 'remove'. edges defaults to true; edge_size_mm is the outside chamfer, omitted to size it from each part. parting_from_base_mm as for physics_export_cast. Calling it again re-applies from the originals, so settings never stack. off=true switches it off (bodies changed since prep are left as they are and named); bake=true keeps the prepared shapes and forgets the originals.

Returns how many parts were treated, the largest chamfer and fillet used, edges too short to break, and parts skipped with the reason.

physics_set_reference_image.summary:
Pin a picture in the viewport to model from: a photo of the thing being copied, a drawing, a sketch. It stands in the plane of a drawing view and shows in the viewport and in physics_get_screenshot, so you can line the model up against it and compare the two in one frame. It is only drawn: it takes no part in the physics, any export, the DFM checks or selection. It is saved, shared and undone with the scene.

To add one, pass `path`, an image file on this machine (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF or BMP), read by the server like physics_import_stl's path. It is stored cut down to 1600 px on its long side. To change one, pass the `imageId` an earlier call returned (as `id`), with only the fields to change. `remove: true` with an `imageId` takes that one off; `clear: true` takes them all off.

`plane` is 'front' (XZ facing -Y, default), 'side' (YZ facing +X), or 'top' (XY facing +Z). `center` is [x,y,z] in world metres; `width` or `height` in metres sets scale; `opacity` 0..1 (default 0.5); `overlay` default true.

details.planes_and_scaling:
plane is 'front' (the XZ plane, facing -Y: what physics_set_camera's 'front' preset looks at; the default), 'side' (YZ, facing +X: the 'side' preset) or 'top' (XY, facing up: 'topDown'). The picture reads the right way round from that view. center is the middle of the picture, [x, y, z] in world metres. width is its width in metres; give height instead to size it by its height, and the other follows from the picture's own proportions. With neither, a new picture comes in as wide as the scene's contents and centred on them, standing on the floor (lying on it for 'top').

TO SCALE A PHOTO TO A MODEL, measure in pixels: if a part D mm across spans p pixels of an image W pixels wide, the whole picture is width = W / p x D mm, and its center sits where that part's middle is, offset by the part's distance from the image's middle at the same scale. opacity is 0..1 (default 0.5). overlay (default true) draws the picture over the model so it can be traced; false lets the model hide it. hidden: true keeps it without drawing it.

Returns the picture's id, plane, center, widthMm, heightMm, opacity and overlay, and `referenceImages`: every picture in the scene. physics_get_scene_summary lists them too.

physics_split_for_print.summary: Cut `body_id` (plus optional `with_ids`) into sections that each fit the 3D printer bed (`bed_mm`), oriented for minimum support, with alignment joinery (`joinery`: 'dowel' | 'peg' | 'none'). Pass `apply=true` to replace the body with its split sections and exact pin/socket colliders, or `test_assembly=true` to verify assembly in MuJoCo at print fidelity.

details.joinery_and_parameters:
Cut a body into sections that each fit the 3D printer's bed, the same as the Split for Print dialog (bottom bar, FDM). Each section is turned to whichever way up needs the least support, and the cut faces get joinery: 'dowel' (default) bores matching blind holes in both faces for bought dowels; 'peg' prints a chamfered peg on one face and a hole in the other, the peg going on whichever side's print pose minds it least; 'none' leaves plain faces to glue. Pins are placed as deep in each shared face as they fit, two per face when it is wide enough (so the joint cannot turn), and only where both sections are solid behind the face to the hole's bottom plus min_wall_mm; none when there is no such room (a warning names it). A peg joint where a peg would stand either section off the bed gets holes both sides for a loose dowel instead (a warning says so).

body_id defaults to the selection. with_ids lists more bodies to split together with it as one part (a box and its lid, say), in body_id's frame; on apply they are replaced by the sections too. Bodies rigidly attached under any of them (children with no joint) are included automatically. bed_mm is [width, depth, height] and defaults to the bed set in the bottom bar (256 cube unless changed). margin_mm (5) is kept clear round the bed edge; both are recorded on the sections, and physics_export_print plates them inside that margin. max_sections (64) caps the count. diameter_mm (6), length_mm (20, the whole dowel; a peg stands half of it proud), clearance_mm (0.2, on the diameter) and min_wall_mm (2) shape the joinery. The overhang limit comes from the loaded filament.
details.verification_and_apply: Without apply it only reports: each section's printed size, support area, pose (up vector and spin), volume (mm3) and hole/peg count; the cuts (normal and offset, body frame); the joints between sections; and exact Manifold checks (overlap between printed sections, mm3; how far the sections differ from the original; pins without a partner). test_assembly=true also puts the sections back together in MuJoCo at print fidelity, one cut at a time: dowels dropped into their holes, then each side dropped onto the other under gravity, then pushed and twisted. Each stage reports gapMm (how far short of its seat it came to rest; about a pin length means a pin missed its hole), playMm and twistDeg ('unbounded' for a plain cut, which glue holds), rotates (a single pin), and notes. apply=true replaces the body with its sections: the first keeps the body's id, the others are new siblings named <name>_part2, _part3..., all in place, in the part's colour with its paint and other geoms' colours carried on as paint, carrying printPose (which the 3MF export uses to lay them out on the bed) and exact pin/socket colliders. Jointed or bought-in bodies hung off the part or off a body taken into it are kept, re-hung from the section they sit in; welds and connects to any of them go to that section. A body that fits whole is not rebuilt: apply only records its printPose. placement='beside' keeps the original and puts the sections next to it along +X; center_origin=true puts each section's origin at its middle. One undo step.

physics_timber_breakdown.summary:
Break a solid, cabinet or box, or framed furniture (table, chair, flower stand), into wooden parts you can cut on a saw: a cut list with joinery, hardware and a glue-up guide. Optional CNC setups for the pockets.

`mode`: 'auto' (default; frame when it finds legs and rails, planks otherwise) | 'planks' | 'frame'. Targets `body_id` plus `with_ids`, or the selection, or the whole scene.

`clearance_mm` is the fit allowance for both. `apply: true` splits the body into one scene body per part (`placement`: 'replace' | 'beside').

details.planks_and_frame_options:
- PLANKS (box / shell): `hollow_interior` (true: a 6-wall shell of `wall_thickness_mm`, 18; false: solid layers of `board_thickness_mm`, 18). Walls wider than `max_board_width_mm` (180) or longer than `max_board_length_mm` (1200) split along the grain. `joint_type`: 'glue' (flush, no dowels) | 'butt' (with alignment dowels, `dowel_dia_mm` 8, `dowel_length_mm` 30; 0 for none) | 'rabbet' | 'miter' | 'finger' (`finger_width_mm` 24). Returns every plank's size and grain, a lay-flat sheet and a BOM.
- FRAME (legs, rails, top): `joint_mode`: 'mortise_tenon' (default) | 'dowel' | 'dado' | 'glue' (butt joints glued flush, no joinery, no CNC). `tenon_length_mm`, `shoulder_mm`, `tenon_corner_fit` ('dogbone' | 'round_tenon' | 'chisel_square'), `tenon_cut_method` ('bandsaw' | 'cnc'), `edge_profile` ('roundover' | 'chamfer' | 'square') with `edge_radius_mm`, `tabletop_clips` (Z-clip slots in the aprons, M&T and dado only). Wide tops split at `max_board_width_mm`. Returns parts with cut sizes and F1/F2 reference faces, joints, stock bars (`stock_length_mm`, 1800), hardware, a build guide, and CNC setups for the mortises sized to `cnc_bed_mm` [X, Y, Z] (default: the CNC bed in Machine Setup). Pass `include_gcode: true` to get each setup's G-code.

physics_export_machining.summary:
Produce a three-axis CNC program for the whole scene and report what the job needs: the stock it wants, the part size and volume, how much of the part no setup can reach, how many holding tabs were placed, the cut distance and the estimated time, plus one G-code program per setup.

Key args: `sides` (1 or 2) or `setups` ('auto' or face list like '+z,+x,-x' for multi-face indexing), `toolDiaMm`, `finishingToolType` ('flat'|'ball_nose'|'v_bit'), `material` ('aluminium'|'hardwood'|'softwood'|'plywood'|'acrylic'|'foam'), and optional `out_dir` to write the .nc files. Uses the bench stock from physics_set_environment.

details.stock_and_cutters:
sides is 1 or 2. The stock is the bench board (set it with physics_set_environment), as in the dialog: refused, with the size the part needs, when it cannot hold the part; used as it is, the part centred, when it is about the size the part wants; and when it is much bigger, or a side setup needs the block flush with the part, the job is planned on the smaller block and summary.boardPrep says what to cut the board down to first. Per-call stock sizes are refused. toolDiaMm sets both the roughing and the finishing cutter. finishingToolType is the finishing cutter's shape: flat (the default), ball_nose or v_bit. Flat leaves walls square and flats flat, which suits a part made of faces and pockets; a ball nose is what makes a curved surface smooth — a dome, a dish, a sculpted face — where a flat end mill leaves a staircase, at the cost of a radius in every inside corner. Roughing is always a flat end mill. material drives the feeds and speeds: aluminium, hardwood, softwood, plywood, acrylic, foam. The part is cut at its modelled size, millimetre for millimetre, as in the dialog; scale_percent is refused. To cut it bigger or smaller, resize it in the scene. Over 1 m any way is refused with the scale that fits.

Pass out_dir to have the .nc files written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file sizes only.

It always surfaces the whole part before it profiles it. For something flat that only needs its outline cut — a stencil, a gasket — that is most of the quoted time and none of the useful work.
details.multi_face_setups: SETUPS FROM ANY FACE: setups 'auto' plans as many setups as the part needs instead of sides: it looks at the part from all six faces of the block with the finishing cutter (reaching tool_stickout_mm, or 8 diameters), gives each bit of material to the face it is shallowest under, and keeps the fewest setups that reach the part (it may also lay the part another way up: summary.upChosen). Use it for anything a top-down cut leaves solid: a slot that leans back, the hole in an upright letter, a hook. setups may also be a list of faces, '+z,+x,-x', named as the block stands for setup 1 (+z top, -y front, -x left end). clearance_mm is the room under the spindle; a setup that would stand the block taller than it is left out. The summary then has plan (one line), setups (per setup: face, faceUp, standingHeightMm, depthMm, lengthOverDia, estimatedTimeSeconds, clearedMm3, skinMm left for the turn's error, locate, datum, instructions; each datum touch has wallMm, 0 for a sawn face or the size of the datum notch the first setup cut in a waste corner, and the work position for it is wallMm minus the bit's radius, touched from inside the notch), remaining (what no face reaches and where; a fillet in corners sharper than the cutter is normal), redesignHint, and dropped faces with the reason. Files are machining-setup-<n>-<face>.nc. Before planning extra setups, prefer a redesign the hint names (make the leaning face vertical): one setup is always cheaper. Only setup 1 can be run over MCP; every later setup is turned and zeroed by the operator at the machine, and the machine refuses it otherwise.

physics_export_relief.summary:
Plan a relief carve of the scene — the model carved into the top of a board, as the Relief Carve dialog does it — and report how the job splits: the roughing cutter, strategy, layer count and its share of the time, the finishing cutter and pass count, the total estimate, and the 1-based line of the tool change.

Uses the Relief Carve dialog's last plan or bench stock by default. Key args: `vertical_scale_mode` ('auto'|'model'|'fill'|'proportional'), `fit_mode` ('fit'|'actual'), `background_mode` ('auto'|'carve'|'skip'), `roughingToolDiaMm`, `finishingToolDiaMm`, `finishingToolType` ('flat'|'ball_nose'|'v_bit'), `carveDepthMm`, `material`, and `out_dir`.

details.height_and_scale_modes:
By default it uses exactly the settings the Relief Carve dialog last planned with this session — the stock, fit, depth, cutters and any feed typed over — so it reproduces the program the operator would send; optionsFrom says which. If the dialog has not been opened, it starts from the scene's own carve settings and the bench's stock and material.

HEIGHT AND SIZE: by default (vertical_scale_mode 'auto') a model that fits the stock is cut AS MODELLED — 1:1 in X, Y and Z, centred, as deep as the lowest point a cutter coming straight down can see — so a tray, sign or plate with a pattern already on its face needs no depth or scale set at all; carveDepthMm is ignored and summary.heightMode says 'model'. A model bigger than the stock (footprint, or deeper than the stock less 1 mm) falls back to 'fill' (its height stretched onto carveDepthMm, plan fitted to the stock) and a warning says so. Force one with vertical_scale_mode 'model', 'fill' or 'proportional' (with vertical_exaggeration); fit_mode 'fit' (to the stock) or 'actual' (its modelled size, cropped at the stock's edge) sets the plan scale for fill/proportional; scale_percent is refused: resize the model in the scene instead; background_mode 'auto' (leave the stock round a true-size model, carve it otherwise), 'carve' or 'skip'. summary.undercut reports material hidden under an overhang (a leaning slot, a lip) that a 3-axis cut leaves solid: areaMm2, volumeMm3, maxMm, boundsMm. A true-size cut also says it in warnings. Set the bench stock to the real board first (stock_width_mm etc.).
details.cutter_options_and_undercuts:
Anything passed is laid on top: roughingToolDiaMm, finishingToolDiaMm, finishingToolType (flat, ball_nose or v_bit), carveDepthMm, material, roughingStrategy (adaptive or raster), roughingEnabled, stockWidthMm, stockDepthMm, stockThicknessMm. Changing a cutter, the material or the depth works the feeds and speeds out again for it. A probed bed is not applied.

Pass out_dir to have relief-carve.nc written there. Without it you get the numbers and the file size only.

An undercut as modelled is not something relief can cut: relief is a single face. Machine it as a part instead: physics_export_machining with setups 'auto' and the same board and cutters stands the block on the faces that reach under the overhang. A feature that runs off the model's edge below the top face (a groove open at both ends) is cut out past the board edge by half a millimetre plus the cutter's radius, and a warning names the edges: keep clamps clear of them.

physics_export_print.summary:
Export the scene, or chosen bodies, as a print file: STL or 3MF, the toolbar's Export STL / Export 3MF without the dialog. ids: body ids or names, each with every body fixed below it; omitted, every body. format 'stl' (default) or '3mf'. STL carries no colour; a 3MF carries each body's colours, materials and paint as filaments. Parts come out at TRUE SIZE in millimetres, Z-up, the set centred on the origin and standing on z = 0, keeping their places relative to each other; there is no rescale prompt, so to print at another size scale the bodies first. Bought-in hardware (bearings, screws, nuts from physics_add_hardware) and simulated cuts are left out; booleans, cuts and surface patterns (lettering included) are in. separate=true writes one file per body, a split section's stood the way it prints.

Pass out_dir to have the files written there; the reply gives each one's path. Without it you get each part's triangles and sizeMm and the file sizes only: the mesh is never returned into the conversation.

Before handing a file over, read `watertight` on every mesh geom in physics_get_scene_summary: a slicer refuses or mangles a mesh that is not closed, and the viewport will not show it.

details.colour_and_material: A 3MF carries colour and material: each body is one object, and its geoms are grouped by colour into volumes, each volume set to its own filament (Bambu Studio / OrcaSlicer model_settings.config, PrusaSlicer's config too), so a part whose inside is a different material from its outside — a core, a liner, an insert — gives each its own geom with its own rgba. Paint is carried as well, on the painted surface, stamped with the filament it prints in; filaments: how many the printer has (default 5, an AMS and the external spool; 9 for two AMS; up to 32), further colours snapping to the nearest; the reply's summary.filaments lists each file's filaments (number, sRGB hex, triangles), which is what to load in which slot. The file names no filament type: Bambu Studio fills slots it adds with a copy of the project's last filament preset, so say which material goes in each slot when handing the file over. STL carries no colour.
details.split_sections: A 3MF of a scene with sections made by physics_split_for_print (apply=true) is laid out on the print bed: each section stood the way it prints, every other chosen body as it stands, all with their colours and paint, as the 3MF button offers to; plate=true lays out bodies with no sections too, plate=false exports everything where it stands instead. The plate keeps to the margin the sections were split with (margin_mm overrides) and is the bottom bar's bed unless bed_mm ([width, depth, height]) is given; a warning says when that is not the bed the sections were split for. With separate=true each body gets a file of its own, laid on the bed the same way.

physics_add_simulation.summary:
Cut a machining, carving, slicing, mold, sheet, tube or timber job back out and add what is left to the scene as a body, to look at, measure and set against the model before any material is spent. The same as the Add Simulation button in the dialogs.

kind picks the job: 'relief' (physics_export_relief's program), 'machining' (physics_export_machining's setups; optional stage=0..k|'all'), 'laser' or 'contour' (extruded panels/layers), 'mold' (adds generated 3D mold), 'mold_cast' (simulates cast piece via method='rigid'|'silicone'|'sand'|'lost-pla' or into an existing mold body_id), 'sheet' (folds sheet-unfold net along bend lines), 'tube' (pipe frame from cut list), or 'timber' (milled mortise/tenon or dado frame from physics_timber_breakdown).

placement 'beside' (the default) stands the part at the size it comes off the machine beside the model, past any earlier simulation; 'overlay' undoes the fit (scale, and a relief's vertical exaggeration) and lays it over the model, where an over-cut or a missed area is plain.

The body is static and collides with nothing, gets a section on the scene's note card, and is left out of every later export, so it never changes the next plan. Delete it like any body. A big relief takes a few seconds.

details.relief_machining_mold_basics:
kind picks the job: relief (the program physics_export_relief would hand over, with the same options — vertical_scale_mode, fit_mode and background_mode too and the Relief Carve dialog's last plan by default), machining (physics_export_machining's, with the same stock and the same defaults, sides 1, aluminium and a 3 mm flat, unless told otherwise; with sides 2 side B is turned over as the operator turns it, so holes, tabs and any step at the seam show), laser or contour (the panels or the stacked layers, extruded at material_thickness_mm, which for contour defaults to the bench stock's thickness; with machine='router' they are laid out as the router dialog lays them out, no kerf and dogbone corners for bit_dia_mm, every inside corner keeps the bit's radius and a slot narrower than bit_dia_mm is never cut), mold (adds the generated 3D mold to the scene), or mold_cast (simulates what would be cast from a mold — either an existing mold body via body_id, as the Cast button pours into the selection, or a newly made mold, as the Mold dialog's Rigid tab simulates it — and adds the cast body to the scene; mold_type is 'auto' when not given (a one-part open mold when that keeps the part as well as two halves would, otherwise a two-part clamshell), or 'clamshell' or 'open' to insist; either way the mold opens along whichever of the part's axes fills in the least of it, so an upright bust splits front to back, and the reply names the type and direction it used (moldType, pullDirection, setupNote); trim_channels trims sprue/vent runner stubs).

For kind mold, and mold_cast without body_id, the new mold is of master_id (a body, or several comma-separated), else every body that is not a simulation (never the UI selection), and the reply's molded names what was used.

Returns the body's id and name and the volumes: for relief, what the program removes and how many rapid moves cut material (anything but 0 is a fault in the program); for machining, the part's volume over its footprint against the model's (partVsModel, tabs included); for contour, the stack against the model stretched the same way (stackVsModel); for mold or mold_cast, the mold/cast dimensions, cavity depth, and volume.
details.sheet_tube_timber:
kind 'sheet' folds the net the Sheet Unfold dialog would hand over (sheet_mode 'papercraft' (default), 'sheet_metal' or 'soft_goods'; material_thickness_mm (default 1.5), bend_radius_mm (1.5), k_factor (0.44), scale_factor (1)) back up along its own fold lines: each bend's arc is the neutral length (R + K T) x angle centred on the file's bend line, the rest of the drawn zone left flat, so a wrong allowance or setback shows as a flange standing off the model. The model is taken as the part's outside. The reply's maxDeviationMm and meanDeviationMm are how far, fitted to the model, a model corner lies off its folded face or a cut edge off its folded line: under 0.05 the net is right. Glue tabs are left off.

kind 'tube' makes the pipe frame from its cut list (the Pipes dialog's, for the scene's pipes; pipe_standard_id, default 'pvc_sch40_3_4'): every tube cut to length and pushed home against its start hub's shoulder. The reply's maxGapMm and worstJoint are how far a tube's far end is short of (+) or past (-) the far hub's shoulder, and clashes the hubs where two tubes' ends run into each other.

kind 'timber' makes the frame physics_timber_breakdown plans (body_id, with_ids, joint_mode 'mortise_tenon' or 'dado', cutter_dia_mm, tenon_length_mm, shoulder_mm, clearance_mm): each member its finished blank with its tenons sawn on, every CNC window's program milled in the frame the part really sits in on the bed, then each tenon pushed into its mortise as milled. The reply's largestShoulderGapMm and worstJoint are a shoulder standing off the face because its tenon bottomed or missed the pocket (0 when every tenon goes home), tooTight the tenons wider than their pocket, mostOffCentreMm how far a pocket is off its tenon, setupFaults any window whose setup sheet the part cannot be put on as written, and mortisesByHand those on parts too big for the CNC, which are not simulated. It takes a few seconds.
details.machining_stages_and_pouring: With setups 'auto' (or a list of faces) a machining simulation cuts every setup in its own frame and keeps what all of them leave, so a slot cut from the block's ends shows as cut. One setup, or the top and the flip, are simulated as before. STEP BY STEP: for kind machining, stage adds one step of the job instead of the finished part: 0 is the stock as it goes on the machine (only the registration pin holes bored), k the block after setups 1 to k, stood as the block stands on the bed for setup k (so a turned block shows turned); 'all' adds every step not yet in the scene, in order, left to right. Steps are always placed beside. The reply lists each step's stage, title, id, volumeMm3, removedMm3 and rapidMovesThatCut, and stages (the stock plus one per setup). A re-plan is a new set of steps. With body_id, pour_direction ('+z', '-z', '+x', '-x', '+y', '-y'; default the best side) and fill_mm (default: to the rim) set the side poured from and how deep; a pour into a master and its pour box from physics_make_pour_box, standing upright, defaults to the top and to the box's fill line (fillFrom: 'pour box' in the reply); a box from an older version has no fill line and fills to the rim. Passing cast_material records it on the cast, and a pour into a cast made of silicone refuses a silicone cast_material, which would stick to it. A mold_cast without body_id (any method) stands the finished piece the way the master stands, and the reply's deviationMm ({maxMm, meanMm}) is how far its surface strays from the master's, both ways. A pour into an existing mold (body_id) is set as it came out of that mold, so its orientation says nothing about which way up the casting is meant to be: before judging how text or art reads, turn it (physics_update_object quat) the way it will actually stand.
details.one_click_chains: ONE CLICK TO THE FINISHED PIECE: for kind mold_cast, method (not with body_id, which pours into a mold already there; an unknown method is refused) picks the Mold dialog tab whose chain runs. 'rigid' (default): a printed mold is made and poured, as before. 'silicone': a pour box round the master, silicone poured to its fill line (silicone: 'platinum' default or 'tin'; hole, hole_dia_mm and hole_at_mm as physics_make_pour_box takes them; the box the one physics_make_pour_box apply=true put round the master, else one at default sizes; pourBoxFrom says which), the silicone mold taken off, turned over, vented where air would be trapped, and cast_material (default epoxy; no metals, no silicones) poured in through the master's foot. It refuses a foot with no part 6 mm across (thin legs or a blade count as narrow), pointing to the rigid mold with dissolvable_liner or a pour hole; with a pour hole from physics_make_pour_box's hole='pour' it is poured through the hole the way it was made instead (pouredThrough). Adds the piece and the silicone mold (left selected); the reply has siliconeMold {id, name, vents, silicone grams and A/B}. 'sand' or 'lost-pla': the printed pattern in the smallest flask that holds it (sand: 25 mm round the sides and below; lost PLA: the investment flask), filled round, the pattern taken away, cast_material (a metal, default aluminium) poured down the sprue; draft_deg (sand 2, lost PLA 0) and shrink_percent as for physics_export_cast; parting, sprue, riser and gating are those last planned for the method (Mold dialog or physics_export_cast), else defaults, as optionsFrom says. Adds the piece as the pour reached it, cut off its gating and shrunk to size: a body the gating does not reach is left out. The reply has flask {shape, sizeMm}, sandG or investmentPowderG, filledShare (the share of the part the metal reaches from the sprue; below 0.97 a warning says what was left out; null when gated by hand, which is not poured) and pourWeightG, what to melt: the part, the gating and a margin, as physics_export_cast's pourWeightG. The flask is illustrative: a real one is often bigger, which changes only the sand or investment. Every chain's reply has volumeMm3, weightG, mixG where the material is mixed, gating {volumeMm3, weightG} for metal (the gating and pour margin, cut off and remelted), deviationMm and materialNotes. A wrong cast_material for the method is refused with the ones that fit.
details.dissolvable_liner: For kind mold, dissolvable_liner=true prints the mold as a PLA shell with a dissolvable PVA liner, for a two-filament printer: every undercut is kept, the shell lifts straight off along the pull, and the PVA left on the casting dissolves in warm water. liner_skin_mm (1.2) is the PVA between the casting and the PLA. cast_material is 'epoxy' (the default), 'polyurethane', 'platinum' or 'tin' (silicones; 'silicone' means platinum), 'wax', 'chocolate', 'water', 'plaster', 'concrete' or 'jesmonite'; with a liner the water-based ones are refused, because they dissolve PVA while they cure. Metals are always refused: they go in sand or investment (physics_export_cast). For mold_cast with body_id, passing cast_material adds the pour's weightG, mixG (the parts to weigh out, where it is mixed) and materialNotes to the reply. The reply adds liner: pvaGrams, plaGrams, pvaVolumeMm3, castVolumeMl, thickestPvaMm, dissolveHours (a rough guide, at about 1 mm an hour) and the steps to use it; files names the two-material 3MF (PLA shell on filament 1, PVA liner on filament 2, set for Bambu Studio/OrcaSlicer and PrusaSlicer), written to out_dir when one is given.
details.rigid_mold_draft: For kind mold and the rigid mold_cast, draft_deg tapers the cavity walls (default the Mold dialog's last setting, else 0), with dissolvable_liner and allow_undercuts too. draft_mode says which way: 'remove' (default) keeps the opening's size and takes depth x tan(angle) off the casting at the bottom of each wall, so a thin wall can all but vanish (1 degree over 111 mm is 1.9 mm a side); 'add' keeps the bottom's size and puts the taper on, widening the opening, so nothing is undersize; 'centre' pivots each wall about its mid-height. The reply's minDraftDeg is the taper the cavity has. An 'add' or 'centre' draft that reaches the mold's side wall is warned about: raise the wall margin.

physics_get_camera.summary: Return the 3D viewport camera's live `position` and `target` in MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z], active `preset`, `dims` (whether the Dims overlay is on), and `dimensions` (every drawn measurement in an orthographic drawing view with `dims: true`).

details.dimensions_format: Return the 3D viewport camera's current position and look-at target, both in MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z] (same convention as every other pos field). Reflects the LIVE view, including manual orbiting/panning a human has done in the browser since the last physics_set_camera call or preset change. Call this before a screenshot if you're not sure what's currently framed, or after asking the user to orbit to a specific view themselves. Returns position and target in MuJoCo world space, plus which preset is active. Also returns dims (whether the Dims overlay is on) and dimensions: what it is drawing right now, one entry per figure ({body, kind:'linear'|'diameter'|'radius'|'angle'|'location'|'gear', direction:'width'|'height', row:'chain'|'overall', count, sides, from, sharedWith, label, lines, valueMm or valueDeg}). Sizes are true sizes along the body's own axes, even when it is turned or tilted; With the viewport's Section button on, the figures are of the cut face of a plane square to the view (depths, wall thicknesses, a round floor's radius), not of the outside; 'radius' is a rounded corner or fillet seen square on (count: how many equal ones); 'diameter' with sides is a regular polygonal hole (6 for a hex), valueMm across its flats, labelled like 'hex 5 A/F', and an arc of more than half a circle (a D-shaft bore) is a 'diameter'; 'gear' is the gear data a generated gear, rack or GT2 pulley was cut to, one entry per part with `lines` as the drawing prints them (teeth, module, pressure angle, profile shift x, pitch/tip/root diameters d/da/df, backlash; a rack's pitch p; a pulley's pitch diameter PD and outside diameter OD), given in every view, with the pitch circle drawn when the gear is seen end on; a chain link labelled like '3× 42' stands for count equal steps, valueMm one step; 'angle' is its long axis against the sheet's horizontal or vertical, or a slanted edge's angle from the nearer of them (a draft, a dovetail flank, a gusset; count: how many equal ones), a chamfer labelled like '5 × 45°'; 'location' is its origin from its parent body's origin (`from`, or 'origin'). A figure two bodies share at the same place (walls whose faces line up) is listed once, the other bodies named in sharedWith — empty in perspective, with Dims off, or once the camera is orbited off the view's axis.

physics_get_history.summary: Return simulation telemetry history (sampled every 10 steps, up to 5000 frames held; default returns at most 200 evenly strided frames). Filter with `since_time`, `last`, `stride`, `max_frames`, `bodies` (names or ids), and `include` (['bodies','joints','contacts','aero']). Use `physics_get_telemetry` for just the latest single frame.

details.frame_shape_and_filters:
Return the simulation telemetry history, sampled every 10 physics steps (up to 5000 frames held). Reply: { total, returned, stride, frames }, where each frame has time, bodies: { id: { pos, vel, angvel, quat, xfrc_applied } } (pos: the body origin in the world, m; vel: the world-frame velocity of that same point, m/s; angvel: the body's angular velocity in the WORLD frame, rad/s; bodies and joints are read at the same instant, the end of the step), joints: { name: { body, pos, vel, qfrc_applied, ctrl?, actuatorForce?, clutchTorque? } } (hinge/slide: numbers; free: pos [x,y,z,qw,qx,qy,qz], vel [vx,vy,vz,wx,wy,wz]; ball: pos [qw,qx,qy,qz], vel [wx,wy,wz]; angular rates of free/ball joints in the body frame. A hinge/slide with an actuator adds ctrl, its control value, and actuatorForce, the actuators' force on the joint in N or N*m (MuJoCo's qfrc_actuator); qfrc_applied shows only api.applyJointForce, never an actuator's effort; a torque-limited velocity motor, which drives its joint through a slip clutch from a hidden driver, reports the driver's ctrl and actuatorForce (the motor's effort) and adds clutchTorque, what the clutch puts on the joint: the effort while it holds, forceLimit while it slips), contacts: [{ geom1, geom2, dist, body1, body2 }] (body ids; 'world' for the floor and other world geoms) and aeroDiagnostics. The history is one continuous run: a build that starts over from t = 0 (a new scene, a preset, Reset, an undo, a structural edit) clears it and records the opening frame; an edit made mid-play that keeps the simulation running keeps it.

BY DEFAULT YOU GET AT MOST 200 FRAMES spread evenly across the whole history (stride raised to fit; the newest frame is always included). A full buffer is ~14 MB, so narrow it rather than lifting the cap:
- since_time: only frames at or after this sim time (s).
- last: only the newest N recorded frames.
- stride: keep every kth frame (counted back from the newest).
- max_frames: cap on frames returned (default 200; 0 = no cap, the whole window).
- bodies: only these bodies (names or ids): their entries in bodies, their joints in joints, and only the contacts one of them is in. An entry matching no body is named in `warning`.
- include: which sections to return, any of ['bodies','joints','contacts','aero'] (default all).

Filters apply in that order: since_time, then last, then stride/max_frames. Use physics_get_telemetry for just the latest frame.

tools.physics_get_lattice:
Read a lattice body back: every face, as the corners it is made of, in millimetres in the cage's frame (see physics_create_lattice; `cageOriginMm` converts to the body frame joints use).

Faces come back as coordinates rather than as indices into a vertex list, so a face from this reply can be handed straight to physics_lattice_extrude or physics_lattice_delete_faces. Each face also reports which way it faces ('+z', '-x', ...), which tells an outward face from one drawn from the wrong side.

Also returns the counts, the bounds and size in millimetres, and `watertight`. Call it before every edit that names an existing face: a corner that is 0.05 mm out is not that corner, and the edit will be refused.
tools.physics_get_note_cards: Return the current array of note card overlays. Each card has { id, markdown, minimized, x, y }.

physics_get_object.summary:
Return a single object by ID from the physics scene graph with large mesh arrays stripped. CONVEX PIECES ARE COUNTED, NOT LISTED: a body that collides as convex pieces carries `collidesAs` ('N convex pieces') and `colliderGeoms` (the count), a split part's exact pin and socket colliders `exactColliders` { pins, sockets }, and the generated `csgScad` of a boolean is left out; pass full: true for every piece and the SCAD (four hollow links of 40 pieces each came to 46 KB listed, under 2 KB counted). Every body, nested ones included, carries `worldPos` (world frame, m) and `worldPosSource`: 'simulation' (the latest frame of a model built from the body as it stands) or 'authored' (its parents' poses composed).

EVERY MESH GEOM IS CHECKED AND THE RESULT IS IN THE REPLY. Alongside vertCount, faceCount and bbox, a mesh carries `watertight`, and when it is not: `boundaryEdges` (edges used by one triangle instead of two), `nonManifoldEdges`, `degenerateTriangles` and `windingInverted`. A closed, outward-wound mesh that passes through itself (a fold) carries `weighedByHull: true` and a note: MuJoCo could not integrate its real inertia, so it is weighed by its convex hull until the surface is fixed. A mesh that is not watertight draws perfectly and cannot be printed, cast or machined, so read it before you rely on the shape — this is the same guard physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt have always given you, extended to meshes built by hand or imported.

MESH PAGES: pass geom (and offset, limit) for that geom's triangles, a page at a time, in world metres.

details.mesh_pages: geom names one of the body's geoms as drawn (a body with holes gives its evaluated solid); with a single geom it may be left out, and offset or limit alone ask for its pages. The reply adds meshPage {geom, triangleCount, offset, triangles, nextOffset}: triangles holds up to limit rows (default 2000, at most 20000) from offset, each [ax, ay, az, bx, by, bz, cx, cy, cz] in world metres to the micron, wound outward, the body's and its parents' poses applied; nextOffset is where the next page starts, null on the last. This is how to read the surface of a body too big for physics_get_scene: a scanned or sculpted master of a few hundred thousand faces is past what the MCP link carries in one reply.

tools.physics_get_objects: Return all objects in the physics scene graph with large mesh arrays stripped (useful to get SCAD and scripts without massive payload).
tools.physics_get_scene: Return the full scene graph (bodies, joints, geoms, scripts), including raw mesh vertex/face arrays. Can be a very large payload for scad/mesh-heavy scenes. Prefer physics_get_scene_summary unless you actually need the raw arrays. The answer is the scene object { nodes, ...what the scene says about itself (simFidelity, referenceImages, castPrep, name), environment (gravityZ, wind, density, floor), noteCards }. Pass that whole object back to physics_update_scene to put the scene back exactly as it was. A reply over 30 MB, past what the MCP link carries, comes back as an error instead of dropping the connection; read such a scene with physics_get_objects, and a big mesh with physics_get_object's geom, offset and limit.

physics_get_scene_summary.summary:
Return a lightweight scene summary: per-node id/name/pos/quat/euler/joints, plus worldPos and worldPosSource ('simulation' or 'authored') wherever a body's world position differs from its pos (a nested body, whose pos is in its parent's frame, or one the simulation has moved), and per-geom type/size (plus `fromto` for a capsule or cylinder written end to end, whose size is then only its radius), or for mesh geoms vertCount/faceCount/bbox instead of the raw vertices/faces arrays. Lengths are rounded to the micron. Generated geoms are counted rather than listed: a curve track (isCurve) gives `curve` { segments, controlPoints, widthMm, thicknessMm } and an empty geoms list, and a decomposed body's convex pieces are `colliderGeoms` (a count) beside `collidesAs`. Use this for routine checks (did it compile, roughly what size/shape is it) instead of physics_get_scene.

Also reports per-mesh `watertight` (plus `boundaryEdges`, `nonManifoldEdges`, `windingInverted`, `weighedByHull`), per-body compiled `inertial` (`massKg`, `comMm`, `principalInertiaKgM2`, `stale`), `collidesAs` / `collisionPending` / `cavitiesFilled` / `openingsNarrowedMm`, fabrication `stock` fit, `hardwareList`, and `referenceImages`.

details.mesh_watertight_checks: EVERY MESH GEOM IS CHECKED AND THE RESULT IS IN THE REPLY. Alongside vertCount, faceCount and bbox, a mesh carries `watertight`, and when it is not: `boundaryEdges` (edges used by one triangle instead of two), `nonManifoldEdges`, `degenerateTriangles` and `windingInverted`. A closed, outward-wound mesh that passes through itself (a fold) carries `weighedByHull: true` and a note: MuJoCo could not integrate its real inertia, so it is weighed by its convex hull until the surface is fixed. A mesh that is not watertight draws perfectly and cannot be printed, cast or machined, so read it before you rely on the shape — this is the same guard physics_get_lattice and physics_get_sculpt have always given you, extended to meshes built by hand or imported.
details.fabrication_stock: For a FABRICATION scene (one with carve settings, print fidelity, or no hinge, slide or ball joint anywhere: parts on a bench rather than a mechanism) it also reports `stock`. Loose parts set up as an experiment are not fabrication: without carve settings or print fidelity, any body with shatterImpulseNs, a geom's dentYieldNs, a crumple joint, loadStrength, joinMaterial, a non-zero joint initialVelocity, a control script or an actuator leaves `stock` out, and so does a free body that starts in the air resting on nothing (a drop test). `stock` gives the bench stock (widthMm, depthMm, thicknessMm), the design's size (designMm) and whether it fits, with a note naming by how much it does not. Set the stock with physics_set_environment. designMm is the whole scene, which is what physics_export_machining cuts. With more than one top-level body, `stock.parts` also gives each one's sizeMm and whether it fits on its own (turned 90° if need be), and `partsNote` names any that do not.
details.inertial_and_collision_status:
EVERY BODY CARRIES `inertial`: what the solver actually uses, read back from the compiled model. massKg; comMm, the centre of mass in the body's own frame; principalInertiaKgM2, the inertia about the principal axes; principalAxesQuat, those axes in the body frame [w,x,y,z]. `totalMassKg` sums every body that can move; bodies fixed to the world (a wall, a bench) are left out and given as `fixedMassKg`. This is the figure after densities, hand-set masses and convex decomposition are all applied, so check it instead of running a drop test to infer the mass. These figures are from the model last compiled. When the scene has changed since then (an edit whose compile has not landed yet, or one that failed), the bodies it no longer describes carry `inertial.stale: true` and the reply has a top-level `modelStale` { bodies, compiling, note }: ask again once `compiling` is false, and if it stays stale read physics_get_state.lastCompileError.

A mesh body's `collidesAs` is 'convex hull', 'N convex pieces', or, while its convex decomposition is still running in the background, a 'pending: ...' string with `collisionPending: true`. Until it lands the body collides as its hull, so wait for it before testing anything that depends on the cavity. A boolean body still compiling has `csg.pending: true`.

When the scene holds reference pictures (physics_set_reference_image), `referenceImages` lists them: id, plane, center, size in mm, opacity and overlay.

tools.physics_get_schema: Return this app's reference doc, one section or subtopic at a time. Called bare it returns `overview`, `workflow`, `coreGotchas` (the must-know scene rules), `sections` (sizes in chars), and `subsections` (available dot-paths). Pass `section='<name>'` for a top-level section (`gotchas`, `nodeFields`, `geomFields`, `geomSizes`, `jointFields`, `openScadNotes`, `meshNotes`, `tips`, `examples`, `machining`, `sculpting`, `lattice`, `buoyancy`), or a dotted path like `section='gotchas.collision'`, `section='nodeFields.features'`, or `section='tools.physics_cut.hardware'` (pass `'<name>.all'` for a whole multi-part section, or `section='all'` for everything).
tools.physics_get_screenshot: Capture the current rendered frame of the Physics Sim's 3D viewport as a PNG image, exactly as a user would see it (camera angle, colors, lighting). Use this to visually verify a scene's layout, spacing, or shape instead of only inspecting the scene graph numerically. See physics_set_camera to frame a specific view first, and physics_get_camera to check what's currently framed. The frame is rendered on request, so a paused simulation or an idle viewport still gives the scene as it is now. Pass show_colliders: true to outline, for that one frame, what the physics actually collides — each convex piece a hollow body is broken into in its own colour, plus any collision-only or invisible proxy geoms — so a piece bridging a slot or a stale proxy shows at a glance. The viewport's Colliders button shows the same.
tools.physics_get_sculpt: Return a sculpt body's base (for any other mesh body, the name of the geom the brushes work on), whether it has been edited, and its mesh statistics: vertex and face counts, bounds and size in metres, and watertightness. Cheap. Call it between strokes to see the shape growing rather than pulling the whole scene graph, which carries every vertex.

physics_get_state.summary: Return full Physics Sim state: `sceneGraph` (meshes stripped unless `include_meshes: true`), `isPlaying`, `isLoaded`, `gravity`, `wind`, `density`, `lastCompileError`, and `worker` (live build/frame health, `realtimeFactor`, and `scriptProblems` listing compile/runtime errors in control scripts).

details.worker_and_script_diagnostics: Return full Physics Sim state: sceneGraph, isPlaying, isLoaded (true only when the physics worker holds a model built from the scene as it now stands), gravity, wind, density, lastCompileError (string | null: the most recent MJCF/MuJoCo compile failure message, or null if the last compile succeeded). `worker` says whether the simulation is really running this scene: sceneBuilt (the installed model was compiled from the current graph), staleBodies (bodies it does not describe: new, or changed since), compiling (a build is in flight), lastBuildAgoMs, lastFrameAgoMs and simTime (the last frame the worker sent), stalled (playing in a visible tab with no frame for 2 s: the worker is not stepping) and a note when something is wrong. simTime is the installed model's: a new scene (build_scene, a preset, Reset) starts it at 0 rather than leaving the previous scene's clock. CONTROL SCRIPTS: worker.scriptProblems lists what the live scripts got wrong since the run started (or the script changed): [{ body, message, firstAtTime, count }], one entry per body and message (a compile error; 'runtime error: ...' with count = the steps it failed on; an unknown body, joint or actuator name, with the names the model has; a force or control that is not a number); moreScriptProblems counts any beyond 20. worker.realtimeFactor (sim seconds per wall second over the last second of play; 1 is real time), worker.scriptMsPerStep (mean wall time all scripts took per physics step) and worker.slowestScript { body, msPerStep } say what play costs, and while playing below 0.8x the note says whether the scripts are the reason. The worker pushes these twice a second while playing, so they can lag by that much. Read it rather than trusting isPlaying after physics_play. The sceneGraph has its mesh vertex/face arrays stripped, as physics_get_objects does, so the reply stays small; pass include_meshes: true for the raw arrays (one carved part runs to megabytes).

physics_get_telemetry.summary: Return only the latest single frame of simulation telemetry (recorded every 10 physics steps): time, bodies: { id: { pos, vel, angvel, quat, xfrc_applied } } (pos: the body origin in the world, m; vel: the world-frame velocity of that same point, m/s; angvel: the body's angular velocity in the WORLD frame, rad/s; bodies and joints are read at the same instant, the end of the step), joints: { name: { body, pos, vel, qfrc_applied, ctrl?, actuatorForce?, clutchTorque? } } (shapes by joint type, actuator and clutch fields: see details), contacts: [{ geom1, geom2, dist, body1, body2 }] (body ids; 'world' for the floor and other world geoms), and aeroDiagnostics. Also scriptState: every scripted body's api.state now, by body id (absent when all are empty), and scriptLogs: the latest api.log lines [{ t, body, msg }], oldest first (up to 50; scriptLogsDropped counts older lines no longer held). A new scene, a preset load or Reset starts the history over: the reply is then the new scene's opening frame at t = 0, never the previous scene's last one. Lightweight alternative to physics_get_history.

details.joint_fields: Hinge/slide: numbers; free: pos [x,y,z,qw,qx,qy,qz], vel [vx,vy,vz,wx,wy,wz]; ball: pos [qw,qx,qy,qz], vel [wx,wy,wz]; angular rates of free/ball joints in the body frame. A hinge/slide with an actuator adds ctrl, its control value, and actuatorForce, the actuators' force on the joint in N or N*m (MuJoCo's qfrc_actuator); qfrc_applied shows only api.applyJointForce, never an actuator's effort; a torque-limited velocity motor, which drives its joint through a slip clutch from a hidden driver, reports the driver's ctrl and actuatorForce (the motor's effort) and adds clutchTorque, what the clutch puts on the joint: the effort while it holds, forceLimit while it slips.

tools.physics_import_stl: Import a binary or ASCII STL file into the 3D physics simulation. Parses sub-components to infer array spacing and customizer UI parameters (`importMode='scad_parametric'`), raw OpenSCAD polyhedron (`'scad_raw'`), raw 3D mesh (`'mesh'`), or primitive shape approximation (`'primitive'`). Pass path to import an STL file from disk (a Windows path works from WSL); stlData takes the file inline instead and only suits small files. For a big mesh (a sculpt or a scan, tens of thousands of triangles and up) use importMode='mesh': the OpenSCAD modes turn every triangle into script. A part over 200,000 triangles always comes in as a mesh, whatever importMode asked for (the reply's warnings say so): every triangle is drawn, measured and exported, and it collides as a simplified copy of about 50,000 triangles (colliderFaceCount), because the full mesh would take most of the physics engine's 2 GB memory and the first rebuild or physics_run_headless would run out. Import it dynamic (the default): a static one keeps its full mesh in the physics model.
tools.physics_lattice_bevel:
Cut the corners off a face, turning an n-gon into a 2n-gon. `amountMm` is how far back along each edge the cut goes.

Use it to make a round face: smoothing a four-cornered cage gives a rounded square, not a circle. Bevel a square into an octagon and smooth that; extrude the octagon first for a cylinder. Bevel again for sixteen corners if the part is big enough to show it. For most round faces physics_lattice_circle is simpler.

Only for a face whose corners belong to no other face, such as a lone plate before it is extruded. Its edges must run along an axis or at 45 degrees, and the cut must be under half of every edge.
tools.physics_lattice_bevel_edges:
Chamfer or round EDGES OF THE SOLID, stitching the faces back on either side. `edges` is a list of edges, each a pair of corners [[x,y,z],[x,y,z]] in millimetres, or three corners and up for a whole face's border, so "chamfer that rim" is one call. `radiusMm` is how far back the cut goes; `mode` is 'chamfer' (default) or 'fillet'; `loop: true` grows a single edge to its whole ring first; `mirror` cuts the reflection too.

Use this for edges of a solid, not physics_lattice_bevel. That one cuts the corners off a single FACE whose corners belong to nothing else. This one pulls BOTH faces back from the edge and stitches the gap.

Chamfer and fillet are the same cut and differ only under smoothing: a chamfer's strip is held sharp so it stays a flat chamfer; a fillet's is left soft so physics_lattice_smooth rounds it to an arc of about the radius you asked for. A fillet with smoothing at 0 looks like a chamfer.

Pass every edge you want cut in ONE call. A bevel has to see its neighbours to get the corner where two of them meet right, and calling it once per edge cuts the second from a shape the first already moved. Each edge needs exactly two faces on it, must run along an axis or at 45 degrees, and the cut must leave room on the edges either side (half of each where both ends are being cut). A radius that will not fit is refused and changes nothing.
tools.physics_lattice_bridge:
Join two faces with a band of quads, opening both. Both faces are named by their corners in millimetres, and both are consumed: they become the openings of what is now a tube.

On faces of two SEPARATE shapes it makes them one: a neck, a handle, a strut. On two faces of the SAME shape it bores a tunnel through it. With physics_lattice_inset first, this is how a hole through a part is made.

The faces must have the same number of corners and share none of them. Two whole opposite walls of a box share edges through the walls between them, so they are refused: inset each of them first and join the smaller faces.

Corners are paired by the rotation that puts them closest overall, so the band has no twist, and the result is wound consistently whether it joined two shapes or tunnelled through one.
tools.physics_lattice_circle:
Place a circle, or any regular polygon, as one face. `centre` is [x,y,z] in millimetres, `diameterMm` the diameter, `axis` the plane it lies in ('x'/'y'/'z', the plane's normal, default 'z'), `sides` 0 for a circle or 3/4/6/8… for a regular polygon, `mirror` to place the reflection too. Returns `corners` in millimetres. Pass those straight to physics_lattice_extrude for a cylinder, or physics_lattice_inset for a rim.

At the 0.1 mm grid a polygon rounded to it is within 0.05 mm of the true arc. With `sides: 0` the corner count is worked out from the radius against that budget, so a 2 mm hole stays light and a 60 mm disc is smooth, capped at 64.

What lands is an ORDINARY FACE. Extrude it, bridge two of them for a taper, dimension it, mirror it. Prefer this to drawing an octagon by hand with physics_lattice_faces or bevelling a square twice.
tools.physics_lattice_delete_faces:
Remove faces from a lattice body, named by their corners in millimetres, in any order (a face found reversed counts as the same face). Corners that no longer take part in any face stop being part of the shape.

Use it to open a solid up before bridging it, or to take off a face that was drawn inside-out (physics_lattice_faces can also re-draw that one the other way round). Reports how many were removed and which could not be found.

DO NOT EMPTY THE CAGE. Delete every face and the body has no vertices left, MuJoCo refuses the whole scene with 'at least 4 vertices required', and the body is dropped — while these tools go on reporting ok, because the cage edit itself succeeded. Clearing the starter box to revolve or draw something else is the usual way to hit it. Add the new geometry FIRST and delete the box afterwards; the body is then never empty for a moment.
tools.physics_lattice_dimension:
Set the size or the position of part of a lattice shape by saying the number, rather than by pushing it there. `corners` is the corners to measure, as [x, y, z] points in millimetres — a face's four, an edge's two, or any handful — exactly as physics_get_lattice reports them.

mode 'size' scales them about their own middle on that axis, so both ends move and the rest of the part stays where it is. mode 'position' moves them, measured at the middle of the selection — which for a face is the plane it lies in, so "put this face at 20" is one call.

This is how a part gets to be 40 mm across because the thing it bolts to is. Arriving at that by extruding 7 mm and then 3 mm more is arithmetic nobody should be doing in their head.

Every corner named must be a corner of this shape: a dimension applied to three of the four you meant does not fail, it quietly pulls the part out of square, so a name that matches nothing is refused. Values land on the grid like any other placement — ask for 6.35 on a 0.1 mm grid and the reply reads back 6.4. `changed: false` means the request meant nothing: a size on an axis the selection is flat along, or a number it is already at.
tools.physics_lattice_extrude:
Push one face of a lattice body out along its own axis, walling in the gap it leaves. A box becomes an L, a plate becomes a boss, in one call.

`face` is the face's corners in millimetres, in any order; take them from physics_get_lattice. distanceMm is rounded to whole grid steps and may be negative to push the face in. axis ('x', 'y' or 'z') overrides the direction; by default a face travels along whichever axis it faces.

The face itself is consumed: what was the outside becomes the new cap, and the reply gives the cap's corners so the next extrusion can be chained straight onto it. mirror extrudes the reflected face by the same amount.

A single quad extruded is still an open shell: the side it was pushed off is a hole. Cap it with physics_lattice_faces, wound the other way, or start from the box physics_create_lattice gives you, which is already closed.

physics_lattice_faces.summary: Draw faces on a lattice body: `faces` is a list of faces, each 3+ corners `[x,y,z]` in mm in the cage's frame (snapped to the 0.1 mm grid; prefer quads for clean Catmull-Clark smoothing). Corners must run counter-clockwise seen from outside the solid. Optional `mirror` ('x'|'y'|'z') adds reflected faces with reversed winding.

details.winding_and_auto_fusion:
Draw faces on a lattice body. `faces` is a list of faces, each a list of THREE OR MORE corners [x, y, z] in MILLIMETRES in the cage's frame. Use quads wherever possible: Catmull-Clark smoothing puts a dimple at every triangle corner — but an outline that is genuinely a polygon should be sent as one face rather than cut into quads, because a profile split into pieces extrudes into pieces with walls between them. A T is eight corners; an L is six.

Corners do not have to exist yet; a corner that lands where one already is reuses it, which joins the new face to the shape. Points are snapped to the 0.1 mm grid and `snappedBy` reports the largest correction made. A snap of half a step is rounding; a snap of five is a mistake in the numbers.

WINDING DECIDES WHICH WAY A FACE POINTS: corners counter-clockwise seen from outside the solid. A face wound the other way is invisible in the viewport and a hole in the exported file. Check the `normal` physics_get_lattice reports rather than assuming.

mirror ('x', 'y' or 'z') also adds each face's reflection through the body origin, with the winding reversed. Returns what was added, what was skipped and why, and the cage's new counts.

As in the editor, every lattice edit then fuses the cage where two faces lie flat against each other facing opposite ways (a leg's top under a seat), and unites closed pieces whose volumes overlap, so boxes drawn flush come out as one watertight solid weighed by its real volume rather than as touching boxes weighed by their hull. The same happens after `ops` on physics_create_lattice.

tools.physics_lattice_inset:
Shrink a face inside itself by `amountMm`, leaving a ring of quads around it. `face` is the face's corners in millimetres, in any order; the reply gives the corners of the new smaller face.

This is the start of every hole. Inset each wall first, then physics_lattice_bridge the two smaller faces to bore a tunnel. Inset and then delete the middle for a hole in a plate. Inset and then extrude for a raised panel or a recess.

Only a face lying flat on to an axis can be inset. The inset must also be less than half the face's width.
tools.physics_lattice_orient:
Turn every face of a lattice body to agree with its neighbours and point outwards, and report how many were turned.

A face's winding decides which side of it is solid. A face wound inwards draws wherever backfaces are shown and is lost wherever they are culled, so a part can look finished and export full of holes. Faces drawn by hand take their winding from the order their corners were given.

Every reply from a lattice tool carries `inconsistent`, the number of faces that are inward or at odds with their neighbours. When it is not zero, call this. It is safe to call when it is zero; it does nothing and says so.

Run it before physics_lattice_wall: a wall is offset along the surface's own normals, so on a shape whose normals disagree it is thickened in both directions at once.

Faces agree with their neighbours only across an edge exactly two faces share. Parts that merely touch along an edge (a back standing on a seat) are each turned outward by their own volume, so a part already wound outward is never turned in because of the part it touches.
tools.physics_lattice_revolve:
Sweep a profile about one of the body's axes, the way a lathe does. `profile` is two or more points [x,y,z] in millimetres in the order they run along the profile, `axis` is the spindle ('x'/'y'/'z', default 'z'), `degrees` is how far round (1 to 360, default 360), `closed: true` joins the last profile point back to the first (a solid ring rather than a shell), `throughMm` moves the axis line off the origin, `segments` overrides how many stops it takes.

Use it for anything turned: a boss, a spigot, a knob, a funnel, a wheel rim. physics_lattice_extrude makes prisms only.

The profile does not have to be drawn first: corners that are not there yet are created, so a whole turned part is one call. HOW FAR EACH POINT SITS FROM THE AXIS IS ITS RADIUS; there is no second number. A point sitting ON the axis becomes the pole, so a cone is a two-point profile: [[0,0,40],[30,0,0]] about 'z' is a 60 mm cone 40 mm tall. Less than 360 leaves both ends open.
tools.physics_lattice_sharpen:
Mark edges of a lattice body sharp, so smoothing rounds everything except them. Pass sharp:false to let them round off again.

Catmull-Clark rounds every edge it is given. Crease the edges that should stay crisp: the rim of a housing, the flat faces of a bracket, the top edge of a knob.

`edges` is a list of edges, each exactly two corners [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]] in millimetres. Take them from the `corners` physics_get_lattice reports; creases already set come back per face as `sharpEdges`. Only an edge some face runs along can be creased; a diagonal across a quad is not an edge.

A corner where three or more sharp edges meet is held in place entirely, so the corner of a box stays square while its faces round. mirror also marks the reflected edge.

loop:true grows each edge into the whole ring it belongs to: the rim of a shell, the top of a cylinder, the seam around a boss. Prefer it to listing a ring edge by edge. A loop runs on through four-way corners and stops where there is no straight on, so on a plain box (every corner three-way) it is just the edge given.

An entry of THREE OR MORE corners is read as a face, and marks that face's whole border. Use that for the rim of a cap: the corners around one are three-way, so no loop runs through them.
tools.physics_lattice_smooth:
Set how many Catmull-Clark passes a lattice body's mesh is built with: 0 (the cage itself, flat faces and hard edges), 1, or 2.

Use this to get curves from a grid: a coarse cage of a few dozen quads, smoothed, rather than a finer grid with thousands of corners.

The CAGE is unchanged and stays what you edit; what changes is the mesh built from it, which is what the physics, the STL and every CAM path see. Quads smooth cleanly and triangles do not, so a shape that will be smoothed should be built out of quads.
tools.physics_lattice_wall:
Give a lattice body a wall thickness in millimetres, turning the surface into a closed shell. Pass 0 to take it off again.

A lattice is a SURFACE. A slicer, a mold and a CAM job all need a closed solid, so a shape that reports watertight:false needs a wall or a cap before export.

The offset runs INWARDS, so a shape drawn as the outside of a part keeps the dimensions it was drawn with. The wall is built after smoothing, so it follows the rounded surface rather than the cage, and the rim where the two surfaces meet is held sharp.

The cage is untouched and goes on reporting itself as open; the mesh built from it is closed. A SHAPE THAT IS ALREADY CLOSED IGNORES THIS, and the box physics_create_lattice hands you is closed. So hollowing that box out means deleting a face first — the one the part opens on, usually the bottom — and then walling the open surface that leaves. Wall a closed box and nothing at all happens.
tools.physics_list_presets: Return available physics scene preset names.
tools.physics_load_preset: Load a physics scene preset. Preset names come from the app's PRESETS registry. Call physics_list_presets for the current list rather than relying on a hardcoded set. Also accepts 'user:<name>' to load a preset the user saved in the app.
tools.physics_machine_arm:
Deliberately CANNOT arm the machine. It exists to give a clear answer rather than leave you guessing why motion is refused.

Arming is a click in the app, by the person standing next to the machine: ARM. That is the one thing in this tool set an agent may not do for itself. If you need to move the machine and it is not armed, ask the user to click it — do not retry, and do not look for another route.

The permission lasts about an hour and covers jogging, zeroing, probing, framing and carving. They can end it at any moment with DISARM in the same banner, which also cancels whatever is running.
tools.physics_machine_cancel: Stop the job and drop the rest of the program. Never gated. The line it reached is kept, so it can still be picked up with physics_machine_resume_from_line. Soft-resets the controller, which leaves it in alarm if it was moving — unlock and re-home before cutting again.
tools.physics_machine_connect:
Open the link to the machine. `transport` is 'usb' or 'wifi'; WiFi also needs `deviceId`.

USB opens a native port-picker that only the person at the keyboard can answer, so it only works if they are sitting there. WiFi has no such prompt and is the transport to prefer — and on a carve it is the better one anyway: through a Tekno Box the device runs the program itself, so a four-hour job survives the laptop being shut.
tools.physics_machine_disarm: Give the permission back before it lapses, and stop anything running. Needs no arming itself. Worth calling when a carve has finished and nothing further is planned.
tools.physics_machine_disconnect: Close the machine link. Does not stop a job — cancel or e-stop first if one is running.
tools.physics_machine_estop:
Emergency stop: soft-reset the controller and stop the spindle, at once. Never gated and never refused.

Reach for this the moment something looks wrong — a cut in the wrong place, a sound that is not right, the user saying stop. Position is lost and the machine needs re-homing and re-zeroing, which is a small price. Do not deliberate about it.
tools.physics_machine_frame_job:
Trace the outline of the stock with nothing cutting. Needs the machine armed.

On a laser the guide beam is lit for this — `guidePower` sets how bright — so the operator can watch exactly where the outline falls on the material. That is the whole point: it answers 'is the stock where the job thinks it is, and is it big enough' in seconds, before anything cuts.

Do this after zeroing and before physics_carve_scene.
tools.physics_machine_goto_origin: Lift to a safe height, then travel to the work origin. `safeZMm` default 5. Needs the machine armed.
tools.physics_machine_home:
Run the homing cycle ($H) against the limit switches. Needs the machine armed. Only works where homing is enabled ($22=1).

Homing establishes machine coordinates; it does not set the work origin and does not make a stale Z datum trustworthy.
tools.physics_machine_jog:
Move the tool by a relative distance: x, y and z in mm, optional feedRate (default 1000). Positive Z is up. At least one axis required. Needs the machine armed.

A GRBL `$J=` jog, so it leaves modal state alone and can be cancelled mid-move. The reply carries the position after the move, read back from the controller rather than assumed.
tools.physics_machine_list_devices: List the Tekno Boxes paired to this account, with whether each is online. Pass one of these ids as physics_machine_connect's deviceId to cut over WiFi. Read-only.
tools.physics_machine_pause:
Feed hold: decelerate and stop without losing position or discarding the planner. Never gated.

The spindle is deliberately left running and the tool is left in the cut — a stationary bit in contact with the work is what burns wood and welds itself into acrylic. Resume with physics_machine_resume.
tools.physics_machine_preview_resume:
What a resume from a given line would do, without doing it. Read-only, never gated.

Returns the preamble it would send and whether the reconstructed state is uncertain. The depth in that preamble is the number worth checking against the workpiece in front of the operator before committing. A program that was streaming when the browser went away is restored from a checkpoint on the next load, so this and resume_from_line now work across a reload, a sleep or a power cut — not only within the session that started the job.
tools.physics_machine_probe_surface:
Probe a grid across the stock and return the heights, for levelling a carve against a bed or workpiece that is not flat. Optional `cols`/`rows` (default 3x3) and `bounds`. Needs the machine armed.

A 0.2mm dish across a 300mm bed is enough to cut through a 0.4mm veneer at one end and not scratch it at the other.
tools.physics_machine_resume: Pick a paused job back up. Needs the machine armed. A tool-change or material pause parks the machine, so resuming drives it back to the cut first; a feed hold only needs releasing.

physics_machine_resume_from_line.summary:
Restart a job that ended badly, part way through. Needs the machine armed. `fromLine` is the program line to pick up at.

Reconstructs modal state (units, coords, feed, spindle, Z depth) by replaying earlier lines without sending them, then sends a safe preamble. Always call `physics_machine_preview_resume` first and re-zero Z if the tool was changed or the controller power-cycled.

details.preamble_and_restored_jobs:
This is the tool that turns a dead three-hour carve into twenty lost minutes. Line eleven thousand of a program means nothing on its own — the units, coordinate system, feedrate, spindle speed and depth were all established thousands of lines earlier — so the program is replayed WITHOUT being sent to work out that state, and a short preamble puts the machine back into it: retract, spindle up to speed, move over the point it stopped at, then descend at a feedrate rather than a rapid.

Call physics_machine_preview_resume first and read out the depth it names. And note what this does NOT check: a resume after a snapped cutter is a resume onto a different tool, whose length makes the existing Z datum wrong in the direction of driving into the work. Re-zero Z first.

A job interrupted by the tab closing, the laptop sleeping or the power going off is also resumable: the program and the line it reached are checkpointed to this browser's storage as it streams (and to the account on PhysBox Pro, which is the only option for a program too big for localStorage). The app offers it back on load and on tab focus. That kind of resume is flagged `restored`, and it is the dangerous one: the controller has been through a power cycle, so it is not homed, its tool is unknown, and the work must still be clamped exactly where it was. Home, confirm the work origin and re-zero Z before resuming one.

tools.physics_machine_settings:
The controller's `$$` settings — max rates, accelerations, steps/mm, homing configuration — as read when the link opened. Read-only.

An empty result with a `note` means the controller never answered `$$`, which is NOT the same as a controller with no settings: the figures are unknown, so do not reason about travel limits or feed ceilings from their absence. This app's run-time estimates depend on these, and says when it is falling back to an assumed profile.
tools.physics_machine_status:
Report the machine: whether it is connected, its GRBL state, work and machine coordinates, live feed and spindle, the trim percentages, and how far through a job it is. Read-only and never gated.

`armed` is the field that decides what else you can do. False means every command that moves an axis will be refused until the person at the machine allows it; `armedUntil` is when that permission lapses on its own. Call this before anything else here.
tools.physics_machine_trim:
Trim a running job without stopping it: `feed` and `spindle` take a step of 10, 1, -1 or -10 (percent) or 'reset'; `rapid` takes 100, 50 or 25. Never gated.

What to reach for when a carve is chattering or a cut is scorching, where the alternative is aborting onto material that has been cut into and can no longer be registered.

STEPS, NOT TARGETS: GRBL has no command to set a figure, so 87 is rejected rather than silently ignored. Nudge and check with physics_machine_status.
tools.physics_machine_unlock:
Clear GRBL's alarm lockout ($X). Needs the machine armed.

Routine after a boot lockout. NOT routine after a limit trip or a reset mid-motion: the machine has lost its position and unlocking does not give it back. Home it before cutting.
tools.physics_machine_zero_all: Set X, Y and Z all at once where the tool is standing. Needs the machine armed. The quick setup when the tool is already parked at the corner of the stock at cutting height.
tools.physics_machine_zero_xy: Set the current XY position as the work origin. Needs the machine armed. Jog the tool over the corner of the stock first. Written with `G10 L20`, a real work offset that survives a reset.
tools.physics_machine_zero_z:
Set work Z0. Needs the machine armed. Two ways:
- `touchPlateMm` (default 12): probes down onto a conductive plate of that thickness and puts Z0 the plate's thickness below the contact point. Pass the real figure — a wrong one is a wrong datum, silently.
- `here: true`: records where the tool is standing right now as Z0, with an optional `offsetMm`. This is what to use when the operator has wound the tool down onto the stock by eye, which on a carve is common and perfectly legitimate.

Either way this is what clears the app's `needsZZero` flag. The flag is set the moment a connection opens and again at every tool change, because GRBL keeps the Z offset in EEPROM across sessions, tools and stock — a datum that reads back as valid may belong to a different setup entirely, and nothing in a status report says whether this operator has zeroed this Z since.

physics_measure.summary:
Measure a distance between two points, or the angle at a corner between three. `start` and `end` are points [x,y,z] in METRES in the world frame (the same frame physics_get_objects reports); `corner` turns it into an angle measured at that point; `withinMm` is how far it may snap (default 3); `snap: false` measures exactly the points given.

Snaps to box corners, cylinder axes/ends, mesh vertices, or hole/circle centres on the evaluated scene (`movedByMm` reports the snap distance).Or pass `body` (and optional `axis` 'x'|'y'|'z') instead of `start`/`end` to measure a body's tilt (`fromVerticalDeg`, `fromHorizontalDeg`, `headingDeg`).

details.snapping_and_drawn_scene:
Each end snaps to the nearest feature: a box's analytic corners, a cylinder's axis and end centres, a mesh vertex, or THE CENTRE OF ANY CIRCLE the neighbouring vertices lie on. That last one makes hole-centre-to-hole-centre measurable on a boolean result, where the document no longer holds the cylinder that cut the hole.

It measures the DRAWN scene, not the document: transforms applied, booleans evaluated, lattice cages smoothed, walled and recentred. Every reply says what each end landed on and how far it had to move (`movedByMm`). If `movedByMm` is large, you aimed at the wrong thing. Distances come back in millimetres and metres, with the per-axis parts in `deltaMm`.
details.orientation_mode: ORIENTATION: pass `body` (id or name) instead of start/end to ask which way a body points — "how far is the phone leaning". `axis` picks one of the body's own axes, 'x', 'y' or 'z' (default z). Returns fromVerticalDeg (angle between that axis and world up), fromHorizontalDeg, headingDeg (direction of its horizontal part, from +X towards +Y, null when vertical), axisWorld and quat. Read from the simulation's latest frame when it has run (source 'simulation', atTime), else from the body as authored (source 'authored'). physics_run_headless reports every body's final tilt in `final` without a separate call.

tools.physics_paint: Brush colour onto PART of a geom's surface, as dabs at points on it. Use it for markings: the pips of a die, a stripe down a roller, eyes on a head.
