Paint adds no geoms, no collisions and no mass. at is [x,y,z] or a list of them, in the GEOM'S OWN frame in metres (the same frame as the geom's pos/size, so a box of size [0.01,0.01,0.01] has its +Z face at z=0.01 and its corners at x,y=±0.01), and every point in one call is one stroke: the five pips of a die face are a single call. radius is the brush radius in metres (default 0.008). rgba is [r,g,b], each 0..1. flow is how much coverage one dab lays down, 0..1 (default 1, full strength; lower values tint, and dabs that overlap build up). Pass erase:true to take paint off instead. Paintable geom types are box, sphere, ellipsoid, cylinder, capsule and mesh; a mesh is painted on the vertices it already has, so a coarse mesh holds only coarse marks. Painted geoms are re-tessellated finely, which is visual only. Errors if no vertex falls within radius of any point; that means the point is not on the surface, usually because it was given in world space instead of the geom's frame.

physics_apply_pattern.summary:
Lay a surface pattern or TEXT — lettering in any Google font, wood grain, flutes, fish scales, kumiko, cracked earth and the rest of the Generators patterns — on ONE FACE of a part that already exists, the way the T key does in the app. The pattern is drawn and exported (STL, 3MF, relief carve, solid machining, slicing, the laser's engrave layer) but the PHYSICS SEES THE PLAIN SHAPE: it is surface detail, not geometry the simulation pays for.

`at` is a point on the face in the body's frame in mm and `normal` is the face normal (optional). The pattern floods out to the part's sharp edges (or seams from physics_knife). Key args: `pattern` ('text', 'image', or any generator id; pass an unknown id to list all), `depthMm` (default 1.5), `emboss` (default false = engrave), `borderMm`, `cellMm`, `color`, `options`, `remove`, `preview`.

details.face_flood_and_edit: `at` is a point on the face in the BODY's own frame in millimetres, as for physics_cut; `normal` is the way the face looks (optional — without it the nearest surface in any direction is taken). The face is grown from that point out to the part's sharp edges and covered whole: a box's whole top, a cylinder's whole side, a dish and over a rounded rim. A part with no edges at all (a sphere, a capsule, a sculpted blob) cannot be covered whole without tearing the pattern, so there it covers the side within 75° of the point and the reply says `capped: true`. `stopAtDeg` sets that limit on any face (180 is none); it is rarely needed. Calling it on a face that already has a pattern EDITS that pattern: only what you pass changes. `remove: true` takes it off. `preview: true` builds it and reports, without changing the scene — use it to see what face and size a point picks.
details.generators_and_layout: `pattern` is a pattern id; a wrong one is refused with the full list and each pattern's options. `options` are that pattern's own settings (sizes in mm, e.g. fluted {pitchMm, profile}, scales {scaleMm}). `depthMm` (default 1.5) is how deep it is engraved, or with `emboss: true` how far it stands proud. `borderMm` (default 2) leaves a plain rim round the face. `cellMm` (default 0.4) is the detail: smaller is crisper, slower and heavier. `twistDeg` turns it on the face; `scale` multiplies every feature's size. `color` ([r, g, b] each 0..1, or '#rrggbb') paints the part the pattern moves in a colour of its own: the letters of text, engraved or embossed, or the sunk ground of an engraving / the raised ground of an embossing; the untouched face keeps the body's colour. It is drawn in the viewport and written to the 3MF as paint, so a multi-filament slicer gets it as a second filament. 'none' takes it off; on an edit, leaving it out keeps it. The reply gives it back as hex. Every pattern also takes the layout options: layoutAlign ('fit' stretches the pitch to whole repeats edge to edge, 'centre', 'free'; on regular repeats only), frameMm with frameStyle ('plain', 'groove', 'raised', 'sunk') and frameGrooveMm, symmetry ('none', 'mirror_x', 'mirror_y', 'quarter', 'k3'..'k12' kaleidoscope), fadeMm and softenMm. Patterns include ornament (lotus_mandala, thai_tiles, rosette), board-fitted layouts (raised_panel, tiles, contour_rings, spiral), parquet/herringbone, weave, tartan, water_drop, ocean, landscape, cobblestone, honeycomb, greek_key, truchet and star_lattice.
details.text: TEXT: `pattern: 'text'` puts lettering on the face, in any Google font (shift+T in the app). Options: text (newlines for more lines), fontFamily (a Google Fonts family name, e.g. 'Roboto', 'Cinzel', 'Pacifico'; default Roboto), fontWeight ('300','400','500','700','900'; the nearest the family has), heightMm (capital-letter height, default 8), letterSpacingMm, lineSpacing (baseline to baseline in letter heights, default 1.6), align ('left','centre','right'). path is the line it runs along: 'straight' (default); 'arc' round a circle of arcRadiusMm centred on the face, arcSide 'top' (over the top, reading clockwise) or 'bottom' (under it, reading left to right, sharing the same ring -- one of each makes a seal); 'wave' with waveAmpMm and waveLengthMm; 'custom' along pathD, an SVG path in mm, y down as SVG draws it, placed by pathAlign ('start','centre','end'). pathOffsetMm slides it along its path. offsetXMm/offsetYMm move it from the middle of the face; boxMm draws a rectangle line round straight text, boxPadMm from it. On a cylinder the text is placed once, centred on `at`, not repeated round. Engrave (default) cuts the letters in; `emboss: true` raises them; depthMm is the depth or height. cellMm defaults to 0.25 for text. The font is fetched when the call is made; an unknown family is refused (ok:false). The reply's options leave out the saved letter outlines.
details.projection_and_reply:
`projection` is how a curved face is laid flat for the pattern: 'auto' (default) projects a flat face, unrolls a cylinder's side, and unwraps anything else so the pattern's cells stay square; 'planar', 'cylindrical' and 'unwrap' force one. A pattern taken all the way round a cylinder is resized slightly so it meets itself (`wrap.scaled` in the reply); one that does not repeat is blended across the join (`wrap.blended`). A tube that is not a cylinder is cut open on the far side from `at`, and the cut is left plain (`seam`).

The reply gives the face's size (`faceMm`), its area, the projection used, how much the layout stretches the pattern (`stretchPercent` — above 15 means it visibly distorts), the depth actually used (less than asked on a tight curve) and any warnings. ok:false with the reason when it cannot go on: the face is already patterned by an overlapping pattern, or the depth would fold the surface through itself.
details.image: IMAGE / HEIGHT MAP: pattern 'image' raises a picture from the face (emboss) or cuts it in (engrave), light parts high. Give the picture as image_path (a PNG or JPEG on disk, read by the MCP server), or options.image as a data URL or an http(s) URL. It is decoded once into a grey grid of at most 1024 px a side and the file is not kept. Options: mapping 'white-high' (default) or 'white-low'; fit 'stretch' (default: over the whole face), 'contain' (keep its shape, centred) or 'width' (widthMm wide), with offsetXMm/offsetYMm for the last two; blurPx 0-8 smooths pixel steps. Round a cylinder's whole side (pick the side with stopAtDeg 180) it goes once round, stretched to the circumference, the middle of the picture on the point picked: draw a height map as the cylinder's unrolled side, its left and right edges matching, and it closes on itself with no seam. cellMm defaults to 0.25; fine detail on a big face is limited by the triangle budget, and a warning says when the detail was coarsened.

physics_knife.summary: Divide a part with a flat plane at `at` (mm) and `normal` in the body's own frame. By default leaves a face seam (so `physics_apply_pattern` stops at the seam); `cut: true` slices right through into separate bodies; `remove: true` removes the seam nearest `at`.

details.seams:
Divide a part with a flat plane, the way the K key (Knife) does in the app: leave a SEAM on its faces, or with `cut: true` cut it right through into separate bodies.

`at` is a point the plane passes through and `normal` the direction square to it, both in the BODY's own frame (`at` in millimetres), as for physics_cut and physics_apply_pattern. By default the plane leaves a seam: the part stays one solid with the same physics, but every face the plane crosses (as far as that face's sharp edges) becomes two faces, and a pattern laid with physics_apply_pattern stops at the seam as it stops at a sharp edge. That is how to put two different patterns on one face, or a pattern on half of one: halve a sphere through its middle, then pattern each half. Seams are listed per geom as `faceSplits` in physics_get_object. The reply lists the geoms divided and how many faces each. `remove: true` takes off the seam passing nearest `at` (within 5 mm; `normal` is not needed).
details.cutting_into_bodies: `cut: true` cuts right through: every separate piece becomes its own body in place, keeping the part's colour, with its mass shared out by volume and exact convex colliders. The first piece keeps the part's id. Each piece keeps the patterns and seams of the faces it was cut from: a pattern the cut ran through is laid afresh on both pieces, each over its own part of the face. The reply lists the pieces with their ids, volumes and how many patterns and seams each kept. ok:false when the plane does not cut right through the part, or for a seam when it divides no face (it misses the part, or runs along an edge).

tools.physics_play: Start the physics simulation. Returns { ok, isPlaying, sceneBuilt }; when sceneBuilt is false the worker is not running the scene as it now stands (never built, a compile in flight, or the last compile failed) and `warning` says which. Call physics_get_state a moment later and read `worker` to confirm frames are arriving.
tools.physics_probe_sculpt:
Find where the surface is. Pass `at`: [x, y, z] or a list of them in the body's own frame, and get back, for each, the nearest point ON the surface, the outward normal there, and how far off the guess was. Nothing is changed.

Use it to get coordinates to sculpt and paint with. The bounding box from physics_get_sculpt locates only the extremities; the belly of a bird, the side of a head, the inside of a hand have to be probed for. Probe a handful of guesses in one call, then sculpt with the points it returns. physics_paint errors if no vertex falls within its radius, so probe before painting too.
tools.physics_reset: Reset the physics simulation to its initial state.

physics_run_headless.summary: Run the physics simulation headlessly for N ticks without affecting the live view. Waits up to 45 s for pending convex decompositions first. Pass `stride=N` (e.g. 10), `bodies=[...]` and `include=['bodies','joints']` (no contacts) to decimate the returned trajectory (~500 KB per 900 full ticks); `final` is judged every tick whatever the stride. Returns `trajectory`, `final` (`settled`, `moving`, `creeping`, `constraintsHeld`, per-body `posMm`/`tiltDeg`/`rocking`/`creepMmS`, worst constraint/limit errors), `shattered`, `dented`, `breaks`, `logs`, `scriptState`, `warnings`, and truncation diagnostics (`truncated`, `truncationReason`).

details.trajectory_and_shattering:
Run the physics simulation headlessly for N ticks. A body whose convex pieces are still being worked out (queued or running) would collide as its hull, so the run first waits up to 45 s for them, and if any are still pending says so plainly in warnings (and that the run does not show their real contact). Returns trajectory: [{time, bodies:{id:{pos,vel,angvel,quat,xfrc_applied}} (pos: the body origin in the world, m; vel: the world-frame velocity of that same point, m/s; angvel: the body's angular velocity in the WORLD frame, rad/s; bodies and joints are read at the same instant, the end of the step), joints: { name: { body, pos, vel, qfrc_applied, ctrl?, actuatorForce?, clutchTorque? } } (hinge/slide: numbers; free: pos [x,y,z,qw,qx,qy,qz], vel [vx,vy,vz,wx,wy,wz]; ball: pos [qw,qx,qy,qz], vel [wx,wy,wz]; angular rates of free/ball joints in the body frame. A hinge/slide with an actuator adds ctrl, its control value, and actuatorForce, the actuators' force on the joint in N or N*m (MuJoCo's qfrc_actuator); qfrc_applied shows only api.applyJointForce, never an actuator's effort; a torque-limited velocity motor, which drives its joint through a slip clutch from a hidden driver, reports the driver's ctrl and actuatorForce (the motor's effort) and adds clutchTorque, what the clutch puts on the joint: the effort while it holds, forceLimit while it slips), contacts: [{ geom1, geom2, dist, body1, body2 }] (body ids; 'world' for the floor and other world geoms), aeroDiagnostics:{name:{relSpeed,alpha,CL,CD,force,torque}}}], warnings:[string], and wallMs (the run's wall time). Does not affect the live view. SHATTERING AND DENTING ARE SIMULATED HEADLESS, as live: the run stops at the tick of every blow, judges it as the live run does, and a body hit past its shatterImpulseNs is cut into the same pieces (shatterPieces, shatterSeed) and rebuilt as them at that tick, carrying their velocities; the run goes on with time continuous. The shards are bodies of the trajectory from then on, with the ids the live run gives them (<name>_shard0, _shard1 ...), and asking for the broken body in `bodies` keeps its shards too. `shattered` lists each break: { id, name, time, impulseNs, shards: [ids] }. `dented` lists each surface marked: { body, geom, time, impulseNs, depthMm } or pierced: true for a hole. Dents are cosmetic here as they are live; a surface with deformCollision is the exception, since live its damage is rebuilt into the solver and headless it is not, and `warnings` names such bodies. None of it reaches the live scene or physics_get_breaks. Use this to verify scene behaviour programmatically (a projectile lands in the right place, a pendulum reaches the right angle, a body comes to rest at the expected position) before calling physics_play for visual presentation. PAYLOAD CONTROL: pass stride=N to keep only every Nth trajectory frame (plus the final frame) and bodies=[...] to include only those bodies per frame (with their joints, and only the contacts one of them is in) and in final.bodies. Each entry may be a body's name or its id; one that matches neither is named in `warnings`, with the scene's bodies, rather than silently matching nothing. The filter only trims what is returned: final.settled is always judged on every body and joint in the scene. A full per-tick all-body trajectory is ~500KB per 900 ticks and long runs can blow the response window without decimation. For most verification (final position, trajectory shape, lap progress) stride=10 loses nothing that matters, and `final` is judged on every tick whatever the stride. `include` (any of ['bodies','joints','contacts','aero'], default all, as physics_get_history's) leaves the other sections out of every frame; contacts are most of a frame on a scene of a few bodies, so include: ['bodies','joints'] lets a long run keep a fine stride.

A BODY STILL BEING BROKEN INTO CONVEX PIECES collides as its hull until they land, so the run first waits up to 30 s for them; if any are still not ready it runs anyway and its first warning names those bodies. Run again once physics_get_scene_summary no longer reports collisionPending.
details.truncation_and_divergence:
EVERY REPLY SAYS WHETHER IT FINISHED. `ticksRequested` is what you asked for, `ticksSimulated` is what actually ran, and `truncated` says whether the run stopped early; when it did, `truncationReason` is 'diverged', 'nan' or 'frame-cap' and `truncationDetail` explains it in words.

'diverged' is the one to expect. MuJoCo does not throw when a model goes unstable — it silently resets the state and the clock back to zero and keeps stepping. A run over a scene that blows up therefore used to come back as a full-length trajectory that was really several restarted runs stitched together, with times that climbed, jumped back and climbed again. Now the first tick that fails to advance the clock ends the run and says so. A blow-up on the VERY FIRST tick is caught too, though the clock cannot show it (MuJoCo's reset lands on one timestep, exactly where a good first step does): it comes back truncated with truncationReason 'diverged', ticksSimulated 0 and no frames, and truncationDetail names any joints whose initial velocities the reset zeroed - the run never started from the state the scene sets up. Live play stops the same way, with an error saying so. If you see it, the scene is unstable: look for very light bodies, stiff contacts, huge scripted forces, or a composite with too many segments.

A run can also blow up WITHOUT going non-finite: a body flung metres into the air or spun at hundreds of rad/s by a contact that went wrong. That run is not truncated, but it carries `unstable: {gainedJ, limitJ, tick, timeS, body, speedMS}` and a warning: the contacts and constraints put more energy into the scene than lifting every moving body a quarter of the scene's size. Contacts cannot add energy (motors, scripts and wind are not counted against it), so treat the trajectory from `timeS` on as the solver failing, not physics.

Kept frames are exactly `stride` ticks apart, always in ascending time order, with the final tick appended.
details.final_and_settled:
The reply also carries `final`: whether the run ended at rest and how each body ended. final.settled is true only when every body moved under 1 mm/s and turned under 0.5 °/s throughout the last half second, and no body was rocking (its tilt reversing twice in the last second by more than 0.2°) or creeping; it is false for a run shorter than half a second. CREEP: soft contacts let a body below its friction angle slide at a steady 0.2-0.8 mm/s, and a self-locked wedge back out at 0.25-0.5 mm/s indefinitely - under the 1 mm/s limit, but not at rest. A body that drifts steadily by more than 0.05 mm/s through the last half second is reported `creeping: true` with `creepMmS`, is not settled, and is listed in `final.creeping` as well as `final.moving`. Before calling a held or self-locking pose a failure, run it again at physics_set_environment fidelity:'print', which stiffens contact and cuts creep about tenfold; creep that stays is the mechanism's. Every hinge and slide joint must also have stayed under those speeds (rad/s for a hinge, m/s for a slide), and when the run did not settle `final.moving` lists the body ids and joint names still moving. final.bodies[id] gives `name` (when it differs from the id), posMm, tiltDeg (its own +Z against world up), turnedDeg (the total it turned through over the run, every step added up: a wheel that went round twice says 720), netTurnedDeg (the angle between where it started and where it ended), speedMmS, angSpeedDegS, peakSpeedMmS and peakAngSpeedDegS (the fastest over the run), settled, rocking and (when it is) creeping with creepMmS. `final` IS JUDGED ON EVERY TICK, NOT ON THE KEPT FRAMES, so stride changes nothing in it: read it rather than working turns or speeds out of a strided trajectory, which aliases (a fast spinner sampled every 500 ticks shows a fraction of its turn). Read it instead of scanning the trajectory: the first still-looking frame of something rocking is one end of a swing.

AN EMPTY SCENE is refused with ok: false and an error saying so: there is nothing to run, so nothing can be reported settled.
details.broken_constraints: BROKEN CONSTRAINTS ARE REPORTED. MuJoCo's pins, welds, couplings and joint stops are soft, and a linkage loaded past what they hold stretches instead of failing: a scissor lift whose loop-closing pins opened 23 mm folded through the floor and still came to rest. Every tick of the run measures each active equality's error, and `final.constraints` lists the worst per constraint, worst first (up to 20; `moreConstraints` counts the rest): name (connect_constraint_N, weld_constraint_N, explicit_coupling_N, gear_coupling_N ...), kind ('connect' | 'weld' | 'joint' | 'tendon'), bodies (body names, 'world' for the ground), joints for a coupling (kind 'tendon' for every coupling the compiler writes), worstMm/finalMm for a position error (a slide coupling's too), worstDeg/finalDeg for a weld's rotation or a hinge coupling, worstAtS, peakForce/finalForce (what it carried, largest over the run and at the end, from the solver's constraint force: a pin's or weld's force at its anchor in N, a coupling's in its first joint's units - N on a slide, N*m on a hinge - which on a rope or pulley coupling is the rope's tension; forceUnit says which; a weld's moment is not given), and broke: true for one that broke during the run. `final.limits` lists every limited hinge or slide that went more than 2 mm or 2° past its range: joint, body, range, unit, worstPast, worstAtS, final and finalPast. Anything over 1 mm or 1° (2 mm or 2° for a stop) is also a warning naming it. `final.constraintsHeld` is false when any did. final.settled says only that the run came to rest: a mechanism can be settled and broken, so read both. `breaks` lists every weld, member, join blob and crumple zone that gave way during the run, in order: { key, nodeId, targetId, kind ('weld' | 'crumple' | 'member' | 'joint'), cause?, time, forceN, torqueNm }, keyed as physics_get_breaks keys them. They are the run's own: the live scene is not broken by them, and physics_get_breaks does not list them.
details.control_scripts: CONTROL SCRIPTS. The run starts every script from an empty api.state and leaves the live scene's alone. Each mistake a script made is one warning, with when it started and how often: "Script on 'cart': runtime error: x is not defined (first at t=0.301 s, failed on 700 steps)"; an unknown body, joint or actuator name is a warning too, naming what the model has. `logs` is the api.log output [{ t, body, msg }], oldest first: the last 200 lines, with `logsDropped` counting earlier ones. `scriptState` is every scripted body's api.state at the end of the run, by body id. `scriptMsPerStep` is the mean wall time the scripts took per step; when they take most of the run and live play could not keep real time, a warning says so, with the live speed to expect.

tools.physics_save_preset: Save the current active physics scene graph and note cards as a custom user preset, the way the Save button does: in this browser and, when signed in, in the account too; a scene too big for the browser goes to the account alone. Waits for the account and returns `savedTo` ('browser', 'account' or 'browser and account'), `message`, and a `warning` when signed in but the account did not take it. A failure returns `error` with what to do about it.

physics_sculpt.summary: Brush the surface of a sculpt or any mesh body (primitives and boolean bodies are refused). `at` is [x,y,z] or a list of points in the body's own frame in metres. `brush`: 'draw' (push/carve along normal; supports `depthMm` cap and `hardness` 0..1), 'inflate', 'smooth', 'flatten', 'pinch', or 'grab' (requires `delta`). `invert` reverses the brush. `symmetry` ('x'|'y'|'z') is OFF unless passed (figure bases face +X, so left/right is 'y'). `radius` is in metres (default 1/6 of longest side), `strength` 0..1 (default 0.5), `dynamicTopology` default true.

details.surface_snapping_and_brushes:
Brush the surface of a sculpt body or of any other mesh body: an imported STL, a mesh loaded from a scene file, a compiled OpenSCAD part. On a body with several meshes it brushes the first one that is not the output of a boolean. A primitive and a boolean body are refused. A stroke on a big imported mesh (500k triangles) takes about half a second; pass dynamicTopology false on a mesh that is already dense enough. `at` is [x, y, z] or a list of them in the BODY'S OWN frame in metres (the same convention as physics_paint). Each point is one dab, and the whole call lands as a single stroke and a single undo step. Points do not need to be exactly on the surface: each is snapped to the nearest point on it, and the normal there sets the brush direction.

A point further from the surface than one brush radius is reported in `missed` rather than applied, and each miss carries `nearest`, the point that would have worked. Feed that back in. This matters on the animal and figure bases, where a coordinate guessed from the bounding box is often off the surface.

brush is one of: draw (push out along the normal; the general-purpose one), inflate (swell the whole area, for mass rather than a feature), smooth (average out lumps and brush marks), flatten (pull the area onto a plane, for a facet or a flat face), pinch (draw the surface together for a ridge, a crease or a sharp edge), grab (take hold and drag; the brush for gross shape, and the only one that needs `delta`, without which it does nothing).
details.symmetry_and_depth:
invert reverses the brush: draw carves in, inflate deflates, pinch spreads. symmetry mirrors every dab across a plane through the body's origin: pass 'y' for anything with a left and a right. THE FIGURE BASES ALL FACE +X, so their left and right lie along Y. Mirroring 'x' on a head reflects front to back. MIRRORING IS OFF UNLESS YOU PASS ONE: omit symmetry and each dab lands once. radius is in metres (default a sixth of the body's longest side), strength is 0..1 (default 0.5). dynamicTopology (default true) lets the brush add triangles as it goes, so detail is not limited by the base's resolution; turn it off once the shape is settled and you are only smoothing. detail is the target edge length as a fraction of the radius (default 0.25); smaller is finer and much more expensive.

AN EXACT DEPTH: depthMm (draw only) is the most one stroke raises or carves, measured from the surface where the stroke began. Keep dabbing and the surface stops there, a flat floor at that depth, so 'draw' with invert and depthMm 2.5 carves a 2.5 mm groove in one call instead of a bowl that deepens with every pass. A second stroke goes on from the new floor. hardness 0..1 (default 0) is the share of the radius that works at full strength before the edge falls away: 0 is a soft blend, 0.8 a flat-ended punch with a steep wall, for crisp eye sockets and slits. For a feature under about 2 mm, use a radius about half its width with hardness 0.7 or more.
details.replies_and_watertightness:
Returns the new vertex/face counts, whether the mesh is still watertight, how many dabs landed, and the misses. Check the count is growing as you expect: a stroke that reports applied:0 changed nothing at all. An inward stroke (draw or inflate with invert) stops short of the clay behind it and will not fold a pit's walls over, so repeating it deepens the pit less each time rather than pushing through. A `warning` in the reply (also in physics_get_sculpt) means the surface now passes through itself: it is still watertight, but it is weighed by its convex hull until fixed, so take the stroke back with physics_undo_sculpt.

`maxDisplacement` is how far the furthest vertex travelled, in metres, and it is NULL whenever `topologyChanged` is true — which is most strokes, because dynamicTopology is on by default and a brush that adds triangles renumbers the mesh, leaving nothing honest to measure against. Null means not measured, not nothing happened; read `applied`, `moved` and the vertex count for that.

physics_sculpt_cut.summary:
Cut a sculpt body, or any other mesh body physics_sculpt can brush, with scissors: a polygon swept straight through the whole body, taken out. A polygon in the middle of the body makes a hole through it; one that runs over the edge cuts that piece off. The body stays a sculpt, so you can go on brushing it, including the new cut faces. Prefer this to physics_cut on a sculpt: physics_cut turns it into a boolean, which ends sculpting.

`polygon` is three or more [x, y, z] points in the BODY'S OWN frame in metres, the same convention as physics_sculpt. It is projected onto a plane and swept along `direction` (default: the polygon's own normal) far enough to go right through the body both ways, so only its outline matters, not its depth. For example, a square of side 0.04 in the XY plane with direction [0, 0, 1] drills a square hole straight down through the top of a base.

details.modes_splitting_and_undo:
mode 'remove' (the default) takes the swept prism out; 'keep' keeps only what lies inside it and takes everything else away. cap (default true) closes the cut with new flat faces so the body stays a solid; cap false leaves the hole open, so the sculpt becomes a shell you can see into. An open shell will not print or machine, and reports watertight false.

A CUT THAT SPLITS THE CLAY MAKES ONE BODY PER PIECE. The largest piece stays on this body; each of the others becomes a new sculpt body at the same pose, listed in `bodies` (this body first), so any of them can be moved, brushed or removed with physics_delete_object on its own. A split cannot be taken back with physics_undo_sculpt (its history for the body is cleared); the editor's undo reverses it.

Returns facesBefore/facesAfter, `pieces`, `bodies` when it split, the usual sculpt summary (of this body) and undoDepth. A cut that does not split the clay is undone with physics_undo_sculpt, which shares its history with physics_sculpt. A cut that would remove all of the clay, or a polygon that encloses nothing, is refused with an error and changes nothing.

tools.physics_set_camera: Point the 3D viewport camera at an explicit pose: position and optional target, both MuJoCo world-space [x,y,z]. Or pass preset to reset to a built-in view (this also clears any prior explicit pose): 'perspective' (the diagonal 3/4 pose, not aligned to any world axis), or one of the orthographic drawing views — 'topDown' (looking down -Z, +Y up the screen), 'front' (looking along +Y from the -Y side, +Z up) and 'side' (the right-hand view, looking along -X, +Y to the right, +Z up). The drawing views are framed on the scene's content; an explicit position always goes back to perspective. dims=true|false switches the Dims overlay, alone or with a preset: in a drawing view it marks the selected body (or every body when none is selected) in mm — true sizes along each body's own axes (overall width and height, a chain between the face edges, hole centres and the steps of round parts, ⌀ on rounds seen side on), the diameter of every hole, sphere or rod seen end-on with equal holes counted ('2× ⌀8'), the angle of a turned part, and each body's origin from its parent's. physics_get_camera returns what it drew as `dimensions`. Use this rather than rotating a body to line a face up with a fixed camera.
tools.physics_set_color: Set a body's base colour. rgba is [r,g,b] or [r,g,b,a], each 0..1; alpha below 1 renders translucent. Omit geomName to colour every geom of the body, which is usually what you want after physics_import_stl: an imported mesh often arrives as several geoms. Colour is decorative only: it never reaches the physics, the MJCF or any exporter. For markings on part of a surface (pips, stripes, a logo, eyes on a face) use physics_paint instead of adding decorative geoms.

physics_set_environment.summary: Update physics environment and bench stock (all fields optional): `gravityZ` (default -9.81), `windX`/`windY`, `density` (kg/m3 fluid drag only — does not add buoyancy; see schema.buoyancy), `floorFriction`, `floorBounce` (0..1), `fidelity` ('standard'|'print'), and bench stock `stock_width_mm`, `stock_depth_mm`, `stock_thickness_mm`.

details.parameters_and_stock: Update physics environment. gravityZ is negative for downward gravity (e.g. -9.81). windX/windY add lateral fluid drag. density is the density of the surrounding fluid in kg/m3 and it adds DRAG, not buoyancy: MuJoCo's fluid model here pushes back against motion and lifts nothing. A balloon in a scene with density 1.2 still falls. To float something, apply the weight of the fluid it displaces yourself, from that body's script: `api.applyForce([0, 0, rho * volume * 9.81])`. See schema.buoyancy. floorFriction controls ground grip. floorBounce: 0=no bounce (default), 1=maximum bounce. Sets floor dampingRatio to (1-floorBounce), averaged with each contacting geom's own dampingRatio. fidelity is 'standard' (default) or 'print': print makes contact as stiff as the 1 ms timestep allows (resting penetration about 0.04 mm instead of millimetres) and brings Split for Print's exact pin and socket colliders to life, so dowels and pegs really go into their holes; use it for millimetre parts that have to fit together. It is saved with the scene and undoable. All fields optional. STOCK: stock_width_mm, stock_depth_mm and stock_thickness_mm set the board on the bench — the stock every carve and export uses and the design is checked against (the same numbers as the status bar). Describe the user's real board here rather than modelling it into the design; the reply and physics_get_scene_summary's `stock` then say whether the design fits it (designMm, fits, and a note such as 'The design is 5 mm wider than your stock.').

physics_set_note_cards.summary: Replace the note card overlays. Pass noteCards: [{ id, markdown, minimized, x, y }]. One card is the norm; id can be any unique string, minimized false, and x/y in the 20-40 range put it clear of the toolbar. Call this after every physics_build_scene or physics_update_scene, and again whenever an edit changes what the card claims. Pass an empty array to clear all cards. Format each card with `# Title`, a 1-2 sentence summary, `## Dimensions` (exact mm/kg), `## Physics`, and `## Try it`.

details.house_style:
The markdown should read like a museum label for THIS scene, in this shape:
- `# Title` naming the actual thing built ("Ball Bearing Race"), not its category.
- A sentence or two on what it is and what it does when you press Play.
- `## Dimensions`: the sizes that matter, in millimetres and kg, as a short list or table: overall extent of the assembly, the size and mass of each significant body, and any gap, radius, or spacing a reader would want the number for. Read them off the geoms you just wrote (geom `size` is a HALF-extent for box and ellipsoid, so a size of [0.1, 0.1, 0.1] is a 200 mm cube) rather than restating the prompt.
- `## Physics`: the mechanism: which joints, what constrains what, the equation or effect being demonstrated, and any figure worth quoting (period, gear ratio, equilibrium speed).
- `## Try it`: two or three specific things to change, naming the actual body or field to change and what will happen.

Write the numbers you built with; do not round them into vagueness ("about a metre wide") and do not describe the plumbing ("built via MCP", "MuJoCo convex hull"). The built-in presets' cards are the house style: physics_load_preset one and physics_get_note_cards to read it.

tools.physics_set_sculpt_base: Swap a sculpt body's base shape. DESTRUCTIVE: the mesh is replaced outright and any sculpting done on it is gone, so ask the user before calling it on a body they have worked on. Use it to start again, or to correct a base chosen wrongly at the outset. The new base comes out at the size the body already is.
tools.physics_resize_sculpt: Scale a sculpt body so its longest side is sizeMm millimetres (1 to 2000), or give sizeMm as [width, depth, height] to size each axis on its own (null keeps one as it is): [null, null, 58] squashes a ball into a pumpkin, the panel's Clay mm X/Y/Z. Everything scales together, sculpting included, about the body's origin, so a base sitting on z = 0 still does. Not destructive. Use it when the clay came out the wrong size; it is better to give physics_create_sculpt the right sizeMm at the start, since a brush radius chosen for one size is wrong for another. It clears physics_undo_sculpt's history for the body (its entries are at the old scale); the editor's undo reverses the resize.

physics_sculpt_carve.summary: Carve or add clay with a swept cutter along `path` (points in body-frame metres, snapped onto the surface), `widthMm` wide and `depthMm` deep. `profile`: 'round' (default), 'v', or 'flat'. `fill: true` pockets the area inside a closed path; `mode: 'add'` sweeps a round clay tube along `path`; optional `symmetry`, `taper` (0..0.5), `angleDeg`.

details.profiles_and_modes:
Carve the clay with a cutter dragged along a path: the panel's Carve tool (key 8). The cutter is swept along `path` (points in the body's own frame, metres, each snapped onto the surface; give enough points to follow a curve, as the stretch between two is straight) and subtracted, so the groove has the cutter's own clean walls and rim, exactly widthMm across and depthMm deep along the surface normal, whatever the clay's triangles are. Use it for anything that must be crisp or exact: a mouth, an eye socket, a rib valley, a lettered line. Brushes (physics_sculpt) are for soft form.

profile 'round' (default: a ball-nosed U), 'v' (a crease) or 'flat' (square walls, flat floor). fill: true treats the path as a closed outline and cuts out the whole area inside it to the depth, with a rounded edge: the cutter's centre runs on the outline, so the pocket reaches widthMm/2 beyond it. symmetry mirrors the path. taper (0 to 0.5) narrows and shallows the cutter to a point over that share of the path at each end: a rib valley that fades into the stem. angleDeg leans the cutter to one side of the path, for a slanted cut or an undercut.

mode 'add' joins clay on instead: a round tube widthMm across swept along the path, which may leave the surface. Start just inside the clay and run out into the air for a stem, a horn or a handle; with taper it thins to its tip. depthMm is not used.

Runs in a worker. Replies like physics_sculpt_cut: facesBefore/facesAfter, pieces, bodies when it split, and the sculpt summary. Undo with physics_undo_sculpt.

tools.physics_toggle_play: Toggle play/pause of the physics simulation.
tools.physics_undo_lattice:
Take the last lattice operation back off. The last 8 made through these tools are kept per body, newest first, and every reply carries `undoDepth` so you know how far back you can go.

Separate from the editor's own undo, so it never swallows a person's work. Use it for an extrusion that went the wrong way rather than building over it: an extrusion in the wrong direction leaves side walls inside the solid.
tools.physics_undo_sculpt:
Take the last stroke or cut back off. Use it for a stroke that landed wrong rather than correcting it with more strokes.

The last 8 strokes and cuts made through physics_sculpt and physics_sculpt_cut are kept, per body, newest first; every stroke's reply carries `undoDepth` so you know how far back you can go. This is separate from the editor's own undo, so it never swallows a person's work.
tools.physics_update_object: Update a single object by ID in the physics scene graph. The updates parameter is a partial object containing any fields from nodeFields (such as scad, pos, euler, script, joints, or geoms) to update and recompile on-the-fly. A field set to null is removed: on the body, or, inside a geoms entry (merged into the geom of that name), on that geom alone, e.g. geoms:[{name:'plank', friction:null}] puts the plank back on default friction (id, name and pos cannot be removed; a null there is ignored). A script that does not compile is still saved, and the reply carries scriptWarnings: ["Script on '<body>' does not compile: <error>. ..."]; runtime errors surface in physics_get_state.worker.scriptProblems and in physics_run_headless warnings. A target id in the update that resolves to nothing (a typo in coupleTargetId, pulleyWheelId, weldTargetId ...) is dropped and listed in referenceWarnings. A reply of 'Timeout waiting for ...' does not mean the command failed: it may still have run, or still be running. Check physics_get_scene_summary before retrying.
tools.physics_update_scene: Replace the full scene graph. sceneGraph is a bare array of SceneNode objects (same convention as physics_build_scene's bodies param), or the whole object physics_get_scene returns. A bare array replaces the bodies and keeps the scene's reference pictures and fidelity (not its cast prep or name), and clears the note cards. The object form restores everything it carries: fidelity, reference pictures, environment, cast prep, name and note cards. Full control but requires complete valid structure. Waits for any scad bodies to finish compiling and for MJCF to settle before responding. The response is { ok, error?, nodeCount, topLevelCount } (nodeCount is every body, nested children included; topLevelCount only the top level), so check `ok`/`error` directly rather than polling physics_get_state. Can take several seconds for scenes with multiple scad bodies. After the scene lands, write its note card with physics_set_note_cards; nothing else does. The default card says "Interactive 3D rigid-body physics scene". Replace it as part of building the scene. A script that does not compile is still saved, and the reply carries scriptWarnings: ["Script on '<body>' does not compile: <error>. ..."]; runtime errors surface in physics_get_state.worker.scriptProblems and in physics_run_headless warnings.
tools.physics_load_scene_file: Load a Mesh scene from a JSON file on this machine — the format Export JSON writes ({nodes, noteCards, copilotMessages}) — into the connected Mesh tab, replacing the current scene. The MCP server reads the file itself, so a scene of many megabytes (sculpted or carved meshes run to 10-20 MB) never passes through a tool call; prefer this to physics_update_scene for any scene you already have on disk. `path` is a path on the machine the MCP server runs on (absolute or ~-relative), in that OS's own form. Loads like the app's Import JSON: the whole graph as written (no default-filling), its note cards and chat, the sim stopped, and no preset selected, so Save will not overwrite one. Waits for the model to compile and returns {ok, error?, nodeCount (every body, nested ones included), topLevelCount, noteCardCount, file, megabytes}. Size limit: none from the session that owns the hub; about 32 MB when called from a secondary MCP session, whose commands are relayed through the hub (the tool refuses up front rather than lose the connection). The scene starts from rest at t = 0 with an empty telemetry history.
tools.physics_validate_scad:
Validate OpenSCAD code and return whether it compiles successfully. On success also returns vertCount, faceCount, and boundingBoxM (the compiled mesh's bounding box in meters) so you can sanity-check real-world size before loading it into a scene. If the compiled bounding box is implausibly large (diagonal >20m), the response includes a `warning` field flagging that you likely forgot to wrap the design in scale([0.001,0.001,0.001]). OpenSCAD designs are typically authored in millimeters, but MuJoCo units are meters, so an un-scaled millimeter design compiles ~1000x too large. On failure returns an error message.

COMPILES ARE FAST. The geometry engine is Manifold, so a plate with twenty-seven holes at $fn=32, or an M8 thread through 20 mm, evaluates in a fifth of a second; $fn=180 on a few dozen features is still a second or two. Nothing is rejected for being dense, and this call waits two minutes for it. Leave $fn at what the machines here can show — 32 is finer than anything they can cut.
tools.use_session: Send every later command for an app to one particular browser tab. port is the app's port (5175 for Mesh) and session_id comes from list_sessions. Selecting a tab that has gone away is refused, and the error lists the ids that do exist. The pin holds while its tab reloads: commands fail with an error saying so until it reconnects, and are never sent to another tab instead. An empty session_id unpins. The pin is shared by every agent using the hub; to drive one tab while others drive theirs, pass `session` on each command instead.

choosingTheRightTool.ruleOfThumb: Build detailed scenes in ONE call to physics_build_scene (or add parts with physics_add_object) using declarative body features instead of making 20 sequential tool calls or hand-writing raw triangle arrays.
choosingTheRightTool.mechanicalPartsWithHolesThreadsRounding: Use primitive geoms + declarative `cuts: [...]`, `roundEdges: [...]`, `patterns: [...]`, and `paint: [...]` directly on the body descriptor in physics_build_scene / physics_add_object / physics_update_object, OR boolean geoms (`csg: 'difference' | 'intersection'`).
choosingTheRightTool.extruded2DProfilesWithHoles: Use `type: 'extrude'` (or `'prism'`) with `polygon: [[x,y], ...]` (metres), optional `holes: [[[x,y], ...]]`, and `height` (metres) on a geom or body.
choosingTheRightTool.turnedOrAxisymmetricParts: Use `type: 'lathe'` (or `'revolve'`) with `profile: [[r,z], ...]` (metres) on a geom or body, OR a declarative lattice `{ lattice: { empty: true, subdiv: 1, ops: [{ op: 'revolve', profile: [[xMm,0,zMm], ...] }] } }`.
choosingTheRightTool.conesWedgesToriTubes: Use parametric geom types directly: `cone` (`size: [r, hh]`), `pyramid` (`size: [hx, hy, hh]`), `wedge` (`size: [hx, hy, hz]`), `torus` (`size: [R, r]`), `tube` / `pipe` (`size: [outerR, innerR, hh]`).
choosingTheRightTool.subdivisionAndGridPolyhedra: Use declarative `lattice: { sizeMm: 40, subdiv: 1, thicknessMm: 0, ops: [{ op: 'extrude' | 'inset' | 'bevel' | 'bevel_edges' | 'circle' | 'revolve' | 'bridge' | 'faces' | 'delete_faces' | 'sharpen' | 'dimension' | 'orient' | 'smooth' | 'wall', ... }] }` on the body, or pass `ops: [...]` to `physics_create_lattice`.
choosingTheRightTool.organicClayShapes: Use declarative `sculpt: { base: 'sphere' | 'head' | ..., strokes: [...], cuts: [...] }` on the body, or pass batch `strokes: [...]` to `physics_sculpt`.
choosingTheRightTool.curvedTracksAndRamps: Set `isCurve: true` and `curvePoints: [[x,y,z], ...]` (Z-up metres) on the body.
choosingTheRightTool.customPolyhedra: If you must supply raw triangles (`type: 'mesh'`), pass `verticesZUp: [x0,y0,z0, ...]` in standard MuJoCo Z-up metres (auto-converted to Y-up `vertices` and `renderVertices`, with inside-out closed meshes auto-flipped). Avoid hand-typing hundreds of coordinates when `extrude`, `lathe`, `lattice`, or `scad` can express the shape in 5 lines.

geomSizes.rule: Every size entry a shape reads must be a positive number in metres (a plane's may be 0, meaning infinite). A negative, zero, NaN or text entry is refused with an error naming the geom and the entry, and nothing is changed; it is never replaced with a default. A size left out entirely takes the default.
geomSizes.box: half-extents [hx, hy, hz]. Full dimensions are 2*hx × 2*hy × 2*hz
geomSizes.capsule: [radius, half-height]: a cylinder of half-height hh capped with hemispheres of radius r. Or use fromto to specify endpoints directly. ALWAYS supply both elements (or fromto): a 1-element [radius] does not error, it silently falls back to half-height = radius and collapses the geom into a tiny stub pill at its pos.
geomSizes.ellipsoid: semi-axes [rx, ry, rz]: a sphere stretched independently on each axis
geomSizes.plane: ignored. MuJoCo treats it as an infinite ground plane
geomSizes.cone: [radius, halfHeight] (or `radius` and `height` fields in metres) — closed outward-wound cone mesh
geomSizes.pyramid: [hx, hy, halfHeight] (or `width`, `depth`, `height` in metres) — 4-sided pyramid mesh
geomSizes.wedge: [hx, hy, hz] (or `width`, `depth`, `height` in metres) — right-triangular prism / ramp mesh
geomSizes.torus: [majorRadius, tubeRadius] (or `majorRadius`, `tubeRadius` in metres) — watertight torus ring in XY plane around Z axis. A ring wraps round its hole, so its solidity is well under the 0.92 cut-off at ordinary proportions (about 0.65 at majorRadius = 3 x tubeRadius): it collides as automatic convex pieces, not one hull, so things pass through the hole (physics_get_scene_summary: collidesAs). It is weighed by its true volume, not its hull's.
geomSizes.tube: [outerRadius, innerRadius, halfHeight] (or `outerRadius`, `innerRadius`, `height` in metres; alias `pipe` / `hollow_cylinder`) — hollow cylinder / pipe mesh
geomSizes.extrude: 2D polygon prism (alias `prism`): provide `polygon: [[x,y], ...]` in metres, optional `holes: [[[x,y], ...]]`, and `height` in metres (or `size: [halfHeight]`). Centered on Z by default (`centered: false` spans z=0..height).
geomSizes.lathe: revolved 2D profile around Z axis (alias `revolve`): provide `profile: [[r,z], ...]` in metres and optional `segments` (default 24).
geomSizes.mesh: arbitrary triangle mesh via `verticesZUp` (preferred, Z-up metres) or `vertices` (Three.js Y-up metres) + `faces`. Defaults to `dynamic: true` so body `pos`/`euler`/`quat` and geom `pos`/`euler`/`quat` always position the mesh in Z-up space.

jointTypes.free: 6-DOF unconstrained; body falls freely under gravity. Use for dropped objects.
jointTypes.hinge: 1-DOF rotation around axis. Specify axis:[x,y,z]; left out, it is the body's own Z (MuJoCo's default), and the build or update reply carries a warning naming the joint. Use for wheels, doors, pendulums. For a bearing, lid or arm that should hold its angle, set frictionloss (dry friction, N*m); damping alone only slows it.
jointTypes.slide: 1-DOF translation along axis. Specify axis:[x,y,z]; left out, it is the body's own Z, with a warning as for a hinge. Use for pistons, rails. For a slide that should hold its place, set frictionloss (dry friction, N).
jointTypes.ball: 3-DOF rotation (ball-and-socket). Use with stiffness+damping for springs, sway, or frictionloss for a joint that holds its pose.

geomFields.name: string: unique identifier (required)
geomFields.type: GeomType (required — includes parametric mesh shorthands cone, pyramid, wedge, torus, tube, extrude, lathe)
geomFields.pos: [x,y,z]: local offset from body origin in MuJoCo Z-up space. Works on all geoms including dynamic meshes.
geomFields.euler: [roll,pitch,yaw] degrees: local rotation, alternative to quat
geomFields.fromto: [x1,y1,z1, x2,y2,z2]: capsule/cylinder endpoints in local space, overrides size/pos/quat
geomFields.mass: number: override density-based mass for this geom
geomFields.density: number kg/m3: what the geom is made of. MuJoCo weighs a geom by its volume at a default density of 1000 (water), so a hollow or airy shape left at the default comes out absurdly heavy. Ignored when mass is set. Prefer it over mass for anything that may be rescaled, since it keeps weighing the right thing. Oak ~700, pine ~500, concrete ~2400, steel ~7800, acrylic ~1190, PLA ~1240; a tree crown, a hedge or any other mostly-air volume is single digits. DENSITY IS PER GEOM, so one body can mix materials: an acrylic ring with steel bolts is a ring geom at 1190 plus cylinder geoms at 7800 on the same body. A SCAD body compiles to ONE mesh geom with one density, so for a mixed part keep the SCAD for the main material and add the others as extra primitive geoms on that body (a bolt that should not collide can take contype 0 / conaffinity 0), or split the part into bodies welded together. physics_get_scene_summary's inertial.massKg shows the result.
geomFields.friction: [slide, spin, roll]: contact friction coefficients. slide: tangential sliding (0=icy, 2=rubbery; compiled as at least 0.001, since exactly 0 is unstable in MuJoCo). spin: torsional around contact normal (typical 0.005). roll: rolling resistance (typical 0.0001).
geomFields.contype: integer bitmask: collision group this geom belongs to
geomFields.conaffinity: integer bitmask: which groups this geom collides with
geomFields.solref: [timeconst_s, dampingRatio]: contact spring parameters. timeconst_s: spring time constant in seconds, must be >= 5x timestep (0.005s minimum). Lower = stiffer contact. dampingRatio: 1.0 = critically damped (no bounce), 0.0 = underdamped (max bounce), ~0.2 = lively bouncing. Contact between two geoms averages both dampingRatios: the built-in floor is 1.0 by default (1 - floorBounce), so a ball at 0.2 lands at 0.6 effective; set floorBounce 1 (floor 0.0) to get 0.1. Default (no solref set): [0.02, 1.0] = stiff, no bounce.
geomFields.solimp: [d0, d1, width, midpoint, power]: contact impedance. d0: min impedance (0.8-0.99), d1: max impedance (0.99-0.9999), width: transition width, midpoint: where transition is centered, power: curve shape. Higher d0/d1 = harder contact, less penetration. Typical bouncy: [0.99, 0.9999, 0.0001, 0.5, 2].
geomFields.verticesZUp: number[]: PREFERRED for custom meshes: flat [x0,y0,z0, ...] in standard MuJoCo Z-up metres. Automatically populates Three.js Y-up `vertices` and `renderVertices`, and auto-flips closed meshes if wound inside-out.
geomFields.vertices: number[]: mesh only: flat [x0,y0,z0,...] in Three.js Y-up space (X=right, Y=up, Z=toward camera). Optional if `verticesZUp` or `renderVertices` is supplied.
geomFields.faces: number[]: mesh only: flat triangle indices [i0,j0,k0,...] with outward-facing (CCW) winding. Closed meshes with uniformly negative signed volume are automatically flipped right-side out.
geomFields.polygon: number[][]: for `type: 'extrude'`: 2D `[x, y]` vertices in metres
geomFields.holes: number[][][]: for `type: 'extrude'`: optional array of 2D `[x, y]` hole loops in metres
geomFields.profile: number[][]: for `type: 'lathe'`: 2D `[r, z]` profile points in metres revolved around Z
geomFields.dynamic: boolean: defaults to `true` on all `type: 'mesh'` geoms written over MCP (custom and parametric) so body `pos`/`euler`/`quat` and local `geom.pos`/`euler`/`quat` always position the mesh in Z-up space, and the render follows the body. `false` (static) is opt-in, for scenery baked in world space; it changes only how the mesh is drawn, never whether it collides (see meshNotes.staticMesh).
geomFields.role: 'visual' | 'collision'. 'visual': drawn, never collides, weighs nothing when the body has another solid geom, and is left out of the automatic convex decomposition. 'collision': collides and has mass, never drawn. The way to give a body collision geometry you do not see (a box proxy under a rounded mesh), not alpha 0.
geomFields.renderVertices: number[]: dynamic mesh only: flat [x0,y0,z0,...] in raw MuJoCo Z-up space. Auto-derived from `verticesZUp` or `vertices` if omitted.
geomFields.margin: number: expand contact surface outward by this amount (meters). Useful to prevent sinking.
geomFields.gap: number: dead zone inside margin where no contact force is applied.
geomFields.paint: {res, idx, rgba}: brushed vertex colour laid down by physics_paint or declarative `paint` on the body.
geomFields.dentYieldNs: number — newton-seconds above which this MESH surface takes a permanent crater. Cosmetic: contact keeps using the undented shape. Transient.
geomFields.dentDepthPerNs: number — metres of depth per newton-second over the yield.
geomFields.dentMaxDepth: number — hard cap on how deep one spot can be pushed, in metres.
geomFields.pierceImpulseNs: number — N*s past which the surface is holed clean through instead of dented. Keep it well above dentYieldNs. Cosmetic: contact keeps using the whole surface.
geomFields.deformCollision: boolean — make damage to this surface real to the contact solver rather than only visible. Costs a model rebuild AND a convex decomposition per blow; off by default.
geomFields.csg: 'union' | 'difference' | 'intersection': this geom's part in its BODY'S boolean. Absent or 'union': solid, added in. 'difference': a cutter subtracted from the union of the body's solid geoms (a hole, slot or pocket); it is never drawn, never collides and weighs nothing, even before the boolean has compiled. 'intersection': only what it overlaps survives. A body with a difference or intersection geom becomes a boolean body (csgEnabled is set for you) and is compiled to one mesh through OpenSCAD in the background: physics_get_scene_summary shows csg.pending while it runs, and physics_get_object then reports csgVolume. The primitives stay the source of truth; edit them and the mesh is rebuilt. A boolean is within ONE body: to cut one body with another, physics_combine. How the result collides is the body's `collision` (schema.nodeFields).
geomFields.thread: { pitch: number, left?: boolean, fit?: number } — on any cylinder. On one marked 'difference' the hole is tapped; on any other the cylinder becomes a threaded rod (external ISO thread), which makes the body a boolean one. pitch and fit are in METRES (M6 coarse is 0.001). The cylinder's radius is the thread's MAJOR radius, so an M8 rod (radius 0.004, pitch 0.00125) screws into an M8 tapped hole as drawn. For holes, declarative cuts or physics_cut's threadPitchMm is easier.
geomFields.cutAt: number[3], body frame, metres: on a cutter made by physics_cut or declarative `cuts`, the point on the surface the cut is centred on. With cutNormal and cutDepth it records what the cut MEANS, so when the part changes shape under it (a face pushed out) the cutter is moved to keep it, instead of being left as a sealed void inside the part. A cutter placed by coordinates alone (no cutNormal) is left exactly where it is. You rarely write these by hand: use `cuts` / physics_cut. The geom's own pos/quat/size are still the shape the boolean subtracts.
geomFields.cutNormal: number[3]: the surface's OUTWARD direction at cutAt (any direction, not snapped to an axis). See cutAt.
geomFields.cutDepth: number, metres into the material from cutAt; 0 or absent cuts through. On a boss (a 'union' geom with a cutNormal) it is how far the boss stands OUT of the surface. See cutAt.
geomFields.cutInside: boolean: cutAt is a point INSIDE the part where the cut ends, and the cut runs from there out along cutNormal to the nearest surface, cutDepth past the point (the slot a nut slides into from the side). It stays with the nut when the part changes round it. See cutAt.
geomFields.maxHullVert: number, mesh geoms only: the most corners MuJoCo keeps when it hulls this mesh for collision (MJCF maxhullvert). Drawing still uses every vertex. Lower is cheaper contact between hulls and a coarser hull; shards set it. Leave it unset unless contact cost matters.

core.id: string: unique body identifier (defaults to the name). A body that reuses an id already taken earlier in the scene (depth first) is renamed id_2, id_3 ..., as clashing names are; physics_build_scene and physics_update_scene list any such renames in `renamedIds` and address that body by its new id from then on.
core.mass: number kg: the body's total mass. Shared over its solid geoms in proportion to what each would weigh on its own (stated mass, else volume x density), so the centre of mass stays where the shape puts it; a decomposed mesh body's convex pieces are scaled the same way. Visual geoms stay weightless. On a boolean body it is shared across its colliders, like collisionMass.
core.density: number kg/m3: density for every solid geom on the body that states neither mass nor density of its own. A body `mass` set as well wins over it for the total.
core.name: string: display name and MuJoCo XML name
core.type: always 'body' (or shorthand geom type when `geoms` is omitted)
core.pos: [x,y,z]: position relative to parent (or world for root)
core.euler: [roll,pitch,yaw] degrees: body orientation, alternative to quat
core.static: boolean: if true (or `fixed: true` / `dynamic: false`), omits the default free joint so a top-level body is fixed in world space
core.geoms: SceneGeom[]: one or more geoms defining shape (optional if body-level `type`/`size` shorthand, `lattice`, `sculpt`, `isCurve`, or `scad` is used)
core.joints: SceneJoint[]: joints to parent (empty = fixed to world)
core.scad: string: raw OpenSCAD source code to procedurally compile into a dynamic mesh geometry. In physics_update_object, null or "" removes the source and keeps the last compiled mesh (or the geoms sent in the same call) as a plain mesh.
core.script: string: JavaScript control script running at 1000 Hz (all calls require the 'api.' prefix, e.g. api.getTime(), api.setActuatorControl('<joint>_actuator', v); state persists on api.state). Full API reference in section='nodeFields.scripting'.

scripting.script: JavaScript control script running at 1000 Hz (once per physics step; api.getTimestep() gives the step in s). IMPORTANT: all functions must be called with the 'api.' prefix, e.g. api.getTime(), api.setVelocity([...], 'bodyName'). Bare calls like getTime() will throw ReferenceError. Available: api.isKeyPressed(keyName), api.getPosition(bodyName) (the body origin), api.getVelocity(bodyName) (the world-frame velocity of that same point, m/s), api.getAngularVelocity(bodyName) (world frame, rad/s), api.getOrientation(bodyName) (row-major 3x3 world rotation, 9 numbers), api.setPosition(pos, bodyName), api.setVelocity(vel, bodyName), api.setAngularVelocity(angvel, bodyName) (world frame on a free body, as getAngularVelocity reads it; a ball joint's is in its own frame), api.getMass(bodyName), api.getJointPosition(jointName), api.getJointVelocity(jointName), api.applyForce(forceVec, bodyName), api.applyTorque(torqueVec, bodyName), api.applyJointForce(jointName, forceVal), api.setActuatorControl(actuatorName, ctrlVal) and api.getActuatorControl(actuatorName) (actuatorName is '<jointName>_actuator'; ctrlVal is a velocity actuator's target speed, rad/s hinge or m/s slide, or a motor's torque/force — see schema.jointFields.actuator), api.getTime(), api.getTimestep(), api.getWind(), api.raycast(origin, dir, maxDist = 10, excludeBody) -> { dist, point, geom, body } | null (the first geom along dir from origin, world frame, m; skips the script's own body unless excludeBody names another, or null to skip nothing; fully transparent geoms are not hit; a line follower looks down: api.raycast(api.getPosition(), [0, 0, -1], 0.1)), api.getContacts(bodyName) -> [{ otherBody, otherGeom, geom, dist, force }] (what the body touches now; body ids, 'world' for the floor; force is the normal force in N), api.log(...args) (returned by physics_run_headless as logs and by physics_get_telemetry as scriptLogs). bodyName defaults to the script's own body. A body, joint or actuator name the model does not have, or a force or control that is not a finite number, does nothing and is reported once, naming what the model has, in physics_get_state.worker.scriptProblems and physics_run_headless warnings; it does not throw. Local variables reset every step: keep anything that must last between steps (an integral, a timer, a phase) on api.state, a per-body object that survives edits made mid-play and is cleared by Reset. Mutate it (api.state.integral = (api.state.integral || 0) + err * api.getTimestep()); assigning api.state itself is ignored. Keep it to plain values, arrays and objects — no functions. physics_get_telemetry returns it as scriptState, physics_run_headless as its final scriptState. To launch a body with an initial velocity on the first tick: 'if (api.getTime() === 0) { api.setVelocity([vx, vy, vz], "bodyName"); api.setAngularVelocity([wx, wy, wz], "bodyName"); }' (or set the joint's initialVelocity). To start a hinge or slide at an angle or offset: 'if (api.getTime() === 0) api.setPosition([theta], "bodyName")' (the body's first joint, rad or m).

features.cuts: DeclarativeCut[]: array of hole/slot/dish/hardware cut specs `{ shape?: 'cylinder'|'slot'|'dish'|'counterbore'|'nut_trap'|'nut_slot'|'insert'|'insert_boss'|'bearing', at?: [xMm,yMm,zMm], normal?: [nx,ny,nz], diameterMm?, widthMm?, lengthMm?, depthMm?, threadPitchMm?, size?: 'M3'|'M4'|..., bore?, fitMm? }` applied automatically when the body is built or updated
features.roundEdges: DeclarativeRound[] | DeclarativeRound: `{ edges?: 'all'|'top'|'bottom'|'vertical'|'inside'|number[], sizeMm: number, mode?: 'round'|'bevel' }` (or array of them; alias `roundings`) applied automatically after cuts
features.patterns: DeclarativePattern[]: array of surface textures `{ at: [xMm,yMm,zMm], normal?: [nx,ny,nz], pattern: string, depthMm?: number, emboss?: boolean, options?: {...} }` applied automatically to the body faces
features.paint: DeclarativePaint[]: array of paint strokes `{ at: [x,y,z] | [[x,y,z],...], rgba: [r,g,b,a?], radius?: number, flow?: number, geomName?: string }` (in metres) applied automatically after CSG
features.lattice: { sizeMm?: number, empty?: boolean, subdiv?: 0|1|2, thicknessMm?: number, ops?: LatticeOp[] }: builds a lattice body inline in a single pass. Each op in `ops` is `{ op: 'extrude'|'inset'|'bevel'|'bevel_edges'|'circle'|'revolve'|'bridge'|'faces'|'delete_faces'|'sharpen'|'dimension'|'orient'|'smooth'|'wall', ... }` in mm.
features.sculpt: { base?: 'sphere'|'cube'|'cylinder'|'humanoid'|'quadruped'|'bird'|'fish'|'hand'|'head', sizeMm?: number, strokes?: SculptStroke[], cuts?: SculptCut[] }: builds a sculpted clay body inline in a single pass. sizeMm is the longest side, applied before the strokes; without it the base is 240 mm across and a stroke with no radius uses 0.04. Strokes take depthMm and hardness as physics_sculpt does.
features.csgEnabled: boolean: evaluate this body's geoms as a boolean program (see geom `csg`). Set for you when a geom is marked 'difference' or 'intersection', a cylinder is threaded, or edges are rounded, so you rarely write it.
features.edgeRounds: array — rounded (fillet) and bevelled (chamfer) edges, each { mode: 'fillet'|'chamfer', size (m), edges }. Use declarative `roundEdges` on the body or `physics_round_edges` rather than authoring raw edge geometry by hand.

collision.collision: 'auto' | 'hull' | 'decompose' | 'primitives': how THIS BODY collides, mesh or boolean. MuJoCo collides every mesh as its CONVEX HULL, which fills in any cavity, so a cup, bowl, open-top box, funnel or housing would be solid to contact. 'auto' (the default) measures SOLIDITY, true volume over hull volume, and breaks the shape into convex pieces when it is below 0.92 (a cup is around 0.3, a box 1.0, which keeps its exact cheap hull). 'hull' forces the filled-in hull. 'decompose' forces the split even where auto declines (a very coarse or very dense mesh). 'primitives' is for a boolean body: the authored positive primitives collide and the boolean mesh is visual only (holes do not collide). Decomposition runs in the background and is cached against the mesh; until it lands the body collides as its hull (physics_get_scene_summary: collidesAs, collisionPending). A decomposed hollow body weighs its TRUE volume, often a third of its hull's; set mass or collisionMass for another figure. Not for primitive-only bodies, which collide as their primitives.
collision.collisionResolution: number: V-HACD voxels per chunk of this body's decomposition, clamped to 10,000..1,000,000. Each mesh is first cut into chunks while one is long and thin for its wall or its pieces fill a cavity. Default: enough for a wall two voxels thick, up to 25,000; the inspector's Collision Detail Fine is 50,000 and Finest 100,000. Raise it when a slot comes out solid (cavitiesFilled) or a fit jams (openingsNarrowedMm in physics_get_scene_summary). Costs decomposition time, not simulation time.
collision.collisionHulls: number: the most convex pieces this body's meshes may come out as in all, 1..512. Default: up to 512, or 64 for a body on a free joint. Usually leave it unset: a low cap fills cavities back in.
collision.collisionMass: number, kg: the body's total mass, shared by volume across what it collides as: a mesh body's decomposed convex pieces, and a boolean body's colliders (or its positive primitives in 'primitives' mode, or its mesh as a hull). On a boolean body a body-level `mass` does the same; collisionMass wins when both are set.
collision.csgCollision: DEPRECATED: use `collision`. Still read for older scenes ('auto' | 'decompose' | 'primitives' | 'hull'); `collision` wins when both are set.
collision.csgSectors: number: how many angular sectors a boolean body with a hole axis is split into for collision (default 16). More hugs the bore more closely, with more geoms.
collision.csgHoleAxis: 'auto' | 'x' | 'y' | 'z': the axis a boolean body's hole runs along, for that sector split. 'auto' takes it from the largest cutter.
collision.csgMass: number, kg: DEPRECATED alias of collisionMass on a boolean body, still read so older scenes keep their weight. collisionMass, or a body-level mass, wins when set.
collision.csgFn: number: OpenSCAD $fn (facets round a circle) for the boolean's generated primitives (default 32).
collision.managedCollisionFields: Read-only, written by the app and reported by physics_get_object; never send them: csgHash, csgScad, csgVolume, csgHullVolume, csgCentroid, csgWarning, csgError, collisionHash, collisionDecomposed, collisionSolidity, collisionCavities, collisionIntrusion, collisionWarning, collisionError. Geoms the app generates carry csgDerived ('visual' or 'collider') and colliderOf; they are replaced wholesale on every rebuild, so do not edit them, edit the geoms they come from.

couplings_and_welds.coupleTargetId: id of the body whose first hinge or slide joint this body's first hinge or slide joint is coupled to, as gear teeth or a leadscrew thread couple them: this joint = coupleRatio x that joint. Both bodies need one: a body built with no joints gets a free joint, which cannot be coupled, so the coupling is left out and the build reply's couplingWarnings (and run_headless's warnings) name it. Held rigid (a fixed tendon held at zero length, at MuJoCo's stiffest impedance), so a load deflects it by milliradians and it springs back rather than slipping.
couplings_and_welds.isPulleyRope: boolean: this body is a rope, not a part (no geoms, no joints). A PULLEY ROPE is a body with isPulleyRope: true, no geoms and no joints, naming leftTargetId and rightTargetId (the bodies at its ends, each with a slide joint along the rope) and optionally pulleyWheelId (a body with isPulleyWheel: true, a hinge on its axle and pulleyRadius in metres; else its largest cylinder's radius). It is always taut and held rigid, like gear teeth: each end moved toward the wheel by d takes up strands x d of rope, so leftStrands*dLeft + rightStrands*dRight = 0, and the wheel's rim turns with the rope. leftStrands/rightStrands (default 1) are the strands holding that end: a load hung in a movable pulley is rightStrands: 2 (mechanical advantage 2), a four-fall block and tackle rightStrands: 4. Which way each slide runs toward the wheel, and which way the wheel turns, come from where the bodies are, so either end may be on either side. The rope is drawn from each end's face toward the wheel, over the rim, with an end's further strands drawn up to the wheel's level. An end with no slide, or a wheel with no hinge, is named in couplingWarnings and not coupled.
couplings_and_welds.leftTargetId: a pulley rope's one end: id of a body with a slide joint along the rope.
couplings_and_welds.rightTargetId: a pulley rope's other end: id of a body with a slide joint along the rope.
couplings_and_welds.leftStrands: number, default 1: the rope strands holding the left end (its mechanical advantage). 2 for a load in a movable pulley, 4 for a four-fall block and tackle.
couplings_and_welds.rightStrands: number, default 1: as leftStrands, for the right end.
couplings_and_welds.pulleyWheelId: a pulley rope's wheel: id of a body with isPulleyWheel and a hinge, which turns as the rope runs over it. Optional: without one the ends are coupled directly.
couplings_and_welds.isPulleyWheel: boolean: this hinged body is a wheel a rope can run over (pulleyWheelId).
couplings_and_welds.pulleyRadius: number, metres: a pulley wheel's radius where the rope runs, which sets how fast it turns.
couplings_and_welds.isRack: boolean: this slide body is a rack, coupled to a hinged wheel that meshes with it (see gotchas: GEARS ARE COUPLED BY PROXIMITY). Only a marked body is a rack, whatever its id says.
couplings_and_welds.allowCoupling: boolean, default true. false keeps this body out of the automatic gear and rack coupling (see gotchas: GEARS ARE COUPLED BY PROXIMITY), so it is coupled only where you say with coupleTargetId, or turns by contact alone.
couplings_and_welds.weldTargetId: id of body to rigidly weld (closed-loop constraint)
couplings_and_welds.weldBreakForceN: number — newtons of pull this weld survives before it shears off. Omit and it never breaks. Transient: reset puts it back.
couplings_and_welds.weldBreakTorqueNm: number — newton-metres of twist this weld survives. Either limit alone is enough.
couplings_and_welds.weldBreakHoldSteps: number — consecutive overloaded steps required (default 3), guarding against contact-onset solver spikes.
couplings_and_welds.connectTargetId: id of the body for a ball-socket point constraint (a pin closing a loop: a four-bar's coupler to its rocker, a scissor arm's foot to its slider). Held rigid, however light the links: a gap of microns, not millimetres. A velocity servo much stiffer than the link it drives (kv*0.001 above the joint's inertia) on a pinned or welded body, or on a coupled joint (a gear, a rack, a rope), is driven through a clutch that never slips, so the solver sees it and the loop does not tear or whip the parts coupled to it. A coupling that still opens beside such a servo is reported with its kv*timestep/inertia, not blamed on the load.

curves_and_composites.isComposite: boolean: if true, this body is emitted as a MuJoCo <composite> (a chain of auto-generated, auto-jointed segments forming a smooth curve/cable/rope) instead of using this node's own geoms/joints/children directly. Use this instead of chaining many capsule geoms with fromto to approximate a curve. See compositeType/compositeCount/compositeSize/compositeCurve.
curves_and_composites.compositeType: 'cable'|'grid'|'rope'|'cloth': shape of the composite. 'rope' is remapped to MuJoCo's 'cable' composite type internally; for a smooth 1D curve (rope, cable, mustache, tentacle, vine) use 'cable' or 'rope'. Default 'cable'.
curves_and_composites.compositeCount: string (NOT an array): space-separated segment counts, e.g. "25 1 1" for a 25-segment 1D cable. More segments = smoother curve but more DOF. Default "15 1 1".
curves_and_composites.compositeSize: string (NOT a number): total extent of the composite before curving, e.g. "1.5" for a 1.5m cable. Default "1.5". The segments take MuJoCo's DEFAULT DENSITY of 1000 kg/m3, and nothing here overrides it, so the radius is the only thing setting the mass: a 0.9 m cable at radius 0.003 weighs about 26 g, which is four times a helium balloon and will simply hold it down. For anything meant to read as string or thread, radius 0.0004 or so.
curves_and_composites.compositeCurve: string: MuJoCo composite curve-shape spec (space-separated per-axis codes+params), e.g. "s 0 0" for straight, or a cosine/other MuJoCo composite curve code for a pre-curled shape. Not validated client-side; a malformed string only surfaces as a MuJoCo XML compile error. The chain is laid out along the BODY'S +X before any curve is applied, so a cable meant to hang or stand needs the body turned: euler [0, -90, 0] points it up +Z.
curves_and_composites.compositePrefix: string: name prefix for the auto-generated segment bodies (default `${name}_`). The last segment's auto-generated name is `${compositePrefix}B_last`, needed if you want to weldLastToId it to something.
curves_and_composites.weldLastToId: string: id of another body to rigidly weld the composite's LAST segment to (e.g. anchoring both ends of a rope/cable). Only used when isComposite is true. Compare to the general weldTargetId, which welds this node's own body, not a composite's generated last segment.
curves_and_composites.isCurve: boolean: RIGID curved track. A Catmull-Rom spline through curvePoints is decomposed into many small convex box geoms, so collision follows the real (even concave) curve and balls roll along it. Omit geoms and joints: geoms are auto-generated and the body defaults to static (welded to world). Contrast with isComposite, which makes a floppy rope/cable.
curves_and_composites.curvePoints: number[][]: body-local Z-up control points, e.g. [[-1.6,0,1.4],[-0.55,0,0.45],[0.45,0,0.12],[1.6,0,0.7]]. The spline IS the rolling surface (segment boxes sit half a thickness below it).
curves_and_composites.curveSegments: number: how many box segments approximate the spline (default 28; more = smoother)
curves_and_composites.curveClosed: boolean: wrap the spline into a seamless closed loop (oval/circuit tracks). Default false.
curves_and_composites.curveBank: number: bank (roll) angle in degrees about the travel direction; positive raises the left-of-travel edge. For a counter-clockwise loop use a NEGATIVE bank to raise the outside edge (the oval_track preset uses -18).

breakage_and_sculpt_state.shatterImpulseNs: number — newton-seconds of impulse that breaks this body into pieces. Omit and it never shatters. Transient: reset makes it whole.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.loadStrength: object | material id | true | false — what it takes to break this body by LOADING it (bending, pulling, pushing end-on) rather than hitting it. A material id ('pasta', 'hardwood', 'glass', 'steel', ... — the Deformation materials) takes that material's strength; true takes the body's own deformMaterial's (hardwood if none); or give { flexuralMPa, tensileMPa, modulusGPa, ductile? }. Only a free, long, thin body (one solid cylinder, capsule or box at least 8x as long as it is thick) uses it: the compiler builds it as two halves welded at the middle, which snap there (brittle) or bend for good (ductile: metals, plastic) at the moment, pull and buckling load its cross-section carries. Where it enters a join blob, a brittle one can also snap at the joint. Transient: reset makes it whole. false clears it.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.joinMaterial: 'putty' | 'marshmallow' | 'hotGlue' | 'pva' | 'epoxy' — makes this body (one sphere or ellipsoid geom) a JOINT: at compile time every other part that reaches into it is stuck to it. A rod or bar is held by its end inside the blob; anything else must be pressed in by a tenth of the blob's radius (resting on it is not enough). Strength scales with how much is buried, so a bigger blob holds more. Putty and marshmallow hold what is in them on a PIN (it turns freely; triangulated frames stand, square ones fold) until it is pulled out or pushed out sideways; glue, PVA and epoxy hold it rigid until it lets go. A putty blob moves but never rotates. Nothing is welded in the scene graph: it all happens in the compiled model.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.shatterPattern: 'uniform' | 'radial' — radial crowds the small pieces around the point of impact (default).
breakage_and_sculpt_state.shatterSpread: number — extra outward speed per piece, m/s.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.shatterSeed: number — fixes which pieces, so a scene breaks the same way twice.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.shatterDepth: number — how many times the PIECES may break again when they land (0 default, 2 max). Later generations split into at most four chips that do not collide with each other, and the world holds at most 60 shards.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.isSculpt: boolean: a free-form sculpted body. Its mesh is not derived from parameters; the sculpt tools own it. Set by physics_create_sculpt or declarative `sculpt` on the body.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.sculptBase: string: which base shape it was started from. See schema.sculpting.bases.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.sculptVersion: number: bumped whenever the mesh is replaced wholesale, so the viewport reloads it. Managed for you.
breakage_and_sculpt_state.sculptEdited: boolean: whether any stroke has been applied since the base was set.
